story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Started It All
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through the history of LEGO

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo sat on the floor, snapping bricks together. He was building a LEGO shark. Juno sat next to him, building a LEGO dinosaur. It was way, way past bedtime.

One little brick on the rug began to glow. It glowed bright green, like a firefly caught in a jar.

"Whoa," whispered Milo. "Did you see that?"

A tiny LEGO person popped right up out of the brick. He had a big smile and a hat shaped like a brick. "Hello!" he said. "I'm Click. Want to see where LEGO began?"

Juno grabbed Milo's hand. Milo grabbed the glowing brick tight.

"A carpenter — that means someone who builds things out of wood — named **Ole Kirk Christiansen** started it all," said Click. "In **1932**, in a little town called **Billund, Denmark**, he began making wooden toys."

"Toys, not bricks?" asked Milo.

"Not yet," said Click, winking. "Hold on tight."

Milo squeezed the brick. WHOOOOSH! The bedroom spun into swirls of green light.

When it stopped spinning, they stood in a dusty old workshop. Wood shavings covered the floor like snow. A kind man with a bushy mustache looked up from his workbench and waved hello.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Name Game
chapters.text:
The kind man was Ole Kirk himself. He held up a wooden duck on wheels, its paint still shiny.

"What do you call your toys?" asked Milo.

"Good question," said Click. "In **1934**, Ole Kirk picked a name for his company. He took two Danish words, *leg godt*, and squished them together."

"What does that mean?" asked Juno.

"Guess!" said Click.

Juno thought hard. She loved playing more than almost anything. "Play... good?"

"Close!" said Click, laughing. "It means **'play well.'** That's why his company is called **LEGO**."

Milo grinned. "Play well. I like that a lot."

"Here's a funny bit," said Click. "Long, long ago, people who spoke Latin used a word that sounded just like 'lego' too. It meant 'I put together.' That's probably just a happy accident, not the real reason for the name. But it's a fun one to remember!"

Juno shouted it first, as loud as she could. "PLAY WELL!"

Milo shouted it right back. "PLAY WELL!"

Ole Kirk laughed so hard his mustache wiggled, and he shouted it too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Plastic Splash
chapters.text:
Years rolled by in a blink of green light. Click led them into a busy factory, a place where lots of things get made.

SPLOOSH! Hot, gooey plastic squirted into a big metal mold.

"In **1947**," said Click, "LEGO got a brand-new machine. It squeezes melted plastic into shapes, kind of like pouring Jell-O into a mold."

Milo watched the machine squirt again. SPLOOSH!

"What shape is it making?" asked Milo.

"Guess!" said Click.

Milo looked at the little bumps forming on top. "A brick?"

"A brick!" said Click. "You guessed exactly right."

Juno sniffed the warm, plasticky air. "It smells like hot crayons."

Everyone laughed, even the workers in their striped aprons.

A little plastic brick popped out of the machine, still warm from the mold. Milo held it up to the light. It was shiny and red, nothing at all like the old wooden toys they had just seen.

"This is where the clicking starts," said Click, "even if it doesn't click quite yet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Hollow Brick
chapters.text:
Click led them to a shelf stacked tall with plastic bricks.

"In **1949**," said Click, "LEGO made new bricks called Automatic Binding Bricks. They had little bumps on top, and they were hollow underneath, like a tiny upside-down cup."

Milo stacked three bricks on top of each other, slow and careful.

He gave the little tower a tap.

WOBBLE, WOBBLE... CRASH! The bricks tumbled right down onto the floor.

Juno giggled and clapped. "They don't stay together!"

Milo picked up a brick and peeked underneath it. Just an empty hollow space, nothing to grab onto.

"They need something inside," said Milo, tapping his chin, "to hold onto the bumps below."

Click's eyes twinkled like tiny green lights. "Now you're thinking exactly like a LEGO inventor."

Juno stacked the fallen bricks right back up, giggling the whole time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Tubes Inside
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The green light swirled again. They landed beside a man bent over a drawing desk.

"This is **Godtfred Kirk Christiansen**," said Click. "Ole Kirk's son."

Milo peeked at the drawing. Little round tubes sat drawn inside the bottom of a brick.

"That's just what I said!" cried Milo. "Something inside, to hold the bumps!"

Godtfred looked up and smiled right at him. "In **1958**, I made this new brick official, so everyone would know it was mine."

Juno grabbed two bricks off the desk and lined them up carefully.

She pressed them together.

CLICK!

She pulled hard. They held tight, tighter than any brick had held before.

"IT CLICKS!" Juno yelled, waving the bricks over her head.

"IT CLICKS!" Milo yelled right back, jumping up and down.

Godtfred laughed and clicked two more bricks together himself, just to join in the fun.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Same Click Forever
chapters.text:
Click pulled an old gray brick from his pocket, dusty and worn smooth.

"This brick is from **1958**," he said. "Let's try something."

He handed it to Juno. Juno pulled a brand-new brick from her own pile of dinosaur pieces.

"Try clicking them together," said Click.

Juno pressed the old gray brick onto the shiny new one.

CLICK!

It fit perfectly, snug as can be, like they were made on the very same day.

"No way!" said Milo. "They're from totally different times!"

"That's the magic of it," said Click. "The brick barely changed at all. A brick made long ago still clicks with one made today."

Juno held the two bricks up high, like a shiny trophy. "Old click, new click, same click!" she sang, and she sang it twice more just because it felt so good to say.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: LEGOLAND and Baby Bricks
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! They landed outside a park full of tiny LEGO buildings, towers, and even a bumpy LEGO castle.

"In **1968**," said Click, "LEGO opened a park called **LEGOLAND**, right in **Billund**, next door to the very same factory."

Milo spotted a shark built entirely out of bricks, taller than him, and gasped. "Can we build one that big someday?"

"Someday," said Click, smiling.

Then Juno spotted a big bin of extra-big, chunky bricks, perfect for small hands like hers.

"Those are **DUPLO** bricks," said Click. "Made in **1969**, just the right size for little kids like you, Juno. And guess what? They still click onto regular LEGO bricks too."

Juno grabbed a giant DUPLO dinosaur and clicked it right onto Milo's tiny brick shark.

They both stared at the silly, mismatched monster, then burst out laughing.

"A dino-shark!" shouted Juno, holding it up for everyone in the park to admire.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Tiny People and Going Home
chapters.text:
Inside LEGOLAND, Click held up something brand new: a tiny LEGO person with bendy arms.

"In **1978**," said Click, "LEGO made its very first little people. You can swap their heads and their hats, and move their arms up and down."

Milo picked out a tiny shark hat for his little person. Juno picked a tiny dinosaur hat for hers.

"A boy named **Kjeld** grew up playing with bricks just like these," said Click. "He was Ole Kirk's grandson. He loved it so much that he grew up and led the whole company himself."

"When I grow up," said Milo, "I want a brick job too."

Click's smile glowed brighter than ever before. "Time to go home, you two."

He tapped the glowing brick three times.

WHOOOOSH!

Milo and Juno landed back on their own bedroom carpet, soft blankets waiting beneath them.

On the rug sat one tiny new minifigure, wearing a tiny shark hat, smiling right up at them.

Milo tucked it safely beside his pillow. Juno yawned a great big dinosaur-sized yawn, and curled up close beside him.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: **Ole Kirk Christiansen** was a carpenter who started making wooden toys in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**.
In **1934**, he named his company **LEGO**, from Danish words meaning **"play well."**
In **1947**, LEGO got a new machine that squeezed melted plastic into shapes.
In **1949**, LEGO made early plastic bricks with bumps on top and hollow undersides.
In **1958**, Ole Kirk's son **Godtfred** made the new click-together brick design official, with little tubes inside.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly with a brick made today.
The first LEGOLAND park opened in **Billund** in **1968**, right next to the factory.
Extra-big **DUPLO** bricks for little kids came out in **1969**, and they click onto regular bricks too.
The first tiny LEGO people, with movable arms and swappable hats, appeared in **1978**.
Ole Kirk's grandson **Kjeld** grew up playing with LEGO bricks and later led the whole company.

story.title: Theo and the Pixel That Blinked Back
story.subtitle: One glitchy controller, sixty years of games, and a kid who finally beats his own bedtime.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Green Screen (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was not supposed to be awake. He was definitely not supposed to be in Roblox Studio at 11:47 p.m., trying to fix a glitch that made his obstacle course spawn players inside a wall.

His monitor flickered. Once. Twice.

Then it went fully black, and a single green dot started bouncing across the screen like a ball that had forgotten how to stop. **BLIP. BLIP. BLIP.**

"That's not my game," Theo whispered.

A shape folded itself out of the green light, chunky and square, like a character built from giant LEGO pixels instead of smooth Roblox polygons. It had a controller cord for a tail.

"Correct," the pixel-shape said. "That's the *first* game. Well. One of the first anyone actually played. Name's Byte. You build worlds. I show you where building worlds started."

Theo blinked at it. "You're a glitch."

"I'm a *feature*," Byte said. "Watch the dot."

The green dot bounced between two lines — a net, maybe — on a round little screen shaped like a porthole. "That's an **oscilloscope**," Byte said, noticing Theo squint. "Old lab equipment that draws wiggly lines on glass. A scientist named **William Higinbotham** used one to make a tennis game, back in **1958**, at a place called **Brookhaven Lab**. He called it 'Tennis for Two.'"

"On a science machine? Not even a TV?"

"Not even a TV," Byte confirmed. "You turned a little knob to aim the ball. People lined up for hours."

Theo reached out and turned an invisible knob. The green dot arced over the line, bounced, came back. He grinned. "It's basically Rocket League with one button."

"Everything's basically something with one button, at the start," Byte said. "Ready to keep going?"

Theo looked at his unfinished obstacle course, then at the glowing green net still humming on his screen.

"Obviously," he said, and grabbed the edge of the desk as the room folded sideways like a loading screen.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Dorm Room Space Battle (1962)
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them into a room stacked with machines the size of refrigerators, all humming like a hundred tired bees.

"MIT," Byte said. "**1962**. That computer takes up a whole wall and is weaker than your phone."

A student named Steve Russell was hunched over a screen the size of a dinner plate, two triangle-shaped spaceships drifting across it. Theo's eyes lit up. "Is that — a space fight?"

"'Spacewar!,'" Byte said. "Steve and some friends wrote it to show off what the computer, the **PDP-1**, could actually do besides math homework."

"Wait, there's two ships. Is it two-player?"

"Good eye," Byte said. "Want to try?"

Theo slid onto the stool before anyone could stop him — not that anyone in 1962 could see him anyway, Byte had mentioned something about that, something Theo chose not to worry about at 11:52 p.m. He grabbed a box of switches and nudged his ship around a tiny star in the middle of the screen.

"The star pulls your ship in," Theo said, working it out mid-spin. "Like gravity. You have to fly *around* it, not through it."

"Now you're thinking like a designer," Byte said. "That's the same trick you used in your obstacle course, with the spinning platform nobody can stand still on."

Theo's ship clipped the star's pull and spiraled into Russell's. Little pixel sparks burst across the screen.

"First multiplayer death match in the history of computers," Byte said, "and you just lost it."

"I want a rematch."

"You'll get sixty years of them," Byte said. "Come on. Next stop has a TV in it. An actual TV."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box (1968–1972)
chapters.text:
They landed in a workshop that smelled like solder and coffee. Wires snaked across a workbench toward a cardboard-colored box the size of a toaster, hooked up to an old television.

"This is **Ralph Baer**," Byte said, nodding at a man squinting through glasses at the wires. "People call him the father of video games. He had one weird idea: what if the game lived *inside your television*, not inside a lab?"

Theo stared at the box. "That's it? That's the whole console?"

"They called it the **Brown Box**," Byte said. "Late 1960s. Ugly name, big idea."

Ralph flipped a switch. Two white rectangles — paddles — appeared on the television, with a square ball bouncing between them.

"It's Tennis for Two again," Theo said, "but on a TV in somebody's actual house."

"Bingo. In **1972**, that idea became a real product you could buy: the **Magnavox Odyssey**. First home video game console ever sold."

Theo picked up a plastic overlay sheet — a thin colored sheet you taped right onto the TV screen, since the Odyssey couldn't draw colors itself. "This is so low-tech it's kind of amazing."

"Low-tech built the whole industry," Byte said. "You build worlds with code now. Ralph built one with tape and wire."

Theo taped the overlay onto the screen himself, lining up a cardboard tennis court exactly where the paddles would bounce. It held.

"Nailed it," Byte said. "Ralph would've hired you."

Ralph Baer, without ever noticing the strange boy at his elbow, flipped the switch off and on again, grinning at his own invention like it might vanish if he blinked.

chapters.heading: Level 4: Quarters and Cartridges (1972–1977)
chapters.text:
The next room was loud, bright, and smelled like popcorn — an arcade, rows of machines glowing like campfires.

"Same year as the Odyssey, **1972**," Byte said, "two guys named **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari**. Their first big hit was right there."

Theo turned. A cabinet showed two white paddles and a bouncing square dot, with a crowd three kids deep around it. "Pong. I've literally seen gifs of this."

"Story goes," Byte said, "one early Pong machine got so many quarters stuffed into it that it actually jammed shut. Might be a slight exaggeration — nobody kept perfect receipts back then — but it tells you how fast people fell for this thing."

Theo watched a kid lose, groan, and immediately dig in his pocket for another quarter. "That's basically rage-quitting and re-queuing."

"Some things never change," Byte agreed.

The arcade blinked forward five years, the cabinets replaced by a plain gray box sitting under a TV, with plastic cartridges stacked beside it like library books.

"**1977**," Byte said. "The **Atari 2600**. Before this, a console could basically only play the one game built into it. This one let you swap in a new cartridge whenever you wanted a different game."

Theo turned a cartridge over in his hands. "So this is basically the first time you could *install* a new game instead of being stuck with one."

"That's it exactly," Byte said. "You're standing in the invention of game shelves."

Theo slotted the cartridge in himself, and the TV blinked awake with a game he'd never heard of, in colors that looked like a dream somebody had slightly misremembered.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Invasion and the Pizza (1978–1980)
chapters.text:
Rows of alien shapes marched down a new screen, left to right, dropping one row lower every pass.

"**1978**," Byte said. "Designer **Tomohiro Nishikado** made this one for a company called **Taito**. 'Space Invaders.' The aliens speed up the lower they get — that's not a bug, that's the whole trick."

Theo leaned in, tracking the pattern. "They speed up because there's fewer of them left, so the game has to keep doing less work. That's actually genius. You're basically scaring the player with math."

"Most designers take years to notice that," Byte said. "You noticed it in ten seconds. Showoff."

Theo laughed and shoved the pixel-shape, who wobbled like static.

The screen changed again: a yellow circle chomping dots through a maze, chased by four ghosts.

"**1980**," Byte said. "**Toru Iwatani** made this one for Namco. Story goes he got the idea staring at a pizza with a slice missing. Nobody's totally sure that's true, but it's the story everyone tells."

"Pac-Man came from *pizza*," Theo said, delighted. "I'm never looking at a pepperoni slice the same way again."

He grabbed the joystick and guided the yellow circle around a corner, snapping up a power pellet just as a ghost closed in.

"Eat the big dot," Byte said, "turn the hunter into the hunted."

The ghost turned blue and fled. Theo chased it down, cackling. "This is literally just tag with snacks."

"Welcome," said Byte, "to arcades in 1980. Everybody's playing tag with snacks."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Crash and the Comeback (1983–1985)
chapters.text:
The arcade lights dimmed. Store shelves appeared, stacked with game cartridges nobody was buying.

"**1983**," Byte said, quieter now. "Companies rushed out so many rough, rushed games that people stopped trusting the shelf. Sales crashed. It's called the **video game crash of 1983**."

"So the whole thing just... died?"

"Nearly. Story goes some unsold cartridges, including a famously bad E.T. game, got buried out in a New Mexico landfill. Diggers actually found some of them in **2014** and proved it true. A whole industry, buried in the desert like a time capsule nobody asked for."

Theo winced. "Rough patch notes."

"Big rough patch," Byte agreed. "But watch this."

A small gray box appeared on a new TV, with a cartridge showing a mustached plumber in overalls jumping over a mushroom.

"**1985**. **Nintendo** launches the **NES** in America, bundled with a game designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto** — **Super Mario Bros.** Miyamoto designed this whole plumber hero from scratch. Mario became gaming's most famous face, full stop."

Theo grabbed the controller and bopped a brick block from below. A coin pinged out. "This still feels good. Forty years later and it *still feels good.*"

"That's why it saved the industry," Byte said.

One more flicker: a screen of falling blocks, stacking, clearing, stacking again.

"**1984**, a year earlier, actually — a scientist in Moscow named **Alexey Pajitnov** built this at a computer center. **Tetris.** Simple shapes, falling forever."

Theo rotated a block into a gap with a satisfying **CLUNK**, clearing the row. "It's so simple it's almost annoying how good it is."

"The best ones always are," said Byte.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Blue Blur and Shiny Discs (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
Something streaked across the next screen so fast it left a blur, like a shooting star with sneakers.

"**1991**," Byte said. "Sega needed a hero fast enough to race Mario. Enter **Sonic the Hedgehog**. Blue, fast, built entirely to compete."

Theo pushed the control stick forward and Sonic rocketed through a loop so quick the screen seemed to hiccup. "Okay, this might be faster than taking a penalty kick."

"Nothing in this room is as fast as Sonic," Byte said. "Not even me, and I'm basically made of light."

The screen changed to something sleeker: a gray console, a shiny silver disc spinning instead of a cartridge.

"**1994**. **Sony** jumps into consoles with the **PlayStation**. It uses **CDs** — those shiny discs — instead of cartridges, which meant games could suddenly hold way more video and sound."

Theo turned the disc over, watching rainbows slide across it. "So this is basically when games started looking like actual movies."

"Getting there," Byte said. "Around the same time, a different kind of game was spreading — not on a console at all. **1993**. A shooter called **Doom** let players connect their computers together in the same room and battle each other directly. People called the get-togethers **LAN parties**."

"So basically an offline Discord call, but with monitors stacked on folding tables."

"Exactly that chaotic," Byte said, "and exactly that fun. That's the whole reason your friends come over to play split-screen instead of just texting about it."

Theo grinned, already picturing his own living room full of controllers and cords.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Motion, Blocks, and a Hall of Fame (2006–2015)
chapters.text:
A white remote-shaped controller floated into Theo's hand, light as a TV clicker.

"**2006**," Byte said. "Nintendo's **Wii**. You don't push buttons to swing — you actually swing the thing."

Theo swung it like a soccer throw-in, and on the screen a tiny avatar copied him exactly, a half-second behind. "Wait, this got my whole grandma playing bowling at Thanksgiving."

"That was the whole plan," Byte said. "Bring in people who'd never picked up a controller in their life."

The scene shifted one more time: a blocky green landscape stretching to the horizon, cube trees, cube hills, cube everything.

"This one you'll recognize," Byte said.

"Minecraft," Theo breathed. "Obviously."

"**2011**. A Swedish developer named **Markus Persson** — people called him **Notch** — released it. It went on to become the best-selling video game ever made."

Theo reached out and placed a single block, and the whole landscape seemed to hold still for him, same as it did every afternoon after school. "This is basically why I started building in Roblox Studio in the first place. I wanted to make my *own* block."

"Then you're standing exactly where you were always headed," Byte said. "**2015**. A museum called **The Strong**, in **Rochester, New York**, opens the **World Video Game Hall of Fame** — Pong, Pac-Man, Tetris, Mario, Sonic, Minecraft, all of it, all in one room."

Theo looked around at everything he'd just played, sixty years folded into one long night. "That's basically the whole run. Start to finish."

"Start to right now," Byte said, and the green light folded back in on itself.

Theo landed back in his desk chair with a soft thump, his Roblox Studio window still open, cursor blinking in the exact spot he'd left it. On the desk sat a small gray plastic controller that had not been there before, one cord trailing off into nothing in particular.

He picked it up, turned it over once, and set it carefully beside his keyboard. Then he opened a brand new, empty game file and typed a title into the box: *Level 1.*

His own, this time.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, Theo had a whole game of his own to build.

true_facts.text: In **1958**, a scientist named **William Higinbotham** built a tennis game on a science machine called an oscilloscope, at **Brookhaven Lab**.
In **1962**, students at **MIT** programmed 'Spacewar!,' one of the first two-player computer games.
In **1972**, the **Magnavox Odyssey** became the first home video game console people could actually buy.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started **Atari** and released the arcade hit **Pong**.
A popular story says one early Pong machine got so stuffed with quarters that it actually jammed shut — maybe a bit exaggerated, but it shows how fast the game caught on.
The **Atari 2600**, from **1977**, let players swap in plastic cartridges instead of being stuck with one built-in game.
In **1978**, **Tomohiro Nishikado** created **Space Invaders**, and the aliens sped up the fewer of them were left.
In **1980**, **Toru Iwatani** created **Pac-Man**, said to be inspired by a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, too many rushed, low-quality games flooded store shelves and the North American game market crashed.
**Nintendo** brought the market back in **1985** with the **NES**, bundled with **Super Mario Bros.**
**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed **Super Mario Bros.** in **1985**, starring the plumber Mario, gaming's most famous character.
In **1984**, **Alexey Pajitnov**, a scientist in Moscow, invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris**.
In **1991**, Sega released **Sonic the Hedgehog**, a superfast blue hero made to compete with Mario.
In **2011**, **Markus 'Notch' Persson** released **Minecraft**, which later became the best-selling video game ever made.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Very Old Fish
story.subtitle: A splashy bedtime trip to meet the sharks of long, long ago

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Milo stacked yellow bricks into a wobbly shark fin. Juno stomped her toy dinosaur across the rug, going "STOMP STOMP STOMP."

It had been just one sleep since their tower's last brick went **CLICK** and held.

Now the brick on Milo's shelf began to glow soft red. It gave a tiny click.

"Juno, look!" Milo whispered. "It's doing the thing again!"

The brick popped apart into a tiny glowing shape. It swam through the air like a fish. Two LEGO eyes blinked at them.

"Hello," said the little shark. "I'm Chomp. Want to meet some real sharks?"

Juno gasped. "Real ones? Like dinosaurs, but wet?"

"Even older than dinosaurs," said Chomp, grinning a brick-tooth grin.

Milo's mouth dropped open. "Older? But dinosaurs are SO old."

"Sharks started swimming in the sea a long, long time before dinosaurs ever stomped around," said Chomp.

"YES," said Milo and Juno together.

Chomp glowed brighter. **WHOOOOSH!** The bedroom spun into blue water and bubbles.

When the bubbles cleared, they floated in the sea, safe inside a bubble made of light.

"First thing," said Chomp. "Sharks don't have hard bones like you. They have bendy, squishy bones. Just like the squishy part of your ear!"

Milo squeezed his own ear. "Whoa. Bendy bones."

Juno squeezed her ear too, giggling. "Squishy ear bones!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
A huge shadow drifted below them. Milo's tummy did one quick flip.

"Is that shark going to eat us?" Juno asked, grabbing Milo's sleeve.

Chomp laughed, a bubbly little laugh. "Don't worry. That's just a picture Megalodon left behind. He's not really here."

The shadow faded into swirly light, showing a giant tooth as big as a hand.

"Megalodon was a giant, giant shark," said Chomp. "He swam long, long ago. He's **extinct** now. That means he's not swimming anywhere anymore."

Milo reached out and touched the glowing tooth. It felt warm, like sunshine.

"How do we even know he was real," Milo asked, "if he's not here?"

"Good question!" said Chomp. "His old teeth turned hard as rock in the ground. We call those **fossils**. His teeth are almost all we have left."

Juno held up her toy dinosaur. "Like dino bones!"

"Just like that," said Chomp.

Milo grinned and held the glowing tooth up like a LEGO piece. "I'm gonna build one THIS big when I get home."

"Deal," said Chomp, and the giant tooth shrank down into a tiny sparkly brick, which dropped right into Milo's hand.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Biggest, Gentlest Fish
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** Chomp zoomed them through the blue, and something enormous swam alongside.

Juno's eyes went huge. "THAT is the biggest fish I ever saw!"

"That's a whale shark," said Chomp. "The biggest fish in the whole sea. Longer than a school bus!"

Milo counted its spots. "One, two, three... so many spots!"

"What does it even eat?" Milo asked. "It's gotta eat a WHOLE ocean."

"Just tiny, tiny floaty bits of food," said Chomp. "It opens its huge mouth, gulps up water, then keeps the tiny bits and lets the water back out."

Juno giggled. "Like a giant soup strainer!"

"Exactly like that," said Chomp.

The whale shark rolled gently to one side, and one big eye seemed to look right at Juno.

"Can I pat it?" Juno asked, reaching out.

"We just wave and watch," said Chomp gently. "Sharks like their space, just like you do."

Juno waved instead, both hands. The whale shark gave a slow, happy swish of its tail and swam on.

"Some whale sharks," said Chomp, "live to be a hundred years old, or even more!"

Milo whistled. "That's older than grandpa!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
Something sleek and gray cut through the water ahead.

"Ooh," said Milo, paddling closer inside their bubble. "Is that a great white shark?"

"Good eye," said Chomp. "Great whites grow up to **twenty feet long**. That's a school bus, parked sideways!"

The shark turned, and they saw rows and rows of white, triangle teeth.

Juno counted fast. "One, two, three, four... I lost count!"

"Sharks grow thousands of teeth over a whole lifetime," said Chomp. "When one tooth falls out, a new one slides forward to take its spot."

Milo's jaw dropped. "Like an escalator, but with TEETH?"

"Exactly like a tooth escalator," said Chomp, and even Juno laughed at that one.

"So sharks never get a wobbly tooth and wait for the tooth fairy?" Milo asked.

"Nope," said Chomp. "New teeth, always ready."

Juno bared her own teeth and growled, pretending to be a shark. Milo growled right back, and they both dissolved into giggles, bubbles popping all around them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Hammer-Head Puzzle
chapters.text:
A strange shape wobbled toward them, wide and flat on top.

Juno pointed. "That shark's head looks like a hammer!"

"You got it," said Chomp. "That's a hammerhead shark. Its head is wide and flat, with one eye on each side."

Milo tilted his head, thinking. "Why would you want your eyes so far apart?"

"Try it," said Chomp.

Milo held his hands out wide, one on each side of his head, and peeked around them. "Whoa, I can see almost all the way around!"

"That's the trick," said Chomp. "A hammerhead can see almost all the way around itself, to spot food swimming by."

Juno tried it too, hands out wide, spinning in a slow circle. "I see EVERYTHING!"

The hammerhead shark swam a lazy loop around their bubble, showing off its wide, wraparound view, then swam off into the blue.

"Good job showing us your eyes!" Juno called after it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Walking Shark
chapters.text:
They floated down near some bumpy, colorful rocks.

"Wait," said Milo, squinting. "Is that shark... WALKING?"

A small spotted shark flip-flopped across the rocks on its fins, like tiny paddles.

"That's an epaulette shark," said Chomp. "It uses its fins like little feet to walk across the reef."

Juno clapped. "A WALKING shark! That's the silliest thing ever!"

"It can even hold its breath a long, long time," said Chomp, "way longer than you could, if the water gets shallow."

Milo tried wiggling his arms like fins, flopping sideways along the sea floor inside their bubble. "Look, I'm walking like a shark!"

Juno flopped down next to him, giggling, both of them wiggling across the sandy bottom like two silly fish.

The little shark paused, almost like it was watching them, then flip-flopped on its way.

"I think it likes you," said Chomp.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A soft light bloomed ahead, shaped like an old photograph.

"Who's that?" Milo asked, pointing at a smiling woman swimming with sharks.

"That's **Eugenie Clark**," said Chomp. "People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for a whole lot of years."

Juno tilted her head. "Did she teach them tricks?"

"She sure did," said Chomp. "She showed the whole world that sharks are curious, and smart enough to learn things, just like you."

Milo grinned. "Like how Juno learned to ride her bike?"

"Kind of like that," said Chomp.

"I wanna be a Shark Lady too," said Juno, puffing up her chest. "Or a Shark... kid."

"You're already doing it," said Chomp. "You're asking questions, and watching closely. That's exactly what she did."

Milo gave Juno a high five, and for once, she didn't miss.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Skin Like Sandpaper, and Home Again
chapters.text:
One more shark glided close, and Milo reached toward it, careful and slow.

"Can I touch, just a little?" Milo asked.

"Just a gentle touch," said Chomp. "Feel that?"

Milo ran a finger along the bubble near the shark's side. "It feels bumpy! Like sandpaper!"

"Shark skin is covered in teeny, tiny bumps," said Chomp. "That's why it feels rough, and it helps the shark zoom through the water."

Juno reached out too, careful, and nodded hard. "Bumpy shark!"

"Sharks are like team captains of the sea," said Chomp. "They help keep everything else balanced, so the whole ocean stays healthy."

Milo nodded slowly. "So sharks aren't scary. They're just important."

"Exactly," said Chomp, glowing brighter. "Ready to go home?"

**WHOOOOSH!** The water spun into bubbles, the bubbles spun into bedroom carpet, and Chomp popped back into one small red brick, right on Milo's palm.

On the rug, their giant LEGO tower stood exactly where they'd left it. Beside it sat one new brick, shaped like a tiny tooth, glowing softly before going dark.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn. Milo set the tiny tooth brick on top of the tower. It went **CLICK**, and held.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Sharks have **bendy, squishy bones** instead of hard bones, just like the squishy part of your ear.
Sharks started swimming in the ocean **before dinosaurs even existed**.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark that lived long ago and is **extinct** now, which means it isn't swimming anywhere anymore.
Scientists mostly know about Megalodon from its giant **fossil teeth**, as big as a hand.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the whole sea, longer than a school bus, and it eats tiny floaty bits of food.
Some whale sharks live to be **a hundred years old** or even more.
The **great white shark** can grow up to **twenty feet long** and has rows of pointy, triangle teeth.
Sharks grow **thousands of teeth** over a lifetime, with new ones always sliding forward to replace old ones.
A **hammerhead shark** has a wide, flat head with eyes spread far apart, so it can see almost all the way around.
The **epaulette shark** can actually walk across rocks and reefs using its fins like little feet.
**Eugenie Clark**, nicknamed the Shark Lady, studied sharks for years and showed the world they are curious and smart.
Shark skin is covered in **teeny, tiny bumps**, which make it feel rough like sandpaper.
Sharks are like **team captains of the sea**, helping keep the whole ocean balanced and healthy.

story.title: Theo and the Nine Levels of Soccer
story.subtitle: A bedtime quest through 2,000 years of kicks, cards, and comebacks.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Cuju, Two Thousand Years Deep
chapters.text:
Theo was building a stadium in Roblox Studio at midnight, an hour past when he'd promised to be asleep. He'd just finished the grass texture when the screen flickered — not blue, not black, but a sick, buzzing green, the same green that had carried a message last week: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD.

"Player One," squeaked a voice, and a small green shape made of square pixels popped out of the monitor and landed on his keyboard. "Did you build this stadium, or copy one off the marketplace?"

"Bit!" Theo said. "You're supposed to be a loading screen, not a critic."

"I'm 8-bit," Bit said. "I've got opinions in low resolution. You want a real stadium? I've got nine of them. Each one's a save file from history. Ready, Player One?"

"Born ready," Theo said, and the floor dropped away in a soft **BZZZT**.

He landed in dust and sunshine, in a dirt yard ringed by wooden fences, where a crowd yelled and a leather ball flew between dozens of running feet. Nobody used their hands.

"Where — when — is this?" Theo asked.

"Han China," Bit said. "More than **2,000 years ago**. They called it **cuju** — kickball. Soldiers played it to stay sharp. Nobody touches that ball with a hand."

Theo watched a player flick the ball up with the outside of his foot, a move Theo himself had tried about four hundred times in his backyard with a forty percent success rate. "That's literally a juggle. I do that."

"Called it two thousand years before you did," Bit said.

Theo grinned and jogged into the dust to try it himself — and for one glorious second, the whole yard cheered for him like he belonged there. Then the ball hit him in the face. Soccer, it turned out, had never really changed.

"Noted," Theo said, wiping dust off his nose. "Level complete?"

A gold coin popped into the air and landed in his palm, warm and humming.

"Level complete," Bit agreed. "Eight more save files to go."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The King Who Banned the Game
chapters.text:
The next **BZZZT** dropped Theo into a muddy English street, where what looked like an entire village sprinted after a ball the size of a basketball, elbows everywhere, somebody's hat flying off, a goat watching from a safe distance.

"This is soccer?" Theo said, ducking a guy built like a castle wall.

"This is **mob football**," Bit said. "Medieval England. Whole towns played — no teams, no rules, just everybody chasing one ball from one end of town to the other."

A man in a crown, looking personally offended, stomped past holding a scroll. "That," Bit said, "is **King Edward II**. In **1314**, he banned the game in London. Said it caused too much noise and broke windows."

"Broke windows," Theo repeated. "Soccer got banned for being loud."

"Royally banned," Bit said.

Theo watched the mud-covered crowd roar past again, completely ignoring the king's scroll. "Did it work? The banning?"

"Nope," Bit said. "They just kept playing. Kings can write rules. Kids with a ball don't always read them."

Theo laughed, stepped out of the way of an incoming wheel of cheese somebody had apparently brought as a snack, and caught the gold coin that popped free of the chaos.

"Level complete," he said, grinning. "No royal permission required."

chapters.heading: Level 3: Somebody Write This Down
chapters.text:
**BZZZT** dropped Theo into a smoky room in London, where a dozen serious-looking men argued over a sheet of paper like it was the last slice of pizza.

"Who are they?" Theo whispered.

"Problem solvers," Bit said. "By the 1800s, every school and town played football with different rules. One school let you catch the ball and run. Another said only kicking. Games between schools turned into arguments about whose rules counted."

"Sounds like playing with someone who doesn't believe in gravity settings," Theo said.

"Exactly. So in **1848**, students at Cambridge University wrote the **Cambridge Rules** — one shared rulebook everyone could try. It didn't fix everything. But fifteen years later—"

A man stood up from the table holding a finished page like he'd just beaten a final boss. "That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Bit said. "He personally wrote football's first official rulebook, the **Laws of the Game**, still the ancestor of today's one, in **1863**. Same year, his group made the biggest rule split in the sport's history."

"Which was?"

"No hands," Bit said. "The **Football Association** was founded in London on **October 26, 1863**, and from then on, if you weren't the goalkeeper, your hands were benched."

Theo grabbed the loose page off the table before it blew into the fireplace — and froze. Someone had scribbled a nickname in the margin: *assoc. football.*

"People got lazy saying the whole name," Bit said. "By the **1880s**, English schoolboys had shortened 'association' to 'assoc,' then to **soccer**. You're welcome."

"Wait, soccer is short for *association*?" Theo said. "I've been saying a nickname's nickname my whole life."

"IT'S OFFICIAL!" Bit shouted, as a gold coin popped out of the inkwell.

Theo pocketed it, grinning. "Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Build the League
chapters.text:
The next landing dropped Theo onto a frost-hard field in Scotland, breath steaming, a crowd wrapped in scarves staring at a scoreboard that stubbornly read 0-0.

"Please tell me somebody scores," Theo said.

"Nobody does," Bit said. "This is **1872**, Glasgow — the first-ever official **international match**, Scotland versus England, the first time two countries' teams played each other under one set of written rules. Final score: **nil-nil**."

"That's not thrilling, that's a scoreless draw."

"History doesn't always nail the ending," Bit said. "But it counts."

The scene blinked sideways — same cold, a battered silver cup held over somebody's head. "This one you'll like better," Bit said. "The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871 to 1872**. Still running today. Oldest football competition on Earth."

"It's basically the original tournament bracket," Theo said.

**BZZZT**, and they landed in a wood-paneled office, a man pinning a schedule to the wall. "**William McGregor**," Bit said. "In **1888**, he organized the **Football League**, the world's first one. Instead of random matches, clubs played a real season, with a table and everything."

"A leaderboard," Theo said, delighted. "He built a leaderboard for an entire sport."

"And sixteen years later, in **1904**, seven countries met in Paris and formed **FIFA**, the group that still runs the whole sport worldwide," Bit said. "Four letters, one planet."

Theo scooped the gold coin off McGregor's desk before it could roll away. "Level complete," he said. "This game got organized fast."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Ball in the Castle Wall
chapters.text:
**BZZZT** landed Theo inside cold stone walls, dust floating in a shaft of light, a workman prying open a wooden ceiling beam with a crowbar.

"Where's the soccer part?" Theo asked.

"Patience," Bit said. "This is **Stirling Castle**, in Scotland. Watch."

Something small and leathery, dried out and round, tumbled from the gap in the beam and bounced once on the stone floor. The workman picked it up, baffled.

"A ball," Bit said, "made around the **1540s**, stuffed with a **bladder** — back then, an inflated animal bladder, blown up like a balloon, was basically the beach ball of its day. It got stuck in that ceiling for centuries and nobody noticed."

Theo picked it up carefully. It was smaller than he expected, lopsided, nothing like the ball in his own cleats bag. "Is this really the oldest soccer ball ever found?"

"Might be," Bit said. "Nobody signed a receipt in **1540**, so historians can't be a hundred percent sure. It's probably the oldest one anybody's found — but 'probably' is as far as the evidence goes."

"So it's a legend," Theo said.

"A really good one," Bit said. "The kind that's mostly true and all interesting."

Theo set the old ball gently back on its ledge, like returning a trophy to a shelf it had earned. A gold coin dropped out of the beam gap instead, landing in his palm with a clink that felt four hundred years overdue.

"Level complete," Theo said. "Oldest ball in the game — probably."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Benched for the Wrong Reason
chapters.text:
**BZZZT** dropped Theo into a packed stadium roaring louder than anything he'd heard yet, flags waving, thousands of people pressed in close.

"Please tell me this is a final," Theo said.

"Close," Bit said. "This is a **Dick, Kerr Ladies** match, early 1900s England — a women's soccer team. Look at the crowds."

Up on the field, a sharp-footed forward smashed a shot into the net so hard the keeper didn't even flinch toward it. "That's **Lily Parr**," Bit said. "One of the best players in the country, full stop. Her team was one of the most popular in England."

Theo watched the crowd erupt again. "So why haven't I heard of her?"

Bit's pixels dimmed, just slightly. "Because in **1921**, the FA banned women from playing on their clubs' grounds. Fifty years, Theo. They weren't allowed back on a proper field until **1971**, when the ban finally got lifted."

Theo stopped cheering. "That's not fair. She was better than half these guys."

"Wasn't fair," Bit agreed. "Still isn't a fact anybody should feel good about. But here's the part worth sticking around for."

The stadium flickered forward, decades later, into a packed arena in China, a different crowd, the same roar. "The first official **Women's World Cup**," Bit said, "played in **1991**. Won by the **United States**."

Theo watched a player lift a trophy overhead, and under the cheering he could almost hear Lily Parr's crowd from seventy years earlier. "They got there anyway," he said.

"They always were good enough," Bit said. "The rules just took a while to catch up."

Theo caught the gold coin without looking, like a header he'd actually practiced. "Level complete. About time."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The First World Cup
chapters.text:
**BZZZT** landed Theo on a ship's deck, salt air, a handful of European players staring at a trophy case like none of them quite believed it was real.

"Why's everyone on a boat?" Theo asked.

"Because in **1930**, the only way to reach the very first **World Cup** was by ship, across the Atlantic, to **Uruguay**," Bit said.

"They sailed to a soccer tournament?"

"Thirteen teams did. A French official named **Jules Rimet** had spent years pushing for one real worldwide tournament instead of scattered regional ones. He got his wish — the trophy they played for was even named after him."

The scene shifted to a packed stadium, the host nation's flag waving everywhere, a final whistle blowing. "Uruguay hosted," Bit said, "and Uruguay won, beating **Argentina** in the final, right in front of their own fans."

Theo watched the home crowd erupt, hats flying, a celebration that looked exactly like a server chat blowing up after a clutch win. "Home-field advantage, actual version," he said.

"The original one," Bit agreed. "Nearly a hundred years of World Cups, and it all started with one ship, one trophy, and a guy who wouldn't stop asking for it."

A gold coin rolled off the trophy case. Theo trapped it under his sneaker like a pass he didn't want to lose, then scooped it up.

"Level complete," he said. "Next time I'm seasick, I'm blaming this guy."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Stolen Cups and Red Cards
chapters.text:
**BZZZT** dropped Theo on a London street in front of a glass display case — empty.

"Okay, where's the trophy supposed to be?" Theo said.

"Stolen," Bit said. "**1966**. Someone swiped the actual World Cup trophy out of its case, weeks before England hosted the whole tournament."

"They just lost the trophy."

"For a week," Bit said. "Then a dog named **Pickles**, out on a walk, sniffed it out of a hedge, wrapped in newspaper. Best-dressed dog in football history."

Theo laughed so hard he nearly missed the whistle. The scene blinked to a packed stadium, England's flag everywhere, a final score flashing up. "England hosted **1966**," Bit said, "and England won. Their only title, so far."

"So far," Theo repeated. "I like that you said 'so far.'"

The field blinked again, to a sun-scorched pitch where one player did things with the ball that looked less like soccer and more like Theo's wildest physics glitch. "That's **Pele**," Bit said. "Brazilian forward. The only player ever to win the World Cup on three different winning teams — **1958, 1962, 1970**."

"Three times. On the actual team."

"On the field," Bit confirmed. "Brazil's won the whole thing a record **five times** total — **1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002**."

A referee jogged past, flashing something small and bright from his pocket — yellow plastic, then red. "Also **1970**," Bit said. "A referee named **Ken Aston** got the idea for **yellow and red cards** from a traffic light. Yellow means slow down. Red means you're out."

"Traffic light rules, for soccer. Unreasonably good design."

"Right? And one more thing," Bit said, as Brazil's players lifted a gleaming trophy overhead. "Brazil kept that one forever, after their third title. So in **1974**, FIFA had to build a whole new World Cup trophy, the one they still use today."

Theo caught the gold coin out of the air like a cross he'd been waiting his whole career for. "Level complete," he said. "That was basically four history lessons wearing a jersey."

"Welcome to soccer," Bit said. "It never stops adding content."

chapters.heading: Level 9: Home Server
chapters.text:
**BZZZT**, and Theo's knees hit his own bedroom carpet, right where he'd started, his Roblox stadium still glowing soft and unfinished on the monitor behind him.

"Nine levels," Bit said, floating down to the keyboard, pixels a little watery at the edges, the way they always got right before goodbye. "Not bad for one night, Player One."

Theo opened his fist. Nine gold coins sat warm in his palm — cuju's dust, a banned king's mud, Morley's inkwell, a frozen Scottish nil-nil, a castle's oldest ball, Lily Parr's stadium roar, a ship to Uruguay, a dog named Pickles, Pele's impossible footwork.

"What do I do with these?" he asked.

"Watch," Bit said.

The coins lifted off his palm on their own, spinning together in the dark, melting into one shape, until a small, solid trophy sat cooling in his hands — not the real World Cup, nothing he'd ever seen in a store, but unmistakably a trophy for *this* exact night.

"History's longest-running game," Bit said. "Two thousand years, and it's still going."

"Still adding levels," Theo said.

Bit's pixels blinked, bright and a little misty. "BZZZT. Level complete. All nine."

The screen flickered once more, then settled, steady and green, on a single line: GOOD GAME, PLAYER ONE.

Theo set the little trophy on his desk, right next to his cleats, and climbed back into bed.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a free kick with his name on it.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a kicking game played in **Han China** more than **2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's oldest ancestors.
Medieval **mob football** got so wild that **King Edward II** banned it in London in **1314**.
The **Football Association** was founded in London on **October 26, 1863**, and said players couldn't carry the ball with their hands.
The word **soccer** comes from schoolboys shortening 'association football' to 'assoc' in the **1880s**.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871 to 1872**, is the oldest soccer competition still running today.
The first official **international match** was a **nil-nil draw** between Scotland and England, played in Glasgow in **1872**.
**FIFA**, the group that runs world soccer, was founded in Paris in **1904** by seven countries.
An old leather ball found hidden in **Stirling Castle** might date back to the **1540s**, possibly making it the oldest soccer ball ever found.
**Lily Parr** was a star player for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of England's most popular soccer teams.
Women weren't allowed to play on proper fields in England until the ban was finally lifted in **1971**.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was played in **1991** and won by the **United States**.
The very first **World Cup** was held in **Uruguay** in **1930**, and the host team beat **Argentina** in the final.
The **1966 World Cup trophy** was stolen in London, then found a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**Pele** is the only player ever to win the World Cup on three different champion teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo's nine golden coins fuse into one small trophy that now sits on his desk beside his cleats, with the screen settling on the words GOOD GAME, PLAYER ONE.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Mountain That Glows
story.subtitle: A tiny LEGO brick lights up and three sleepy explorers visit real volcanoes

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Rumble Wakes Up
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime. Juno hugged her dinosaur tight. Milo stacked one more LEGO brick. Theo peeked at his tablet under the blanket.

On Milo's shelf sat a tiny LEGO mountain. He built it with his own hands. One lone orange brick sat right on top.

The orange brick started to glow. It got warm. Then it wiggled.

"Whoa!" said Milo.

POP! A tiny creature hopped out. It looked like a little volcano with eyes.

"Hello!" it said. "I'm Rumble. Let's rock!"

Juno giggled. "You're squishy and orange!"

"A volcano is just a hole in the ground," said Rumble. "Hot rock, tiny bits of ash, and gas puff out of it."

"Can we see one?" asked Theo.

"Hold on tight!" said Rumble.

He grew bigger. He scooped up Juno, Milo, and Theo. WHOOSH! They flew past the stars and landed on a black rocky island.

Steam hissed from cracks in the ground. Orange goo oozed nearby. Juno sniffed the air. "It smells like toasted marshmallows!"

"That orange goo is called lava," said Rumble. "Underground, that same hot melted rock is called magma. Once it pops out on top, we call it lava."

Milo peeked closer. "So it's the same stuff? Just two names?"

"Exactly," said Rumble. "You found it fast!"

This was Kilauea, a volcano in Hawaii. It had been bubbling and flowing for years and years, almost without stopping.

Theo whistled. "That's one hard worker."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Giant Circle of Fire
chapters.text:
Rumble pulled out a glowing map. It curled around the ocean like a bracelet.

"This circle is called the Ring of Fire," he said. "It goes all around the edge of the ocean."

Theo squinted at the map. It looked like a giant soccer field, bent into a circle.

"Most of the world's volcanoes live right here," said Rumble, "where giant rock pieces under the ground bump, pull, or slide past each other."

"Like LEGO plates sliding apart?" asked Milo.

"Just like that," said Rumble.

Theo traced the ring with his finger. He counted little red dots. "There's so many dots over here!" He pointed at one curvy country.

"That's Indonesia," said Rumble. "It has more volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

Juno gasped. "More than dinosaurs stomped on?"

Rumble laughed. "Maybe close!"

Theo grinned. "I just leveled up my volcano knowledge."

The map rolled itself back up. The ground rumbled softly beneath their feet, almost like a drum.

"Next stop," said Rumble, "the biggest volcano of them all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Wide Giant
chapters.text:
They landed on a huge, round mountain. It looked squashed, like a pancake.

"This is Mauna Loa," said Rumble. "It's the biggest volcano on Earth, and it keeps on growing."

Milo looked up. "It's not pointy like I thought."

"Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like this one," said Rumble. "Others are tall and pointy, like Mount Fuji in Japan."

Milo thought about his LEGO builds. "Wide ones need a big bottom, like my castle. Pointy ones stack straight up, like my rocket."

"You got it," said Rumble. "Big and wide just means extra gentle."

"This mountain didn't grow at the edge of two giant rock pieces," said Rumble. "It grew over a hotspot, an extra hot spot deep down, like a stove burner that never turns off."

Juno stomped around the wide slope. "It's not scary. It's just... comfy!"

Theo paced out the distance. "It's taller than four thousand meters! That's like stacking a whole stadium, way up high."

"Good counting," said Rumble.

A little puff of steam floated up nearby. Milo pointed. "Is it going to erupt right now?"

"Nope," said Rumble. "Not today. It's just breathing a little."

Milo relaxed. "Phew. Breathing volcanoes are my favorite kind."

Everybody giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Brand New Island
chapters.text:
Rumble flew them over cold blue water. "Welcome to Iceland," he said.

Juno peered down. "I don't see any island!"

"Watch," said Rumble.

The water bubbled. Steam puffed up. SPLOOSH! Black rock burst out of the waves.

"This really happened," said Rumble. "In 1963, a brand new island popped up right here. They named it Surtsey."

Milo's eyes went wide. "A whole island just... appeared?"

"Yes," said Rumble. "It kept erupting and erupting until the island was big enough to stand on."

Theo looked around at the water. "Why does Iceland get so many volcanoes?"

"Because Iceland sits where two giant rock pieces are slowly pulling apart," said Rumble. "Hot magma squeezes up through the crack."

Juno dipped her toe near the new black rock. "Can I be the first dinosaur to visit?"

"The very first," laughed Rumble.

They tiptoed across the brand new ground. It crunched like gravel under their feet.

Milo grinned. "New islands are kind of like new LEGO sets. Fresh out of the box."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Volcano on Mars
chapters.text:
"Ready for somewhere really far away?" asked Rumble.

WHOOSH! They zoomed past the moon, way out into space.

They landed on red, dusty ground. Above them loomed a mountain so tall it poked out of the sky.

"This is Olympus Mons," said Rumble. "It's on Mars, and it's the biggest volcano in the whole solar system."

Theo's jaw dropped. "How big?"

"About thirteen miles high," said Rumble. "Almost three Mount Everests stacked up."

Theo tried to imagine it. "That's bigger than any tower I've ever built in Roblox."

Milo laughed. "Even bigger than a megalodon shark standing on its tail!"

Juno spun in a circle, staring up. "It doesn't even fit in my eyes! It's the biggest mountain I've ever not-touched."

Everyone laughed.

"Nothing on Earth gets this big," said Rumble. "Mars's ground doesn't shift around as much as ours does, so its volcanoes just keep growing and growing."

Theo nodded slowly. "Okay. That's officially the coolest fact today."

They all agreed, staring up at the giant red mountain.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sleepy Giant
chapters.text:
Back on Earth, they landed in a grassy valley full of bubbling pools.

"This is Yellowstone," said Rumble. "Under here is one gigantic, sleepy volcano."

Milo gulped. "Sleepy like... about to wake up?"

"Don't worry," said Rumble. "Its last big eruption was about 640,000 years ago. Scientists watch it closely, and they see no sign it will wake up soon."

Milo breathed out. "Okay. Phew again."

"How do they watch it?" asked Theo.

Rumble pointed to a little machine blinking nearby. "That's a seismograph. It's a machine that feels tiny ground wiggles. Scientists also use satellites in the sky to check if the ground is puffing up."

Theo peered at the blinking light. "So it's like a volcano alarm clock."

"Exactly," said Rumble.

Juno pressed her ear to the ground. "I hear... bubbles!"

Everyone listened. Little pools nearby went blip, blip, blip.

"That's just steam saying hello," said Rumble.

Juno giggled. "Hello, steam!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Dinosaur-Sized Dirt
chapters.text:
Rumble led them to a hillside covered in bright green plants.

"Old volcano ash turns into super good dirt," said Rumble. "We call that fertile. It just means really good for growing yummy plants."

Juno dug her toy dinosaur into the soft dirt. "It's soft and crumbly!"

"That's why farmers like living near volcanoes," said Rumble. "Even though volcanoes can be a little risky, the dirt grows amazing food."

Milo picked a plump tomato off a nearby vine. "Whoa, this is huge!"

Theo tasted one. "Okay, that's actually really good."

Milo imagined building a whole LEGO farm right on top of a volcano.

Juno planted her toy dinosaur right in the dirt like a flag. "I claim this hill for dinosaurs!"

Rumble chuckled. "Dinosaurs would have loved soil like this too."

The sun was setting, painting the sky orange, just like Rumble's glow.

"Time to go home," said Rumble gently.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back Under the Blanket
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! They zoomed back through the stars.

THUMP! They landed softly on Milo's bedroom carpet.

Rumble shrank back down to a tiny glowing brick. He hopped onto the LEGO mountain, right where he started.

"Did that really happen?" whispered Milo.

Juno yawned, hugging her dinosaur. "My toes still feel crunchy."

Theo smiled, looking at the little orange brick. "I guess some things you just have to believe."

They each picked a favorite fact to tell their friends tomorrow.

The brick gave one last warm flicker, like a wink.

"Let's rock," it whispered, and went dark.

Milo tucked it carefully onto his shelf. Juno climbed into bed. Theo pulled his blanket up high.

Outside, the real stars twinkled, just like tiny volcanoes far, far away.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Let's rock to dreamland.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is just a hole in the ground where hot rock, ash, and gas can escape.
Underground, hot melted rock is called **magma**. Once it comes out on top, it's called **lava**.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been bubbling and flowing almost without stopping for years.
Volcanoes mostly live along the **Ring of Fire**, a huge circle around the ocean.
**Indonesia** has more volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Most volcanoes form where giant rock pieces under the ground bump, pull, or slide.
**Mauna Loa** grew over a **hotspot** instead of at the edge of two rock pieces.
**Mauna Loa** is the biggest volcano on Earth, rising over **4,000 meters** high.
Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like Mauna Loa; others are tall and pointy, like **Mount Fuji**.
In **1963**, a brand new island named **Surtsey** popped up out of the sea near Iceland.
Iceland has so many volcanoes because it sits where two giant rock pieces are slowly pulling apart.
**Olympus Mons** on Mars is the biggest volcano in the whole solar system, about **thirteen miles** tall.
Scientists use a **seismograph** to feel tiny ground wiggles, and satellites to check if the ground is puffing up.
Old volcano ash turns into **fertile** dirt, which is why farmers love growing food near volcanoes.

story.title: Juno and the Golden Hive
story.subtitle: A tiny bee, a big family, and one sweet surprise.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Golden Glow
chapters.text:
Juno lined up her dinosaur toys on the rug. One more roar before bed, she thought.

Then she saw it. A little golden rock glowed on her shelf. Inside it, something tiny buzzed.

Juno tiptoed over and tapped the rock. CLICK!

The glow grew bright. A tiny bee popped out, warm and golden. "Hello, Juno! I'm Buzzy," said the bee. "Want to see my hive?"

"A hive is my cozy home," Buzzy said, "with lots and lots of little rooms."

Juno grinned. "Yes! Shrink me down!"

WHOOOSH! The room spun gold. Juno was bee-sized, with tiny wings of her own.

She landed on a branch buzzing with bees. "Who's in charge?" Juno asked.

"The queen bee," said Buzzy. "She has workers to help her, and some daddy bees called drones too."

Juno counted on her tiny bee legs. "One big family!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Busy Queen
chapters.text:
Buzzy led Juno deep inside the hive. It smelled sweet and warm.

A huge bee sat in the middle, bigger than all the rest. "That's the queen," Buzzy whispered.

She was laying eggs, one after another. Tap, tap, tap.

"How many eggs?" Juno asked.

"Up to two thousand a day," said Buzzy. "She's the busiest mom in the whole hive!"

Juno's eyes went wide. "That's more eggs than my dinosaur book has pictures!"

The queen winked at Juno and kept right on working.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Everyone Has a Job
chapters.text:
Outside the queen's room, bees zoomed everywhere.

One bee swept the floor. Another stood by the door. Another flew off into the sun.

"They're all girls," said Buzzy, "and they take turns doing every job."

"Even guarding?" Juno asked. She loved being a brave dinosaur guard at home.

"Even guarding," said Buzzy. "Want to try?"

Juno puffed up her tiny wings and stood by the door. A big beetle buzzed close.

"STOP!" Juno shouted, stomping her bee feet like a dinosaur.

The beetle zoomed away. The other bees cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: So Many Kinds of Bees
chapters.text:
Buzzy pointed to a fuzzy striped bee, a shiny green bee, and a round black bee.

"There are about twenty thousand kinds of bees," said Buzzy.

Juno thought of her dinosaur book. "Like how there are lots of kinds of dinosaurs!"

"Just like that," said Buzzy. "But only a few of us make honey people eat."

Juno patted her own fuzzy bee tummy. "I'm glad I'm a honey kind today."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Wiggly Dance
chapters.text:
A bee zoomed in and wiggled side to side, round and round.

"That's the waggle dance," said Buzzy. "It's a wiggly dance that tells other bees where the best flowers are."

Juno watched close. "She's pointing with her bottom!"

"Exactly," laughed Buzzy. "A scientist named Karl watched this dance long ago and figured out what it meant."

Juno tried her own wiggle. Her wings buzzed fast, two hundred times every second. BZZZZZ!

"That's the buzzing sound!" Juno giggled. "I'm buzzing like a real bee!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Six Straight Sides
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, Juno saw walls built of tiny rooms. Each one had six straight sides, like a little stop sign.

"Why six sides?" Juno asked.

"Six sides fit together perfectly," said Buzzy. "No wasted space, and lots of room for honey."

Juno remembered stacking her toy blocks. "Like when my blocks fit with no gaps!"

"Just like that," said Buzzy.

Juno helped pat one wall smooth with her tiny leg. It held every drop of sweet nectar inside. Nectar, Buzzy explained, is the sweet juice bees drink from flowers.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bees and Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
"Buzzy," said Juno, "did bees ever meet dinosaurs?"

"They sure did," said Buzzy. "Some old bees got stuck in amber, that hard golden rock, about a hundred million years ago. That's way before people, back when dinosaurs stomped around."

Juno's eyes lit up. "So I AM a bee-dinosaur explorer!"

"You sure are," said Buzzy. "And people have loved bees forever too. Long, long ago in Egypt, people painted pictures of themselves collecting honey from hives."

Juno beamed. "Bees and dinosaurs and people. That's a lot of friends!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sweet Gold, Home Again
chapters.text:
"How much honey does one bee make?" Juno asked.

"Just a tiny drop," said Buzzy. "About as much as fits on your fingertip, her whole life long."

"That's so little!" said Juno.

"But together, bees visit millions of flowers to fill one yummy jar," said Buzzy. "And bees help grow lots of our food too. Every third yummy bite comes from bees helping flowers grow."

The gold light swirled again. WHOOOSH!

Juno landed back on her rug, Juno-sized once more. The amber rock sat quiet on her shelf, one tiny golden drop glowing inside like honey.

Juno yawned a big dinosaur yawn and climbed into bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Buzz home and dream sweet.

true_facts.text: A beehive is one big family: a **queen bee**, lots of **worker bees**, and some daddy bees called **drones**.
The **queen bee** can lay up to **two thousand eggs** every day.
**Worker bees** take turns doing every job, like sweeping, guarding, and flying out for flowers.
There are about **twenty thousand kinds of bees**, but only a few make honey people eat.
Bees do a wiggly **waggle dance** to tell each other where the best flowers are.
A bee's wings buzz about **two hundred times every second**, and that makes the buzzing sound.
Bees build walls of tiny rooms with **six straight sides** that fit together with no gaps.
Some old bees got stuck in **amber** about **a hundred million years ago**, back when dinosaurs were around.
One bee makes only a **tiny drop of honey** in her whole life.
Bees help grow about **one out of every three bites** of food we eat.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Juno returns to her normal size on her bedroom rug, and the amber rock on her shelf glows quietly with one tiny golden drop of light before she climbs into bed.
