scenarios.best_moment: "Why not?" said Nell, grinning. "It worked hard to get here."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Just like that," said Pip, smiling her warm little smile.
editor_notes: Move or cut the final bold shout so the story settles quietly into bed: end Chapter 8 on the petal under the pillow, and put the 'TWELVE BEES' shout where Finn first says it.
Vary Pip's replies and dialogue tags. Replace the repeated 'Just like that' / 'Exactly like that' and 'smiling her warm little smile' with fresh reactions or let a child's line stand alone.
Fix the hummingbird aside (e.g., 'Nobody can, not even a hummingbird!'), and give the shout-along banners a steady rhythm, either after every chapter or only at the three biggest moments.

story.title: Finn, Nell, and the Buzzing Honey Jar
story.subtitle: A honey-sweet bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Jar
chapters.text:
Finn licked a stripe of honey off his toast. It was warm, sticky, and gold.

Nell touched the little yellow flower sticker on her wall. She loved anything yellow, the brighter the better.

"Bedtime soon," Mom called from the hallway. "One more bite, you two."

On the nightstand between their beds sat a small glass jar, half full of honey.

Suddenly the jar glowed. It glowed gold, bright as the sun through curtains.

Then it began to hum. BUZZZZZ.

Finn froze mid-bite. "Nell. Do you hear that?"

Nell nodded, eyes huge. "The jar is singing!"

The lid spun around, click, click, click, faster and faster.

A tiny door popped open right on top.

Out buzzed a small bee, striped like a tiny sweater.

"Hello!" she said. "I'm Pip. I'm a scout bee."

"A talking bee?" Finn blinked twice, just to be sure.

"A talking bee," Pip agreed, "who needs two brave helpers tonight."

She flicked one small wing toward the window. "Want to see how bees make honey? All of it, start to finish?"

Nell clapped her hands. "Yes! Will there be yellow flowers?"

"So many yellow flowers," said Pip. "Hold onto my wings, both of you, nice and gentle."

Finn grabbed one wing. Nell grabbed the other.

The jar's glow swelled bigger and brighter. WHOOOOSH!

Finn and Nell shrank down, smaller and smaller, until they were the size of honeybees.

They landed softly on a wooden step with a tiny plop.

Buzzing filled the air all around them, loud and busy.

Thousands of bees zoomed past, every one with somewhere to be.

"Whoa," whispered Finn. "So many bees!"

"This hive can hold twenty thousand bees," said Pip. "Sometimes even sixty thousand, all buzzing at once."

"That's more bees than I could ever count," said Nell, giggling.

"Come on," said Pip, waving them forward. "Let's go meet somebody very important."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Busy Queen
chapters.text:
Deep inside the hive, bees crowded thick around someone big and gentle.

"That's the queen bee," whispered Pip. "She's the mother of almost every bee you see."

The queen moved slowly, round and busy, bees bowing out of her way.

Finn watched her curl low and lay a tiny white egg into a wax room.

Then another egg. Then another, quick as blinking.

"She lays eggs all day long," said Pip. "Sometimes over a thousand in just one day!"

Nell's mouth popped open. "A THOUSAND EGGS?!"

"That's why there are so many bees here," said Pip, smiling.

Finn tried counting on his fingers, then gave up with a laugh. "Too many for fingers."

"Most of these bees are her daughters," said Pip. "Worker bees. They do every single job."

"Every job?" asked Nell, tilting her head.

"Cleaning rooms, feeding baby bees, guarding the door, making honey," said Pip. "All of it."

Just then, a worker bee zoomed past, carrying something shiny and gold.

"What's she carrying?" asked Finn, pointing with his whole arm.

"Sweet flower juice," said Pip. "We call it nectar. Want to see where she finds it?"

Finn's tummy rumbled, loud and hopeful. He loved anything sweet, especially honey.

"Yes please," he said. "Lead the way, Pip!"

Nell tugged gently on Pip's wing, pointing toward a bright doorway. "Flowers mean yellow. I want to see!"

Pip smiled her tiny bee smile. "Then follow me, little flower-finder."

Together they buzzed toward the sunny hive door, Finn's tummy still rumbling behind them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Yellow Meadow
chapters.text:
Outside, the meadow stretched wide and gold, flowers nodding in a soft breeze.

Nell gasped, spinning in a slow circle. "Yellow! So much yellow!"

Dandelions and sunflowers swayed everywhere she looked, bright as little suns.

A worker bee landed on a yellow flower and dipped in a long, curly tongue, thin as a tiny straw.

"That's called a proboscis," said Pip. "It's long and curly, like a straw, so she can sip the sweet juice hiding deep inside."

"A straw tongue!" Finn laughed. "That's silly and amazing."

"It works perfectly," said Pip. "She sucks up the nectar, that sweet flower juice, drop by drop."

Nell leaned close to a flower, careful to keep her hands behind her back. "Can I smell it?"

"Go ahead," said Pip. "Just don't touch. She's hard at work."

Nell sniffed deeply. "Mmm! It smells sweet, like sunshine."

Finn watched another bee zip from flower to flower without stopping. "She's so fast!"

"She visits lots of flowers before flying home," said Pip.

Nell spotted something past a tangle of grass. "Pip, look! More yellow flowers, over there, nobody's visited yet!"

Pip buzzed up high to check. "Good eyes, Nell! That's a whole new patch."

The nearby bee turned at once and headed straight for it.

"You found her very next stop," said Pip. "Nice work, little flower-finder."

Nell beamed, cheeks pink and proud.

"Now," said Pip, "let's follow that nectar home and see what happens to it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Honey Tummy
chapters.text:
Back at the hive, Finn had a question bubbling up.

"Where does the nectar go?" he asked. "Does she just eat it?"

"Not exactly," said Pip. "She keeps it in a special tummy, just for nectar. A honey tummy."

"A honey tummy?" Finn giggled so hard he nearly fell over. "I want a honey tummy!"

"It's different from her eating tummy," said Pip. "This one is only for carrying sweet juice home safely."

Nell poked her own tummy, curious. "Is my tummy a honey tummy too?"

"Only bees have honey tummies," said Pip, laughing her small buzzy laugh.

The bee landed right by the door, and another bee hurried over to greet her.

They touched their tiny mouths together, quick as a wink.

"What was that?" asked Finn, leaning in close.

"She's sharing the nectar," said Pip. "Passing it along, bee to bee to bee."

"Like sharing a juice box at lunch," said Finn.

"Exactly like that," said Pip. "And every time it gets passed along, it turns a little sweeter."

Nell watched, eyes wide with wonder. "Sweeter and sweeter and sweeter?"

"Sweeter and sweeter," said Pip, "until one happy day, it turns into real honey."

Finn's tummy rumbled again, loud and long. BRRROOOWL.

Nell burst into giggles. "Your tummy is buzzing too, Finn!"

Finn laughed so hard he nearly tipped off the step.

"Come on, silly honey bear," said Pip, grinning. "Let's see where the honey actually gets made."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Honeycomb Rooms
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, Finn and Nell found a whole wall of tiny rooms.

Each little room had six sides, like a small honey window.

"Whoa," said Finn, counting with his finger. "It's like a hundred tiny houses!"

"This is honeycomb," said Pip. "Bees build it from wax, made right inside their own bodies."

"Bees make their own wax?" asked Nell, amazed.

"From tiny spots on their tummies," said Pip. "Then they shape it into these six-sided little rooms."

Finn traced one room's edges slowly. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

"Six sides fit together perfectly," said Pip, "with no wasted space at all."

A bee landed close by and spread shiny nectar into one empty room.

"That's where the nectar waits to become honey," said Pip.

Nell traced a honeycomb shape in the air with one finger. "It looks like yellow lace."

"A bit like lace," said Pip, "but stronger. And a whole lot stickier."

Finn reached a hand toward it, then stopped himself, remembering. "Can I touch it?"

"Better to just look," said Pip gently. "It's sticky work, and it belongs to them."

Finn nodded, tucking his hands behind his back. "Looking is good too."

"Good listening, Finn," said Pip warmly. "Now watch closely. This next part is my favorite."

A gust of tiny wind rustled past their feet, out of nowhere.

"What's that?" asked Nell, holding down her hair.

"Wings," said Pip, grinning wide. "Lots and lots and lots of wings."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Fanning Wings
chapters.text:
Dozens of bees lined up beside the honeycomb, wings ready.

They flapped together, fast as can be. BUZZZZZZZZ!

"Why are they fanning?" asked Finn, holding his hair flat with both hands.

"The nectar is watery," said Pip. "Fanning dries it out, so it turns thick and sticky, like honey."

Nell watched the wings blur into one buzzing, golden cloud. "They're SO fast!"

"A bee's wings flap about two hundred times every second," said Pip. "That's what makes the buzzing sound you hear."

Finn tried flapping his own arms as fast as he could manage. He only made a few floppy waves.

"I can't go that fast!" he laughed, flopping onto the step.

"Nobody can," said Pip kindly, "except bees, and maybe hummingbirds."

Nell leaned close to a honeycomb room, careful not to touch. "It smells different now. Sweeter."

"That's the magic," said Pip. "Watery nectar slowly turning into real, true honey."

Finn sniffed the air too, nose wrinkling happily. "It smells like my toast at home!"

"Soon it will be," said Pip, giving a little wink.

The buzzing wind slowly settled and quieted down. The honey glistened, gold and thick in the light.

"Is it ready?" asked Nell, peeking closer.

"Almost," said Pip. "One more small step, and it will be ready for winter."

"Winter?" asked Finn, puzzled. "Why winter?"

"Come see," said Pip, "and I'll show you exactly why bees save it up."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Wax Lid
chapters.text:
A bee walked carefully along the honeycomb, patting a little wax lid over a full room.

"She's sealing it," said Pip. "A thin wax cap, to keep the honey clean and safe inside."

"Like a lid on a jar," said Finn, thinking of the glowing jar back home.

"Exactly like that," said Pip, nodding.

Nell counted the capped rooms one by one. "One, two, three... so many!"

"Bees fill hundreds of these little rooms," said Pip. "All that honey gets saved for later."

"Why save it?" asked Nell, tilting her head.

"In winter, flowers stop blooming," said Pip. "No nectar to collect anywhere. So bees eat the honey they saved all summer long."

Finn thought of his own kitchen pantry at home. "Like saving snacks for later!"

"Just like that," said Pip, smiling her warm little smile.

Nell patted a capped honeycomb room ever so gently. "Sleep tight, little honey."

Finn burst out laughing. "You're talking to honey now, Nell?"

"Why not?" said Nell, grinning. "It worked hard to get here."

Pip chuckled, a tiny buzzy giggle. "Well said, Nell. Honey really does work hard to get here."

Just then a new bee zoomed in through the door, wiggling and dancing in circles.

"Ooh, what's she doing?" asked Finn, pointing with both hands.

"That," said Pip, eyes sparkling, "is my favorite dance in the whole entire hive. Come and watch closely."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Waggle Dance and the Way Home
chapters.text:
The new bee wiggled in tiny figure-eight shapes, buzzing the whole time she danced.

"That's the waggle dance," said Pip. "A scout bee dances to tell everyone exactly where the best flowers are."

"She's dancing directions?" asked Finn, leaning in close.

"The wiggles and turns tell other bees which way to fly, and how far," said Pip.

Nell wiggled her own hips, giggling happily. "Like this?"

"Just like that," said Pip, laughing. "You'd make a fine scout bee, Nell."

Finn watched other bees copy the wiggle, then zoom straight out the door. "They're listening to her dance!"

"They sure are," said Pip, watching them go.

"Pip," said Finn, "how much honey does it take to fill my toast?"

Pip thought for a moment, counting on tiny bee claws. "It takes about twelve bees, working their whole lives, just to make one small spoonful."

Finn's eyes went wide as saucers. "TWELVE BEES FOR ONE SPOONFUL?!"

"That's a lot of buzzing work," said Nell, shaking her head slowly.

"Bees work hard so you can have sweet toast," said Pip. "Speaking of toast, I believe it's someone's bedtime."

The jar's golden glow shimmered softly all around them.

"Already?" said Finn, yawning despite himself.

"Thank you for showing us everything, Pip," said Nell, giving a tiny wave goodbye.

"Anytime, little flower-finder and little honey-lover," said Pip warmly. "Buzz off to dreamland, you two."

WHOOOOSH! The golden light swirled around them, and Finn and Nell grew back to their regular size.

They landed softly on their own bedroom carpet. The little honey jar sat quiet now, just one small golden drop left on its lid.

Finn rubbed his sleepy eyes. "Did that really just happen?"

Nell pointed down at a tiny yellow flower petal on the carpet, one that definitely had not been there before.

Finn grinned and tucked the petal carefully under his pillow, right next to his honey toast crumbs.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Buzz off to dreamland, little bees.

true_facts.text: A bee hive can hold thousands of bees — sometimes up to sixty thousand!
The queen bee lays eggs all day long, sometimes over a thousand in one day.
A bee sips sweet flower juice, called nectar, with a long curly tongue like a tiny straw.
Bees carry nectar home in a special honey tummy, different from their eating tummy.
Honeycomb rooms have six sides, and bees build them from wax made by their own bodies.
Bees fan watery nectar with their wings until it turns thick and sticky, like honey.
Bees seal full honeycomb rooms with a thin wax lid to keep the honey clean and safe.
Bees save up honey because in winter there are no flowers left to visit.
A scout bee does a wiggly waggle dance to tell other bees exactly where the best flowers are.
It takes about twelve bees working their whole lives to make just one small spoonful of honey.

new_recurring.rule: A small glass honey jar that glows gold and hums like bees whenever real curiosity calls at bedtime. It shrinks the children to match the size of the adventure and always returns them safely to their own bedroom floor when the lesson is…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Finn and Nell returned to their bedroom floor to find a tiny yellow flower petal on the carpet, which Finn tucked under his pillow before sleep.

story.title: Omar and the Hundred-Year Bike Ride
story.subtitle: A glowing wheel hub, nine stops in time, and one very good BMX bike.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wobbly Walking Bike (1817)
chapters.text:
Omar spun his pedals backward in the garage, practicing one more trick before bed. His BMX bike was supposed to be resting against the wall. Instead, the little metal hub in the middle of his back wheel started to glow gold.

"Ready to ride, Omar?" said a tiny voice.

A glowing face blinked up at him from the spokes. "I'm Hub," it said. "I live inside every bike ever made. Spin your pedals backward three times and I'll show you something."

Omar grinned and spun. **WHOOOOSH!** The garage melted into blue light.

They landed on a bumpy German road in **1817**. A man was walking a wooden two-wheeled machine, pushing the ground with his feet.

"Why isn't he pedaling?" Omar asked.

"Because there were no pedals yet," said Hub. "This is the **running machine**, built by **Karl von Drais**. You just run and roll."

Omar tried it. The handlebars turned just like his own bike's. "At least it steers right," he laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Bone-Rattling Ride (1860s)
chapters.text:
Cobblestones clattered under them as Hub spun the wheel forward in time.

"Why not just stick pedals on the wheel?" Omar asked, watching a rider wobble past.

"Somebody already thought of that," said Hub. "In the **1860s**, two Frenchmen, **Pierre Michaux** and **Pierre Lallement**, bolted pedals right onto the front wheel."

The new ride was called a **velocipede** — just a fancy word for an early pedal bike. Everyone called it the **boneshaker** instead, because the bumpy stone streets rattled your whole body.

Omar hopped on one. **BUMP BUMP BUMP!** His teeth chattered on every cobble.

"Okay," he laughed, "my bones officially feel shook."

Hub chuckled. "Lallement even got a patent for his pedal design in America, in **1866**."

"A patent?" Omar asked.

"A paper that says an idea is yours," said Hub.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel (1870s)
chapters.text:
A bike rolled by with a front wheel taller than Omar's dad.

"Whoa!" Omar said, craning his neck. "That wheel is huge!"

"This is the **1870s**," said Hub. "They call it the **penny-farthing**. One turn of the pedals and you fly, because the wheel is so big."

"Penny-farthing?" Omar tilted his head, then guessed. "Is that two old coins? A big one and a tiny one?"

"Exactly right," said Hub. "A big penny and a tiny farthing, just like the wheels."

A rider offered Omar a turn up top. Omar eyed the wobbly seat, way up high.

"If you stop too fast up there, you can tip right over the front," said Hub. "They call that taking a **header**."

Omar grinned and stepped back. "I'll just admire it from down here, thanks."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Bike That Finally Clicked (1885)
chapters.text:
A new bike rolled past with two wheels the exact same size.

"That looks normal," Omar said. "Finally."

"This is the **Rover Safety Bicycle**," said Hub, "built in **1885** by **John Kemp Starley**. A chain connects the pedals to the back wheel, just like yours."

Omar hopped on and pedaled. The chain spun. **CLICK-CLICK-CLICK!**

"No more giant wheel to fall off of," Omar said.

"Right," said Hub. "Lower and even wheels made it way safer. Pretty much every bike after this one copied the idea — even yours."

Omar patted his handlebars like they were old friends. "Nice work, bike ancestor."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Squishy Tire (1888)
chapters.text:
The road turned bumpy again, every wheel made of solid rubber.

"My teeth are rattling again," Omar groaned.

"Not for long," said Hub, pointing at a workshop. "In **1888**, a Scottish man named **John Boyd Dunlop** had an idea."

Dunlop wanted a smoother ride for his son's tricycle. He filled a rubber tube with air and wrapped it around the wheel.

Omar poked a finished tire. **SPLOOSH** — it squished under his finger, then bounced right back.

"It's like a balloon wrapped around the wheel!" Omar said.

"Exactly," said Hub. "Air-filled tires made every bump feel soft. Dunlop's company still makes tires today — maybe even on your dad's car."

Omar bounced the bike once more, grinning. "Best squish ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Everybody's Riding (1890s)
chapters.text:
They landed on a street packed with riders — and tons of them were women.

"Why so many bikes all of a sudden?" Omar asked.

"The **1890s** were the Golden Age," said Hub. "Millions of bikes got sold. And for women, a bike meant going wherever they wanted, whenever they wanted."

A famous rider named **Susan B. Anthony** once said riding a bike gave women more freedom than almost anything else in the world.

"But long skirts kept getting caught in the gears," Hub added. "So women started wearing **bloomers** — puffy, comfortable pants — instead."

Omar looked down at his own shorts, perfect for pedaling. "Comfortable clothes for riding? I get that completely."

He waved at a passing rider, who waved right back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Learned to Fly (1890s)
chapters.text:
A little shop sat crowded with wheels, chains, and metal tubes.

"Whose shop is this?" Omar asked.

"**Wilbur** and **Orville Wright**," said Hub. "They fixed and built bicycles in Dayton, Ohio, in the **1890s**."

In the back corner sat a strange wooden machine with wide, cloth-covered wings.

Omar pointed at the wings' frame. "Those look like bike spokes!"

"Sharp eyes," said Hub. "They used their lightweight bike tubes and spoked wheels to help build it."

"Build what, exactly?" Omar asked.

"An airplane," said Hub. "By **1903**, it actually flew."

Omar stared at the wings, then at his own bike's wheel. "From pedaling... to flying. That's wild."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Hill and the Race (1903–1930s)
chapters.text:
A steep hill rose in front of them. Omar's legs burned just looking at it.

"There's no way I'm pedaling that in one gear," he said.

"You won't have to, soon," said Hub. "By the **1930s**, bikes got **derailleurs** — little shifters that move the chain between gears, so hills get easier."

Omar found a lever, clicked it, and pedaled. The hill suddenly felt half as steep.

"Way easier!" he cheered.

At the top, a line of racers zoomed by in bright jerseys.

"That's the **Tour de France**," said Hub. "It started in **1903** and covers about **3,500 kilometers** across France — more than three weeks of pedaling."

Omar whistled. "That's basically every street in my whole city, times a thousand."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home, With Bumps and Dirt (1970s–Today)
chapters.text:
The ground turned to dirt, with jumps and bumps everywhere.

"Wait," Omar said, grinning wide. "I *know* this place."

"The **1970s**," said Hub. "Riders in the United States built small, tough **BMX** bikes for tricks and dirt racing, like yours. Around the same time, riders in Marin County, California, slapped wide, bumpy tires on bikes to ride rough mountain trails."

Omar spotted a dirt jump and couldn't resist. He pedaled hard, hit the ramp, and caught air. **WHOOOOSH!**

"PERFECT LANDING!" he shouted.

"There are over a **billion** bikes on Earth now," said Hub, "more than any other ride. In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities have more bikes than cars."

Then the dirt faded. Omar landed back in his garage, bike leaning against the wall, hub glowing one last time.

A tiny glowing spoke charm sat looped on his handlebars, warm and humming.

"Thanks, Hub," Omar whispered.

"Pedal on, dream on," Hub whispered back, and the glow faded to sleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Pedal on, dream on.

true_facts.text: The very first bike, called the **running machine**, had no pedals at all. Riders pushed it along with their feet in **1817**.
In the **1860s**, two Frenchmen bolted pedals onto the front wheel, making a bumpy ride called the **boneshaker**.
The **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, popular in the **1870s**.
It was named after two old coins — a big **penny** and a tiny **farthing**.
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the **Rover Safety Bicycle**, with two same-size wheels and a chain.
The safety bicycle's even wheels made riding much easier and safer than the wobbly penny-farthing.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** invented the air-filled tire, making bike rides much smoother.
Riding a bike gave women in the **1890s** new freedom to go wherever they wanted, as **Susan B. Anthony** once said.
**Wilbur** and **Orville Wright** ran a bicycle shop before they built the first successful airplane, which flew in **1903**.
By the **1930s**, bikes got gear-shifters called **derailleurs** to make hills easier to pedal up.
The **Tour de France** began in **1903** and today covers about **3,500 kilometers** across France.
**BMX** bikes, small and tough for tricks and dirt racing, became popular in the **1970s** in the United States.
Mountain bikes with wide, bumpy tires were built in the **1970s** in Marin County, California.
Today there are more than a **billion** bicycles on Earth — more than any other kind of vehicle.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A tiny fridge-magnet robot shows Ada how pulling and pushing really work.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Robot in the Fridge Magnets
chapters.text:
Ada lined up her fridge magnets on a cookie sheet, way past bedtime.

She built a wobbly robot: a head, two arms, a round tummy.

Then the tummy magnet buzzed. It glowed blue-green.

CLICK! A tiny robot popped up on two tiny legs.

"I'm Magna-Bot," it said. "I'm built from real magnets. Want to see my favorite trick?"

"Yes!" said Ada.

Magna-Bot pointed to his own back. "Every magnet has two ends, called poles — a north end and a south end. That's where the pull is strongest."

Ada flipped a magnet around. One side snapped on. The other side scooted away!

"Same ends push away," said Magna-Bot. "Different ends pull close. North and south always want to hug."

"Opposites attract!" Ada shouted, catching the runaway magnet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Invisible Push
chapters.text:
"Watch this," said Magna-Bot. He stood still near a paperclip on the rug.

The paperclip slid across the carpet all by itself and CLICKED onto his arm.

"You didn't even touch it!" said Ada.

"That's my magnetic field," said Magna-Bot. "It's the invisible space around a magnet. It can push or pull things without touching them."

Ada wanted to see it. Magna-Bot sprinkled tiny dark bits, like metal glitter, near himself. They curved into loopy lines from one end to the other.

"Whoa, it's like a rainbow made of metal dust!" said Ada.

She picked up her bendy fridge magnet. "Why does mine bend, but you don't?"

"Fridge magnets are soft rubber mixed with magnet powder," said Magna-Bot. "Bendy, and still sticky."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Tiny Spinning Teams
chapters.text:
"Why isn't my wooden block magnetic?" asked Ada, tapping it on Magna-Bot.

No click. No pull. Nothing happened.

"Good question," said Magna-Bot. "Everything is made of tiny bits, too small to see. Inside those bits are even tinier spinners. Each spinner acts like its own itty-bitty magnet."

"Tiny magnets inside tiny magnets?" Ada giggled.

"In wood, those spinners point every which way, so they cancel out," said Magna-Bot. "But in things like iron, whole teams of spinners line up, all facing the same way. That makes one big strong pull."

Ada lined up her toy robots, facing the same direction, like a parade.

"Like that!" said Magna-Bot. "When the teams line up, you get a real magnet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rock That Started It All
chapters.text:
Magna-Bot's tummy door glowed open, like a tiny window.

"Step through," he said. "I'll show you the very first magnet anyone ever found."

Ada peeked through and saw a rocky hill, long, long ago, near a place called Magnesia. A shepherd's iron staff stuck to a rock!

"That rock is called lodestone," said Magna-Bot. "It's a natural magnet, no robot needed. Some people think that's even where the word 'magnet' comes from."

The window shimmered and showed boats on a river.

"Over in China, people floated little lodestone needles on water," said Magna-Bot. "The needle always turned to point the same way. That was one of the very first compasses — a tool that shows you which way is north."

"A rock that's a map!" said Ada.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Earth, the Giant Magnet
chapters.text:
Back in her room, Ada spun a toy compass. The needle wiggled, then stopped, same direction every time.

"Why does it always point that way?" she asked.

"Because the whole Earth is a giant magnet," said Magna-Bot. "Deep, deep down, there's hot melted metal swirling around, and it makes Earth's own magnetic pull."

"Earth is a magnet?! That's huge!"

"The needle's north end gets pulled toward Earth's magnetic north, way up by the top of the globe," said Magna-Bot. "That's how sailors and hikers find their way, even in the dark."

Ada held the compass steady. "So I always know which way home is."

"Exactly," said Magna-Bot, spinning a happy little circle.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Snap! Two Magnets
chapters.text:
"What if I snapped you in half?" Ada asked, worried she'd hurt him.

"Try it on this bar magnet instead," said Magna-Bot, handing her a toy one.

Ada snapped it — CRACK — into two pieces.

She waited for one half to lose its pull. It didn't!

"Each new piece gets its very own north end and south end," said Magna-Bot. "Break a magnet, and you just get two smaller magnets, not one one-sided piece."

"Magnets don't share," Ada laughed. "They just multiply!"

She tapped a penny and a spoon against Magna-Bot. Nothing stuck.

"Not everything shiny is magnetic," he said. "Gold and silver don't stick, and neither does a soda can."

"So you're a picky sticker," said Ada.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Magnet You Can Switch Off
chapters.text:
Magna-Bot's eyes blinked like tiny lightbulbs. DING-DONG! A toy doorbell on Ada's shelf buzzed.

"That buzz happens because of a magnet too," said Magna-Bot. "Wrap wire into a loop, run electricity through it, and presto — you get an electromagnet. Flip a switch, and it turns on or off, just like that."

"On and off? Regular magnets can't do that!"

"Nope. That's why electromagnets lift giant cars at junkyards," said Magna-Bot, showing Ada a picture of a huge crane. "Flip the switch on, lift the car. Flip it off, and the car drops safely onto a pile."

"Can you be an electromagnet?" Ada asked.

Magna-Bot buzzed, and his glow flickered on, then off, then on again. "Only a little bit!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Cookie Sheet
chapters.text:
Ada yawned a giant yawn.

"One more thing," said Magna-Bot, shrinking back down to magnet-size. "Some animals — birds, sea turtles, even some fish — can feel Earth's magnetic field too. It helps them find their way on long, long trips, the same way your compass helps you."

"So turtles have compasses in their tummies?" Ada giggled.

"Something like that," said Magna-Bot.

He hopped back onto the cookie sheet and clicked into place among the other fridge magnets, his glow fading to a soft little shine.

Ada climbed into bed, thinking about poles and fields and tiny spinning teams, all lining up together.

"Night, Magna-Bot," she whispered.

The little magnet gave one last tiny blink, like a wink.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick with it, buddy!

true_facts.text: A magnet has two ends called **poles** — a north end and a south end — where the pull is strongest.
**Same ends push away, and different ends pull together** — opposites really do attract.
The invisible space around a magnet that pushes or pulls things is called its **magnetic field**.
Bendy fridge magnets are made of **soft rubber mixed with magnet powder**, so they can bend and still stick.
Magnets work because of **tiny spinners** inside everything, each acting like its own little magnet.
In things like wood, those tiny spinners point every which way, so wood isn't magnetic at all.
The first magnet people found was a rock called **lodestone**, discovered near a place called **Magnesia**.
Long ago in **China**, people floated lodestone needles on water to make the first **compasses**.
**Earth itself is a giant magnet**, made by swirling hot melted metal deep down inside it.
A compass needle always points toward Earth's **magnetic north**, which is how travelers find their way.
Snap a magnet in half and you don't get one half without pull — **each piece becomes its own full magnet**.
An **electromagnet** is made by wrapping wire into a loop and running electricity through it, and it can switch on and off.
Electromagnets are strong enough to let giant **cranes** lift old cars at junkyards.
Some animals, like **birds and sea turtles**, can feel Earth's magnetic field to help them travel long distances.

new_recurring.rule: A palm-sized robot built from Ada's own fridge magnets. He glows blue-green and buzzes CLICK to wake up, has a chest door that opens into a glowing window to show real history, and says 'Stick with it, buddy!' as his catchphrase. He…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ada falls asleep picturing poles and fields and tiny spinning teams, while Magna-Bot clicks back into place among the fridge magnets on her cookie sheet, glow fading to a soft shine.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow Hiding in the Mist
story.subtitle: A squirt of water, a flash of light, and the secret order of colors

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Mist That Turned the Lamp Into Colors
chapters.text:
Dev squeezed his water pistol one more time before bed. Priya was drawing a horse on her sketchpad.

A tiny mist floated past the lamp. SPLISH!

The air flickered — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple, all at once.

"Whoa," said Dev. "My water pistol made a rainbow!"

A speck of light popped out of the mist. It spun like a tiny spark, with a grin.

"Not just you," the speck said. "Light did that. I'm Ray. I live wherever light meets water."

Priya poked her pencil at him. "You're a drop of light?"

"Close enough," said Ray. "Want to see how a rainbow really gets made?"

Dev squirted once more. The mist thickened into a shimmery cloud and scooped them up.

WHOOOOSH!

They landed inside something round and clear, with walls like glass.

"Where are we?" asked Priya.

"Inside a raindrop," said Ray. "This is where the magic starts."
chapters.shout_line: MY WATER PISTOL MADE A RAINBOW!

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Bending Like a Bent Straw
chapters.text:
A beam of golden sunlight zoomed straight at them.

"Duck!" shouted Dev, though light can't actually hurt anybody.

The beam hit the edge of the raindrop and bent sideways, like a straw bending in a glass of juice.

"Why'd it bend?" asked Priya.

"Light slows down when it goes from air into water," said Ray. "That slow-down makes it bend. Grown-ups call that **refraction**. You can just call it the bendy trick."

Dev tried bending his own arm like the light did. He wobbled and plopped onto the glassy floor. Everybody laughed.

"Watch," said Ray. "The light bends once coming in, bounces off the back wall of the drop, then bends again on the way out."

Priya traced the beam's path with her finger, like drawing lightning. "It's like a slide with a bounce in the middle!"

"Exactly," said Ray. "Keep watching. It's about to get colorful."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Rainbow Hiding in White
chapters.text:
The beam hit the back wall of the drop. SPARKLE!

Suddenly it wasn't one beam anymore. It was seven.

"Whoa, it split!" said Dev.

Priya squinted, thinking about her paints. "Wait. Sunlight looks white. But it's hiding all the colors inside?"

"Good eye," said Ray. "White light is really every color mixed together. Each color bends a slightly different amount, so the raindrop pulls them apart — like a comb pulling apart tangled hair."

"So the raindrop is basically combing light?" asked Priya.

"Best way I've heard it put," said Ray.

Dev squirted his water pistol straight through the sunbeam. A tiny rainbow flickered across his own hand.

"I made one too!" he shouted.

"You both did," said Ray. "Light plus water plus a little bending, every single time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Red Outside, Purple Inside
chapters.text:
Seven ribbons of light floated in front of them, lining up like kids for a photo.

"Who goes first?" asked Dev.

"Red always does," said Ray. "It bends the least, so it lands on the outside edge."

"And purple bends the most," guessed Priya, "so it gets squished to the inside?"

"Exactly right," said Ray, clapping her spark-hands together.

Dev tried to remember the whole order. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue... then two more I forget."

"Indigo and violet," said Priya. "Indigo's a deep blue-purple, and violet's just purple. Put it together: **Roy G. Biv**. Like a guy's name!"

"Roy G. Biv," Dev repeated, giggling. "Sounds like someone who'd win a pie contest."

"A very colorful pie," said Priya.

Ray laughed so hard a little spark fell off her. "Remember him and you'll never forget the order."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sun Behind You, Rain Ahead
chapters.text:
The raindrop walls melted away. They stood in a wet backyard instead, sunshine warm on their backs.

"Hey, there's no rainbow," said Dev, looking around.

"Check where the sun is," said Ray.

Priya turned in a circle. "It's behind us. And the rain is... in front?"

"Rain is basically Dev's spray, right there," said Ray, pointing at a sprinkler.

Dev aimed his pistol into the sunlight. A rainbow arced across the grass.

"There it is!" he cheered.

"Fun fact," said Ray. "A rainbow is really a full circle. We only see half of it, because the ground blocks the rest."

Priya looked down at the grass under the arc. "So the rest is hiding... underground?"

"Sort of," said Ray. "Which is why pilots get the best view of all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Whole Circle From Way Up High
chapters.text:
Ray scooped them onto a cloud shaped suspiciously like an airplane wing.

"Seatbelts," joked Priya, even though they were sitting on fluff.

They rose above the yard. Below them, the rainbow wasn't an arc anymore.

"It's a whole circle!" shouted Dev. "Like a hula hoop made of colors!"

"From up here, there's no ground blocking it," said Ray. "People in airplanes sometimes see the full circle."

Priya reached toward it. Her hand passed right through.

"Here's a weird one," said Ray. "The rainbow you see isn't the same one Dev sees. You're each standing in a slightly different spot, so the light bounces to your eyes at a different angle."

Dev frowned. "So every rainbow is kind of... mine?"

"And kind of hers," said Ray. "Everybody gets their own private rainbow."

Priya grinned. "Finally, something of mine Dev can't borrow."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Two Rainbows and a Ghostly Night One
chapters.text:
Back on the grass, Priya spotted something above the first rainbow.

"There's a second one!" she said. "But it's... backwards?"

Ray nodded. "Sometimes light bounces twice inside the drops before it leaves. That flips the colors. The second rainbow is fainter, with purple on the outside this time."

Dev squirted a huge cloud of mist, trying to make his own double rainbow. Two faint arcs blinked into his spray.

"Double rainbow, double me," he said proudly.

"Rainbows show up in all kinds of wet places," said Ray. "Misty mornings. Waterfalls. Even your garden hose."

"What about at night?" asked Priya.

"Moonlight can make one too," said Ray. "It's called a **moonbow**. Moonlight is much dimmer than sunlight, so a moonbow usually looks pale and white, almost ghostly, instead of colorful."

"Spooky," said Dev, "but the good kind of spooky."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Man With the Glass Triangle
chapters.text:
Ray led them to a dusty old room full of books and glass.

A man in old-fashioned clothes stood by the window, holding up a triangle-shaped piece of glass.

"That's **Isaac Newton**," whispered Ray. "In the **1660s**, he shone sunlight through that glass triangle, called a prism, and split it into the very same rainbow colors."

Newton turned and noticed them. "Light isn't plain white, children. It's secretly every color, hiding together."

"We know!" said Dev. "We just watched a raindrop do that exact trick!"

Newton chuckled. "Then you've already learned my whole secret."

Priya asked the question she'd been saving. "Is there really a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow?"

"That one's just a fun old story," said Ray gently. "You can never actually reach the end of a rainbow, because it moves whenever you move. People have told that tale for ages anyway, because it's such a good one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Bedroom Floor
chapters.text:
The mist swirled, and WHOOOOSH, they landed right back on the bedroom carpet.

Dev's water pistol lay beside him, one last drop balanced on its tip.

Priya looked at her sketchpad. Without meaning to, she'd drawn a perfect arc of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple.

"When did I draw that?" she asked.

"Maybe some of the trip followed you home," said Ray, now just a tiny sparkle on the lamp.

Dev squeezed his pistol one last time. A small misty rainbow glowed for a second, right over their blanket.

"Bend it, split it, see it shine," said Ray, with a sleepy flicker. "That's the whole secret."

Priya tucked the sketchpad under her pillow. Dev set the water pistol on the nightstand, careful not to spray the lamp again.

"Night, Dev," said Priya. "Thanks for the squirt that started it."

"Night, Priya," said Dev. "Thanks for drawing it."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Bend it, split it, see it shine.

true_facts.text: Light bends as it goes into a raindrop, bounces off the back wall, then bends again coming out.
Light slows down and bends when it moves from air into water — that bendy trick is called **refraction**.
Sunlight looks white, but it's really every color mixed together, and raindrops pull the colors apart.
The rainbow's colors always line up the same way: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet — **Roy G. Biv**.
Red ends up on the outside of a rainbow because it bends the least, and violet ends up on the inside because it bends the most.
To see a rainbow, you need the sun behind you and rain (or spray) in front of you.
A rainbow is really a full circle — we just see half, because the ground blocks the rest.
From an airplane, with no ground in the way, people sometimes see a whole circle rainbow.
Every person actually sees their own rainbow, because the light bounces to each person's eyes at a slightly different angle.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow appears above the first one, with its colors flipped backwards.
Rainbows can show up in mist, waterfalls, and garden hose spray, and moonlight can even make a pale, ghostly one called a **moonbow**.
In the **1660s**, **Isaac Newton** used a triangle-shaped piece of glass to split sunlight into rainbow colors.
The old story about a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow is just a fun tale — you can never actually reach the end, since it moves whenever you move.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Priya and Dev return to their bedroom carpet, where Priya finds she has unknowingly drawn a perfect rainbow on her sketchpad and Dev's water pistol leaves one last glowing rainbow mist over their blanket before Ray fades into a sparkle on the lamp.

story.title: Jack and Ellie Dive with the Shark Lady
story.subtitle: A nighttime swim through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Tooth
chapters.text:
Jack lay on his bedroom floor, flipping through his shark book for the hundredth time. Around his neck hung a real shark tooth, a souvenir from his very first snorkeling trip.

Ellie flopped down beside him, humming her mermaid song. "Sharks are okay," she said. "But mermaids are better."

"Sharks were here LONG before mermaids," Jack said. "Before everything."

That is when the tooth around his neck began to glow bright green. It HUMMED like a seashell held up to your ear, only louder.

"Jack," Ellie whispered, "it's doing a thing."

The glow spread across the carpet like water, and the carpet turned into cool, dark sea. A woman swam up wearing old-fashioned diving goggles, smiling like she had been waiting for them.

"I'm Eugenie," she said. "Folks call me the Shark Lady, because I have spent my whole life studying sharks."

"Are you real?" Ellie asked.

"Real as this tooth," said the Shark Lady, tapping Jack's necklace. "Sharks don't have bones like you do. Their skeletons are made of **cartilage** — bendy stuff, like the squishy part of your ear. That's why old shark skeletons almost never last."

"So how do we know about old sharks at all?" Jack asked.

"Follow me," she said, "and I'll show you sharks from **more than 400 million years ago** — swimming here before there were even dinosaurs, or trees."

Jack grabbed Ellie's hand. Together they kicked off the carpet and into the glowing water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Before the Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
The water here was murky and green, and strange shadowy shapes drifted past.

"Those are some of the very first sharks," the Shark Lady said. "This ocean is **400 million years** old. No dinosaurs yet. Not even trees on land."

Ellie squinted at the shadows. "They don't look very scary."

"Most weren't big," said the Shark Lady. "But they were tough enough to still have relatives swimming today."

Jack noticed something glinting on the sandy bottom — little pointed shapes, scattered like lost buttons.

"Teeth!" he said, scooping one up. "Lots of them!"

"Good eye," said the Shark Lady. "Since shark skeletons are bendy and don't last, almost everything we know about ancient sharks comes from teeth left behind in the sand and rock. Teeth are hard. They stick around."

Ellie picked up a tiny curved one and held it like a treasure. "This is better than any seashell."

"Keep looking," the Shark Lady said, grinning. "There's a much bigger tooth waiting up ahead — and it belonged to the biggest shark that ever lived."

Jack's eyes went wide. He grabbed Ellie's hand again, and they swam toward the deeper, darker water, teeth clinking in Ellie's cupped palms like coins.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
A huge shadow slid across the sea floor, bigger than their whole house.

Ellie froze. "Is it going to eat us?"

"No need to worry," the Shark Lady said gently. "That's just a memory. This giant shark, called **megalodon**, isn't around anymore — it's **extinct**, which just means every single one of them is gone now. This happened millions of years ago."

Jack spotted something huge and triangle-shaped poking out of the sand. He tugged it free. It was a tooth as long as his whole hand.

"WHOA," Jack breathed. "That's bigger than my foot!"

"That's a real megalodon tooth," said the Shark Lady. "Almost everything we know about this giant shark comes from teeth just like that one, since its bendy skeleton didn't last."

Ellie peeked out from behind Jack's shoulder, brave again now that the shadow was only a memory. "So it can't get us?"

"Not even a little bit," the Shark Lady promised.

"That might be a bit of an exaggeration, how huge people say it was," she added, "but one look at this tooth tells you it was REALLY big."

"THAT TOOTH IS AS BIG AS MY HAND!" Ellie shouted, holding it up next to her own fingers.
chapters.shout_line: THAT TOOTH IS AS BIG AS MY HAND!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
The water brightened, and something enormous glided out of the blue — longer than a school bus, with a mouth wide enough to swallow a beach ball.

Ellie grabbed Jack's arm. Then she noticed the giant shark wasn't opening its mouth to bite anything. It just drifted, calm and slow, like a gentle whale.

"That's a whale shark," the Shark Lady said. "The biggest fish in the whole world, over **40 feet long**. But don't worry — it only eats tiny floating bits of food called plankton, by gulping water through that huge mouth and filtering the tiny bits out."

"It's like a giant, gentle vacuum," Jack said.

Ellie reached out her hand but didn't touch — the Shark Lady had already told them to only ever watch, never touch. "It's so soft-looking," she whispered instead.

"Some whale sharks live to be **100 years old or even more**," said the Shark Lady. "Longer than almost any other fish."

"A hundred!" Jack said. "That's older than my great-grandpa."

The whale shark swam a slow loop around them, close but careful, its tail swishing gently like a wave goodbye.

"IT'S GENTLE!" Ellie shouted, waving both arms at the giant fish as it drifted off into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A sleek gray shadow cut through the water, faster and sharper than the whale shark had been.

"Great white shark," the Shark Lady said. "They can grow up to about **20 feet long**."

Jack pressed close to look, careful to keep his distance. "Its teeth look like little triangles with bumpy edges."

"Sharp eyes," said the Shark Lady. "Those bumpy edges are called serrated — like a steak knife — perfect for catching seals and fish."

"Doesn't it run out of teeth?" Ellie asked, remembering the loose ones scattered in the sand earlier.

"Never," said the Shark Lady. "Sharks grow new teeth their whole lives. Thousands of them. New ones keep moving forward to replace any that fall out or wear down."

"So that's why we found so many on the ground back there," Jack said, snapping his fingers.

"Exactly," said the Shark Lady. "You two are turning into proper shark detectives."

The great white swam a slow circle, gave one last flick of its tail, and vanished into the deep blue, leaving only a trail of bubbles behind.

Ellie counted on her fingers. "So it's basically got a never-ending smile."

Jack laughed so hard he swallowed a mouthful of pretend seawater.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Hammer-Headed Swimmer
chapters.text:
Something strange swam toward them — a shark with a head shaped like a flat hammer, an eye poking out on each end.

"That's a hammerhead," the Shark Lady said. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it can see almost all the way around itself."

"Like having eyes on both sides of a ruler," Jack said, holding his hands out wide.

Ellie tilted her head, copying the shark's shape. "Why does it need to see so much?"

"It helps find food hiding in the sand," said the Shark Lady. "And sharks have another trick, too. Little jelly-filled dots on their snouts feel tiny tingles — electricity — made by other animals' bodies. Even a fish holding perfectly still can't hide from that."

"So it's like it can feel heartbeats?" Jack asked.

"Close enough," said the Shark Lady.

The hammerhead swung its strange head side to side, scanning the sandy bottom, then swam off in a smooth S-shape.

"IT SEES EVERYWHERE!" Ellie shouted, spinning in a circle to copy it, until she got dizzy and grabbed Jack's shoulder to steady herself. He caught her, laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Walking on the Reef
chapters.text:
The water grew shallow, warm, and bright with coral shaped like brains and fans.

Jack spotted a small, speckled shark creeping along the coral using its fins like little paddles. "Is it... walking?"

"That's an epaulette shark," said the Shark Lady. "It really can walk across the reef with its fins, even in and out of tide pools. It can even survive for hours with hardly any oxygen — the air we need to breathe."

"No way," Jack said, crouching to watch it waddle along.

Nearby, another shark lay completely still on the sandy floor.

"Is that one asleep?" Ellie whispered, worried it might be hurt.

"Resting," said the Shark Lady. "That's a nurse shark. It can pump water over its gills while lying still, so it doesn't need to keep swimming to breathe, like most sharks do."

Ellie relaxed, relieved. "So it's just having a lazy day."

"Exactly," laughed the Shark Lady.

Jack tried waddling along the sand on his hands and knees, copying the little walking shark, until Ellie laughed so hard bubbles shot out of her mouth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Mermaid's Purses
chapters.text:
Ellie spotted something odd caught in the seaweed — a small, dark, leathery pouch with curly strings at each corner.

"What IS that?" she asked, nose nearly touching it.

"That," said the Shark Lady, "is a mermaid's purse."

Ellie gasped. "A REAL mermaid's purse?"

"Sort of," the Shark Lady laughed. "It's actually a shark egg case. Some sharks lay their babies inside pouches like this one, instead of having live babies the way many other sharks do."

"IT'S A MERMAID'S PURSE!" Ellie shouted, cradling it gently in both hands.

Jack rubbed his palm along a nearby shark's side as it swam past, careful and slow. "Its skin feels like sandpaper!"

"That's because of thousands of tiny tooth-shaped bumps covering its skin," said the Shark Lady. "They help it swim smoothly through the water."

"Sharks really do have teeth everywhere," Jack said, shaking his head.

"Sharks sit at the very top of the ocean's food chain," the Shark Lady added. "That means they help keep every other animal's numbers healthy and balanced — like referees of the sea."

"Are they dangerous to us, though?" Jack asked.

"Barely ever," she said. "Shark bites on people are extremely rare. It's people who need to be gentler with sharks, not the other way around."

Ellie tucked the little purse carefully back into the seaweed, right where she'd found it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
The water began to glow green again, swirling like it had at the very start.

"Time to go home," the Shark Lady said. "But before you do — did you know there are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks swimming in our oceans right now?"

"Five hundred!" Jack said. "We only met about seven!"

"Plenty more adventures left, then," she said, winking.

"How do YOU know so much about sharks?" Ellie asked her.

"I spent my whole life studying them," said the Shark Lady. "I even proved that sharks are curious, clever animals that can learn tricks, just like a puppy can."

"That's so cool," Jack said.

The green glow swallowed them up, and when it faded, Jack and Ellie were back on the bedroom carpet, exactly where they'd started.

Jack's necklace had stopped glowing. But resting beside it on the carpet was one small, curved tooth, and tucked right next to that, a tiny leathery mermaid's purse.

Ellie picked up the little purse and held it against her cheek. "Mermaids and sharks," she said. "Maybe they both win."

"Deal," said Jack, yawning.

They climbed into their beds, tooth and purse tucked safely on the nightstand between them.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.

true_facts.text: A shark's skeleton is made of bendy **cartilage**, not hard bone — like the squishy part of your ear.
There are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks swimming in the oceans today.
Sharks were swimming in the oceans **more than 400 million years ago**, before dinosaurs or even trees.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world, over **40 feet long**, but it only eats tiny floating bits of food.
The great white shark can grow up to about **20 feet long** and has rows of bumpy-edged teeth.
Megalodon was a giant shark from millions of years ago that isn't around anymore, known mostly from its **huge fossil teeth**.
Because bendy shark skeletons don't last, almost everything we know about ancient sharks comes from their teeth.
Sharks grow thousands of teeth over their lives, with new ones always moving forward to replace old ones.
Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny tooth-shaped bumps that make it feel like sandpaper.
Sharks can feel tiny tingles of electricity from other animals' bodies through jelly-filled dots on their snouts.
The epaulette shark can actually walk across the reef using its fins, and can survive a long time with very little air.
The hammerhead shark's wide head spreads its eyes apart so it can see almost all the way around itself.
Some sharks lay their eggs inside leathery pouches nicknamed **mermaid's purses**.
Sharks sit at the top of the ocean's food chain, helping keep all the other animals balanced and healthy.

story.title: Nora and the Glowing Tile of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A hushed, hopscotching journey through a buried Roman town.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Hummed
chapters.text:
Nora sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor. Tiny colored tiles were spread around her like candy. She was making a mosaic coaster, piece by piece. It was way past bedtime, but she just needed one more tile.

She picked up a small gold square. It felt warm in her hand. Then it began to hum, soft and low, like a sleepy bee.

"Ooh," Nora whispered. "That's new."

The tile glowed brighter. Light spilled out, swirling into a window right there on her carpet. A tiny voice crackled from the glow.

"Hello, tile-sorter," it said. "I am Tessera. I am made of a hundred old tiles, and I know a hundred old places."

Nora grinned. "Can you show me one?"

"I can do better," said Tessera. "Step through. I'll pull you home the second you want to come back."

Nora took a breath and stepped into the light. "A window!" she gasped. The carpet disappeared. Sunshine and noise rushed in instead.

She was standing on a busy stone street. Carts rattled by. People called out, selling bread, olives, and fish.

"Welcome to Pompeii," said Tessera, floating beside her like a glowing kite. "A real town, in what is now Italy, near a city called Naples."

"It's loud," Nora laughed. "How many people even live here?"

"Somewhere between eleven thousand and fifteen thousand," said Tessera. "Shops, bathhouses, a theater — a whole busy town."

Nora noticed water trickling nearby, running through a stone fountain on the corner. "Where does the water come from?"

"Pipes," said Tessera, "running under the streets, bringing water to fountains all over town. Pretty clever, for so long ago."

Nora dipped her fingers in the cool water. "Where does the name Pompeii come from, anyway? It's a funny word."

"Nobody's completely sure," said Tessera, "but it might come from an old word meaning five — maybe five little villages that joined into one big town."

"Five friends making one town," said Nora. "That's kind of nice."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Stepping Stones and Rattling Carts
chapters.text:
A cart rolled past, wheels splashing through a puddle. Nora jumped back just in time.

"Careful!" said Tessera. "Pompeii streets get messy."

Nora looked down. Big flat stones poked up out of the street, spaced apart like stones in a creek.

"These must be for crossing without getting muddy," she said, "like turtle-back stones in a stream."

She hopped from stone to stone, testing her idea. Her sneakers stayed perfectly dry.

A cart rattled right through the gaps between the stones, its wheels rolling smoothly through the spaces she had left empty.

"You're exactly right," said Tessera. "The street was built so people could cross without stepping in mud, and carts could still roll straight through the gaps."

"It's basically hopscotch," said Nora, hopping back across. "Ancient hopscotch."

"That is exactly what it is," said Tessera, sounding delighted.

A bell clanged somewhere nearby. Nora looked up a wide street, toward a huge, round building rising over the rooftops.

"What's that giant round thing?" she asked.

"Follow the sound," said Tessera. "Let's find out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Big Round Building
chapters.text:
Nora jogged toward the roar of a cheering crowd. The round building got bigger and bigger as she got closer.

"This is the amphitheater," said Tessera. "A giant oval stadium for watching shows, built around seventy years before the eruption. It's one of the oldest ones ever found."

Nora tipped her head back, staring up at the stone rings of seats. "It's like a stone stadium," she said. "Bet from above it looks like one big mosaic circle."

"You and your mosaics," said Tessera, laughing. "But you're right. Rings and rings, all fitting together."

They climbed partway up the stone steps. Below, crowds filled the seats, clapping and cheering for the show.

"People came from the whole town to watch here," said Tessera. "Games, contests, big performances — it was the place to be."

Nora counted the rows with her finger, tracing circles in the air. "Seven rings," she said. "Eight. It just keeps going."

"That's the fun of a really good circle," said Tessera. "It never seems to end."

Nora laughed. "Just like my mosaic coaster. I keep adding one more tile."

"Speaking of tiles," said Tessera, glow flickering, "there's something you should see on the walls nearby. Come on."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Words on the Wall
chapters.text:
They walked along a sunny street. Painted words covered the walls, bright red and black.

"What's all this writing?" asked Nora, tracing a letter with her finger.

"Ancient advertising," said Tessera. "People painted messages right on their houses — shop signs, election slogans, even jokes. Like a wall full of posters."

"So someone's wall was basically a bulletin board," said Nora. "That's kind of brilliant."

"The Romans thought so too," said Tessera.

Then Nora spotted something odd. A thin curl of smoke rose from a mountain far past the rooftops.

"Tessera, look," she said, pointing. "Is that smoke?"

Tessera's glow flickered. "The mountain," it said quietly. "Vesuvius. It's a volcano — a mountain that can spit fire, smoke, and rock. It's starting to wake up."

"Is everyone going to be okay?" Nora asked.

"Everyone here is safe right now," said Tessera gently. "But it's time for us to watch from somewhere safer. Hold on."

The glowing thread around Nora's wrist tugged. In an instant, the street folded away, and they stood high above the whole bay, watching from a calm, misty distance.

"There," said Tessera. "Now we can watch safely, just like a writer named Pliny the Younger did, long ago. He stood across the bay like this, and wrote down everything he saw, in two careful letters."

"Like a reporter," said Nora.

"Exactly like a reporter," said Tessera. "Thanks to him, we know this happened on one single day — August 24, in the year 79."

Below, ash began to fall, soft and gray, like dirty snow.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Buried in a Blink
chapters.text:
Nora watched the gray snow fall and fall, covering roofs, streets, and stepping stones.

"It happened fast," said Tessera. "Ash and rock piled up high — in some places, as tall as a two-story house."

"That's so much," Nora said softly.

"It covered everything so quickly," said Tessera, "that it froze the whole town in place. Bread stayed right in its oven. Paintings stayed bright on walls. Even writing on walls stayed exactly as it was."

"Like pausing a movie," said Nora.

"A very long pause," said Tessera. "Almost one thousand seven hundred years long."

Nora was quiet a moment, watching the gray curtain settle over the rooftops below. "Did everyone get away safe?" she asked.

"Many people left the town in time," said Tessera. "It's part of why we know so much about how they lived — because the town stayed so carefully kept, like a secret, until people found it again."

Nora nodded slowly. "Okay," she said. "Let's go see what they found."

The light around them shimmered, and the gray scene melted away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sister Town by the Sea
chapters.text:
The light settled into a smaller, breezier town, right along the water.

"This is Herculaneum," said Tessera. "A smaller town nearby, buried by the very same eruption."

"Looks different," said Nora, pointing at dark, solid rock covering everything instead of gray ash.

"Different kind of material here," said Tessera. "It kept things even better in some spots — wooden furniture, even old rolled-up paper called scrolls, stayed in one piece."

"Scrolls? Like ancient books?" Nora asked.

"Exactly like ancient books," said Tessera. "Rolled-up paper, with writing inside. Imagine finding one of those after all this time."

"Can we get a closer look?" Nora asked, stepping toward a doorway. Its wooden frame still stood, dark and shiny like stone.

"It's kind of amazing," she whispered. "Like the sea town kept its own secrets."

"Every buried town keeps a few," said Tessera. "Come on. Let's jump ahead — way, way ahead — to when people finally found them again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Digging Up a Lost Town
chapters.text:
The light swirled, and the world changed again. Now there were tools, ropes, and workers with dusty hands.

"The year is 1748," said Tessera. "Workers digging here found old walls, buried right where the town had been hiding."

"After all that time?" Nora said. "That's so long!"

"Almost seventeen hundred years," said Tessera. "People had nearly forgotten Pompeii was even here."

People who dig up old things to learn about the past are called archaeologists, and a few of them worked nearby, brushing dust from a half-uncovered wall.

Nora crouched close. Something round sat half-buried in the ash.

"Wait — is that bread?" Nora said, pointing.

One of the workers lifted it gently. "Well spotted," she said. "A whole loaf, still marked with the baker's knife lines, like it just came out of the oven."

"It's been down there the whole time," Nora whispered, "just waiting."

Further along, Nora noticed a smudge of red peeking from under crumbling plaster. "There's color under there," she said.

A worker brushed it clean. Red and gold bloomed across the wall.

"A fresco," said Tessera. "A painting made right on wet plaster, so the color sinks in and lasts. There's a whole house nearby with walls full of mysterious painted scenes. Nobody is fully sure what the pictures mean, but they're beautiful."

"I want to make a fresco someday," said Nora.

"You basically already do," said Tessera. "Every mosaic is its own kind of picture that lasts."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Mountain That's Still Watching
chapters.text:
The dusty dig faded, and a new scene bloomed: tall fences, clear paths, and crowds of visitors with cameras.

"This is Pompeii today," said Tessera. "People come from everywhere to walk these streets. Millions of visitors, every single year."

Nora looked around at the ancient walls, still standing in sunshine. "It's like a museum you can walk right through."

"It's protected now," said Tessera, "by a worldwide group that looks after extra-special places. They call it a World Heritage Site."

Far off, over the rooftops, the mountain stood quietly, its top still sometimes smoking.

"Is it still... a volcano?" Nora asked, remembering the gray snow.

"It is," said Tessera. "Vesuvius is still active, and scientists keep a close watch on it, every single day, just to be safe."

Nora nodded, satisfied. "Good," she said. "Somebody should keep an eye on it."

"Somebody always does," said Tessera.

The light began to dim, curling gently back toward its tile shape.

"Time to go home," said Tessera. "You've still got a coaster to finish."

The carpet rushed back beneath her. Nora blinked, back in her own room, the little gold tile warm and quiet in her palm.

She looked down at her half-finished mosaic coaster. Then, carefully, she pressed one more tile into place — a tiny gold square, right in the center, like a little glowing window of its own.

"Goodnight, Pompeii," she whispered. "Thanks for the five little villages."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Sleep tight, and keep your tiles bright.

true_facts.text: **Pompeii** was a real town in what is now **Italy**, near the city of **Naples**.
Somewhere between **eleven thousand and fifteen thousand** people once lived in busy Pompeii.
The town had pipes running under its streets, bringing water to **fountains** all over town.
Streets had **raised stepping stones**, so people could cross without mud, while carts rolled through the gaps between them.
The town's **amphitheater** was built around **seventy years before the eruption**, one of the oldest ones ever found.
A young writer named **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two careful letters about it.
**Mount Vesuvius** erupted on **August 24, in the year 79**.
The eruption buried the town under ash and rock as tall as **a two-story house** in some places.
The ash fell so fast it froze the town in place — **bread stayed in its oven**, and paintings and writing stayed exactly as they were.
Nearby **Herculaneum** was buried by the same eruption, but kept even wooden furniture and rolled-up paper called **scrolls**.
Pompeii was **rediscovered in 1748**, when workers digging there found old buried walls.
Colorful wall paintings called **frescoes** were found, including a house full of mysterious painted scenes.
**Mount Vesuvius** is still an active volcano, and scientists keep a close watch on it today.
Pompeii is protected as a **World Heritage Site**, visited by **millions of people** every year.
