story.title: Maya and the Great Space Race
story.subtitle: From a beeping beach ball to a handshake among the stars.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: A Puddle That Beeped (1957)
chapters.text:
Maya was lying on her bedroom floor, drawing boats, every pencil line a little damp from swim practice. Her hair was still wet, twisted up in a towel on her head. Her swim coach had made them practice backstroke for a whole hour, and her arms still ached in a nice way. She liked backstroke best, since it let her watch the clouds go by. A little puddle had dripped off her towel and onto the rug, right beside her sketchbook.

It had been three quiet nights since Barnacle waved his flipper at her, right when the last rivet clanged into place on that big hungry bridge. Maya still remembered the sound of it.

Then the puddle went *BEEP*.

Maya froze mid-stroke, pencil hovering over a half-finished sailboat. The puddle beeped again — slow, steady, patient, like a clock that refused to be ignored. Two whiskers poked up through the water. Then a round, gray, dripping face.

"All aboard, Maya," said Barnacle the harbour seal, shaking water droplets off his nose and onto her drawing. "You're just in time for the loudest beep in history. Seal of approval, if I do say so myself."

"What's beeping?" Maya asked, scooting closer on her knees.

"A little round ball called **Sputnik 1**," Barnacle said. "On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union shot it way up into the sky, higher than any airplane. It became the very first man-made **satellite** — that's a machine that circles all the way around Earth instead of ever falling back down."

Maya leaned over the puddle. A tiny point of silver light bounced across the water.

"It's so small!" she said.

"About the size of a beach ball," said Barnacle. "Only **58 centimeters** wide, with four long metal whiskers sticking out the back. All it did, all day and all night, was send out one simple beep that people everywhere could pick up on their ordinary radios."

Maya counted along with the beeping. "Beep... beep... beep. It sounds like a heartbeat!"

"That's exactly what people thought back then too," Barnacle said, grinning his whiskery seal grin. "Want to go hear it from closer up?"

Maya didn't need asking twice. She took a deep breath, the same one she took before diving off the high board at the pool, and dove headfirst into the puddle.

**SPLOOSH!**

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika Goes Around (1957)
chapters.text:
They tumbled out of the dark and landed with a soft thump inside a small, round metal capsule. A dog barked happily behind a little round window, tail thumping the wall. The capsule smelled faintly of metal and dog treats, though Maya couldn't say why she knew what dog treats smelled like inside a spaceship.

"Who's that?" Maya asked, pressing her face close to the glass.

"That's **Laika**," said Barnacle. "On **November 3, 1957** — just one month after Sputnik's beep — the Soviet Union sent her up inside a ship called **Sputnik 2**. She became the very first living creature ever to circle all the way around Earth."

"But why her?" Maya asked. "Why a dog?"

"Scientists needed to find out if a living creature could really survive a trip like this," Barnacle said. "Laika went first, so people could follow safely after her."

Maya pressed her nose flat against the glass. Below them, blue ocean slid by, then green land, then ocean again.

"Hey," Maya said slowly, squinting. "I saw that exact same coastline already. That curvy bit, right there!"

"Did you now?" Barnacle's eyes twinkled, the way they always did when he already knew the answer.

Maya watched carefully. Sure enough, the same wiggly shoreline rolled past a second time, right on schedule.

"We're going in a big circle, all the way around the whole Earth!" Maya said.

"That's called an **orbit**," Barnacle said. "Going around and around, instead of flying off or falling back down. You figured that out all by yourself, you know. Out of this world, wouldn't you say, for a first try?"

Maya grinned and pressed her palm flat against the window, right over the smudge where Laika's own paw had fogged up the glass.

"Hi, Laika," Maya whispered. "You're really, really brave."

The little dog wagged her tail so hard her whole back end wiggled, and somewhere far below them, a million radios buzzed with the news.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: America Catches Up (1958)
chapters.text:
Next, the puddle-light dropped them onto a sandy launch pad, lit up with spotlights even though it was clearly nighttime. People in short-sleeved shirts ran back and forth clutching clipboards, talking too fast for Maya to follow.

"Whoa," Maya said. "Why's everybody panicking?"

"The whole country got a big shock from that beep you heard," Barnacle said. "So America hurried to catch up, fast."

Maya hopped from foot to foot, the way she did waiting her turn at the diving board.

A man near a tall silver rocket began counting down from ten, loud through a crackly speaker. Maya joined in without even being asked, shouting right along with him.

"Ten! Nine! Eight!"

On "one," the rocket roared off the pad in a sheet of orange fire, shaking the sand under their feet.

"That's **Explorer 1**," Barnacle said once the roar had faded. "It launched on **January 31, 1958**. And it found something nobody even knew was there — a giant, invisible ring of space weather wrapped clear around Earth, like a hula-hoop too big to ever see."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A hidden ring? Right now? Wrapped around us?"

"Right now," Barnacle said. "Nobody had ever spotted it before Explorer 1 went looking for it. Rocket science," he added, "isn't nearly as hard as it sounds, apparently — just ask Explorer 1."

Later that same year, on **October 1, 1958**, the United States built a brand-new team just for jobs exactly like this one. They called it **NASA**.

Maya saluted the rocket as it shrank to a tiny dot in the dark sky. "Good job, Explorer 1. Good job, me, for counting."

Barnacle chuckled. "Don't think I didn't notice that part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Trip Around (1961)
chapters.text:
They popped up beside a small, round capsule with glowing windows. Inside, a man was smiling so widely his whole face had crinkled up around his eyes.

"Who's that?" Maya whispered.

"**Yuri Gagarin**," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, he became the very first human being ever to fly into space. He went all the way around Earth once, in about **108 minutes**, aboard a ship called **Vostok 1**."

Maya counted on her fingers, the same way she counted laps at swim practice. "That's less time than my whole swim class takes!"

"Faster than any lap you've ever swum," Barnacle agreed. "He was the first **cosmonaut** — that's simply what the Soviet Union called its space fliers, the same way America called its own space fliers **astronauts**."

Gagarin gave a thumbs-up through the round window. Maya thumbs-upped him right back, grinning.

They drifted onward, and the dark sky slowly turned into a stage covered in flags, with microphones everywhere. A tall man in a sharp suit stepped up to speak, and the crowd around him clapped so loudly Maya had to cover her ears for a second.

"That's President **Kennedy**," Barnacle said. "On **May 25, 1961**, he stood up in front of his whole country and dared them to do something enormous."

"What?" Maya asked.

"Land a person on the Moon," Barnacle said, "and bring them home again, safe and sound, before the end of the decade."

Maya tipped her head back and looked up at the pale, round moon hanging in the dark sky above them. She pointed straight at it with her whole arm.

"Let's go there next!" she shouted.

"All aboard, Maya," Barnacle laughed, clapping two flippers together, which for a seal counted as thunderous applause. "Looks like you just picked our very next stop."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The First Woman Up There (1963)
chapters.text:
Before they even got close to the Moon, Barnacle tugged Maya gently sideways, toward a small, bright capsule tumbling slowly in the dark.

"One quick stop first," he said. "You'll want to see this."

Inside the little window, a woman with short dark hair waved down at them, grinning from ear to ear.

"That's **Valentina Tereshkova**," Barnacle said. "On **June 16, 1963**, she became the very first woman ever to fly in space, circling Earth aboard a capsule called **Vostok 6**."

Maya pressed both hands flat against the glass. "A girl went to space? All by herself?"

"A girl went to space," Barnacle confirmed. "All by herself."

"Could I go to space?" Maya asked, almost shy about it.

Barnacle's whiskers twitched into a wide, warm grin. "Why ever not? Valentina didn't start out training to fly rockets, you know. She worked hard at an ordinary job first, and one day, her chance came along."

Maya stood up a little straighter, the exact same way she did before diving off the high board. She decided right then that she would learn every single swim stroke there was, just in case space ever needed a strong swimmer too.

She waved at Valentina with both arms until her shoulders ached.

"Keep going, Valentina!" she shouted.

"Not bad for somebody who used to work in a factory," Barnacle said, nodding with real respect. "Me, personally, I've always preferred working underwater."

Maya giggled. Valentina waved back twice with one gloved hand, and then her little capsule spun on, carrying her around the whole world again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Longest Ten Minutes (1965)
chapters.text:
Next, they floated gently beside a chunky metal ship, bigger up close than it had looked from far away. A figure in a puffy white suit drifted just outside it, turning slow lazy circles, tethered by one long cord.

"Whoa," Maya said. "He's just... floating out there, all by himself!"

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," Barnacle said. "On **March 18, 1965**, he became the very first person ever to leave his ship completely and float free in open space. We call that a **spacewalk**."

"But how does he get back?" Maya asked, a little worried. "What if he just floats away?"

"Good question," Barnacle said. "Want to guess?"

Maya studied the long cord trailing behind him, drifting lazily in the dark. "That rope! It's like when we tie our boat to the dock, so it never floats away on us!"

"Exactly like that," Barnacle said, clearly impressed. "It's called a **tether**. Leonov floated out there for about **ten minutes**, tied on the whole entire time, then pulled himself back home, hand over hand, safe and sound."

Maya grinned, proud of herself. "I knew it! Boats taught me that."

Barnacle, for his part, insisted he'd been doing spacewalks his whole life, underwater, where it hardly ever counted.

Leonov tumbled in one last lazy circle, waved a puffy glove at them, and pulled himself steadily back toward the open hatch.

"See?" Barnacle said gently. "Safe and sound, just exactly like I told you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
They landed near the tallest rocket Maya had ever seen in her whole life, so tall its very top disappeared into the clouds.

"That's the **Saturn V**," Barnacle said. "**363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty, if you stood her right on top of her own pedestal."

Maya grabbed her sketchbook from her back pocket — she never went anywhere without it — and quickly drew the rocket next to a tiny statue for comparison. "It's like ten of me, stacked up, times ten more!"

"Close enough," Barnacle chuckled.

The enormous rocket thundered off the pad with a sound Maya felt rumbling in her own teeth.

**WHOOOOSH!**

Days later — though in Barnacle's puddle-time, it felt like only a blink — they hovered above gray dust and round craters.

"On **July 20, 1969**," Barnacle said, "astronaut **Neil Armstrong** became the very first person ever to walk on the Moon. He called it 'a giant leap for mankind.'"

Maya watched a single bulky white boot press down slowly into the gray dust, leaving a perfectly clear print. Dust puffed up around his boot in slow, silent clouds.

"It's just like my footprints in wet sand!" she said.

"Only this print might stay right there for a very, very long time," Barnacle said. "There's no wind up here at all to ever blow it away."

A second astronaut climbed carefully down the ladder to join him. "That's **Buzz Aldrin**," Barnacle said. "And way up above you both, circling all alone in a ship called **Columbia**, is **Michael Collins**."

Maya looked straight up and waved hard at the tiny dot passing silently overhead. "Hi, Michael! You're doing great too, you know!"

"Being alone up there might sound lonely," Barnacle said gently, "but Michael Collins once said it didn't feel that way at all. He had the whole universe for company, and two friends walking below him. Over the next few years, eleven more astronauts would follow these very same footprints across the Moon."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Rescue (1970)
chapters.text:
The next ship Maya saw looked tired somehow, its lights flickering weakly in the dark.

"In **1970**, this ship, called Apollo 13, was flying toward the Moon when a tank of oxygen suddenly broke apart," Barnacle said, his voice calm and steady. "That left the astronauts inside with a very big problem indeed."

Maya's stomach did a little flip. "Are they okay? Are they going to be okay?"

"They are," Barnacle said quickly. "Because they were clever, every single one of them. Down on Earth, engineers grabbed whatever spare parts they happened to have lying around, and built a fix, piece by piece, like solving a puzzle with absolutely no instructions."

Maya thought of the time her little sailboat's rope had snapped clean in half out on the lake, and how her dad had tied it right back together using an old shoelace from his sneaker.

"Like when you fix something using whatever's lying around?" she asked.

"Exactly like that," Barnacle said, nodding. "The astronauts used spare parts from their very own ship to fix their air, and every single one of them made it home safe."

Somewhere far below, a room full of people in white shirts cheered so hard several of them cried.

Maya let out a long breath she hadn't even noticed she was holding. "Phew."

"Phew is exactly right," Barnacle agreed warmly. "Sometimes the very best part of a space story isn't the going up at all. It's everybody getting safely home again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: A Handshake in Space (1975)
chapters.text:
One more light glowed up ahead of them — two ships, one from each side of the long race, drifting slowly closer and closer together.

"This is our very last stop," Barnacle said. "On **July 17, 1975**, an American ship and a Soviet ship **docked** together up in space — that means they locked together snugly, like two puzzle pieces finally finding their match."

Through the little window, Maya watched two astronauts reach out and shake hands, right there, floating between the bright stars.

"After all that racing," Maya said softly, "they're friends now?"

"After all that racing," Barnacle agreed, "they shook hands, and smiled for all the cameras back home. That's exactly how the whole Space Race ended."

Maya smiled so hard her cheeks hurt. She thought about Sputnik's steady beep, and Laika's wagging tail, and Valentina's wave, and Neil's dusty footprint, all in one happy jumble. She reached out and shook Barnacle's flipper right there in the capsule's open hatch, nice and firm.

"Deal," she said.

The stars blurred together, and then — **SPLOOSH!** — Maya tumbled back through the puddle and landed softly on her own bedroom rug, pencil still somehow in her hand.

The puddle had almost completely dried up by then. Floating in the very last little bit of it was a tiny paper boat Maya didn't remember folding at all — with two tiny stick-figure astronauts drawn right on its sail, shaking hands.

Barnacle's whiskers poked up through the puddle one very last time. "All aboard, Maya. Same time tomorrow?"

"All aboard," Maya whispered back, grinning ear to ear.

Then the puddle dried up completely, and her whole room went quiet, and warm, and still.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard, Maya — sleep tight among the stars.

story.title: Zara and the Humming Rock
story.subtitle: A rockhound's trip to the fire inside the Earth

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Humming Rock
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime, but Zara was still sorting rocks on her rug.

Smooth ones in one pile. Sparkly ones in another. Bumpy ones in the last.

She picked up her newest rock, found on the beach with Mom. It was grey, light as a cork, and covered in tiny holes.

It felt warm. Then it started to hum, low and buzzy, like a bee trapped inside.

"Rocks don't hum," Zara whispered.

The holes glowed soft orange, like tiny campfires.

POP! A small, friendly face blinked open in the rock. "They do if they used to be lava," it said. "Hi. I'm Pip."

Zara's mouth dropped open. "You're really from a volcano?"

"Sure am," said Pip. "Want to see where rocks like me are born?"

Zara didn't even look at her sparkly pile. "YES, please."

Orange light filled her room. The rug turned to warm, black ground under her sneakers.

They stood near a smoking mountain. It smelled like a thousand matches.

"So what IS a volcano?" Zara asked.

"It's a hole in Earth's crust," said Pip. "Crust just means the hard outside skin of our whole planet, like the peel on an orange. Way underground, it's so hot that rock melts. That melted rock is called **magma**. When it pushes up through the hole and comes out, people call it **lava** instead."

Zara spotted a smooth, shiny, black rock by her shoe.

"Pip! Was THIS lava once?" she asked, scooping it up.

Pip's glow brightened. "Good eye. That cooled down and went hard, just like a melted crayon turns solid again."

Zara grinned and tucked it in her pocket. "I'm basically a volcano detective now."

"Rock-solid plan," said Pip. "Let's go find more clues."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring Around the Ocean
chapters.text:
The ground gave a gentle shiver under Zara's sneakers. Not scary. More like a shiver.

"Pip, why do volcanoes bunch up in some spots?" Zara asked. "Why not just anywhere?"

Pip's glow flickered into a glowing map, floating like a light-up puzzle.

"See these lines?" said Pip. "Earth's crust isn't one piece. It's broken into giant puzzle pieces called **plates**. They float around, super slow, on the hot stuff below. Where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other, volcanoes like to pop up."

Zara traced a huge curved line with her finger. It looped almost all the way around an ocean.

"Whoa, it's shaped like a horseshoe!" she said.

"Good eye again," said Pip. "That's the Ring of Fire. It loops around the Pacific Ocean, and it holds about three out of every four active volcanoes on the whole planet."

Zara counted glowing dots along the ring. So many were bunched up in one curvy little country.

"This place has a TON of them," she said, pointing.

"That's Indonesia," said Pip. "It has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

Zara puffed out her cheeks. "I'd never run out of volcanoes to visit there."

"You'd need bigger sneakers," said Pip.

Zara giggled, and the glowing map folded itself into a paper airplane, zooming toward the horizon.

"Follow that map!" said Pip, and they ran.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Hotspot That Never Moves
chapters.text:
They landed on black sand that crunched like cereal under Zara's sneakers.

"Where even are we?" she asked, shielding her eyes from an orange glow ahead.

"Hawaii," said Pip. "But here's the mystery. Hawaii isn't on the edge of a plate at all."

Zara tilted her head. "Then how does it have volcanoes?"

"There's a **hotspot** under here," said Pip. "That just means a spot deep down that stays super hot and stuck in one place, even while the plate above slides over it, kind of like a candle under a moving cake."

Zara watched glowing orange lines creep across black rock, slow as spilled syrup.

"Is that lava?" she gasped.

"That's Kilauea," said Pip. "It's one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. It has been erupting on and off for decades."

Zara counted on her fingers. "That's longer than Mom's whole life!"

"Yep," said Pip.

Zara pointed. "Why's the lava moving so slow? It's not even scary. It's kind of... pretty."

"Exactly," said Pip. "This kind of eruption is usually gentle, not a big explosion. That's why people can watch it safely from far away, like us."

Zara sat on a cool patch of rock to watch the glowing river. "I could watch this forever," she said.

"Careful," said Pip. "You'll turn into a rock yourself if you sit still too long."

Zara jumped up laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Shield and the Party Hat
chapters.text:
As they walked, Zara noticed a giant, wide mountain rising behind them. It wasn't pointy at all. It looked like a shield lying flat on the ground.

"Pip, that mountain's shape is funny," Zara said. "It's not like the drawings in my book."

"That's Mauna Loa," said Pip. "It's the biggest active volcano on Earth, if you count how much rock it's made of. It rises over four thousand meters above the sea."

Zara whistled. "That's not funny. That's HUGE."

"Volcanoes come in different shapes," said Pip. "Wide ones with gentle slopes, like this, are called **shield volcanoes**, shaped like a warrior's shield. Tall, steep, pointy ones are called **stratovolcanoes**, like a party hat. Mount Fuji in Japan is one of those."

Zara grabbed a stick and drew both shapes in the black sand: one low and wide, one tall and pointy.

"So it's like volcano families," she said. "The flat cousins and the pointy cousins."

"Never heard it put that way," said Pip, "but I'll allow it."

Zara patted the wide mountain like it was a sleeping dog. "Good shield volcano," she said.

Pip's glow wiggled, which Zara had learned meant he was laughing.

"Come on, rock detective," said Pip. "Next stop's a pointy cousin. This one's story is almost two thousand years old."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Man Who Wrote It Down
chapters.text:
The ground turned to warm stone steps. A pointy mountain stood across a sparkling bay, puffing a thin trail of smoke.

A man in a long robe stood nearby, scribbling fast, glancing up at the mountain again and again.

"Who's that?" Zara whispered.

"That's Pliny the Younger," said Pip. "He's watching this mountain, Vesuvius, from across the water. In the year **79**, it exploded, burying two whole Roman towns, Pompeii and Herculaneum, under thick ash."

Zara's eyes went wide. "Whole towns? With houses and everything?"

"Whole towns," said Pip. "But here's the neat part. Pliny wrote down everything he saw, in letters to a friend. He described it so well that scientists still use his notes today. Big explosive eruptions like that one are now called **Plinian** eruptions, named after him."

Zara watched the man finish a line, then look up and squint.

"He's basically the first-ever volcano reporter," Zara said.

"Nice way to put it," said Pip.

Zara waved at the distant mountain, staying back with Pip, just watching like Pliny did. "Thanks for writing it down," she called, even though she knew he couldn't hear her, two thousand years away.

"Why'd you say that?" asked Pip.

"Because now I get to visit and know what happened," said Zara. "That seems worth a thank-you."

Pip's glow warmed up, soft and golden. "Rock detective with a heart. Let's keep moving."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Bang Heard Around the World
chapters.text:
A deep BOOM rattled Zara's teeth, even though no mountain was in sight.

"Whoa! Where did THAT come from?" she said, hands over her ears.

"That's an echo," said Pip, "of something that happened on an island called Krakatoa, back in **1883**. It exploded so loudly, people heard it about three thousand miles away, on a tiny island called Rodrigues."

Zara tried to picture that. "That's like yelling in my backyard, and someone hearing it clear across the whole country!"

"Pretty much," said Pip.

The scene shifted. Cold wind replaced warm air. Grey waves crashed below, and smoke puffed up from under the water itself.

"Now we're somewhere chilly," Zara said, hugging her arms.

"Iceland," said Pip. "It has tons of volcanoes because here, two of Earth's plates are pulling apart, instead of pushing together."

Right then, a burst of steam and rock shot up from the sea.

"Pip! Is the ocean making a new ROCK?" Zara shouted.

"Better," said Pip. "It's making a whole new island. In **1963**, an underwater volcano here kept erupting until a brand-new island popped out of the sea. They named it Surtsey."

Zara's jaw dropped. "A volcano can just make LAND?"

"From nothing," said Pip, "but hot rock and time."

Zara watched the baby island steam in the cold wind. "I want to name the next one," she said.

"Get in line," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Summer That Didn't Come
chapters.text:
The wind turned icy again. Old-fashioned houses stood around them, with fields of brown, droopy crops.

"Is it winter?" Zara asked, confused. "The trees look like summer trees."

"It's supposed to be summer," said Pip. "This is **1816**, the year people called the Year Without a Summer."

"Why?" Zara asked. "Where'd summer go?"

"The year before, in **1815**, a volcano called Tambora, in Indonesia, had the biggest eruption anyone's ever recorded," said Pip. "All that ash floated way up into the sky and spread around the whole world, blocking some of the sun's warmth."

Zara looked at the grey sky. "So one volcano messed up summer for EVERYONE?"

"Pretty much," said Pip. "Crops had trouble growing. People remembered that cold, strange year for a long time."

Zara shivered and tugged her sleeves down over her hands.

"That's wild," she said, "that something in one place can mess with weather everywhere."

"The whole planet's connected," said Pip. "Like one big, rocky, breathing thing."

Zara looked at the frosty summer field once more, then turned to Pip.

"Okay," she said. "Take me somewhere warm again. Please."

Pip chuckled, and the icy field melted into golden light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
Warm light faded into daylight, and Zara found herself looking up at a huge, snow-capped mountain.

A man with a backpack and notebook stood nearby, pointing a little device at the mountain's side.

"Who's that?" Zara asked.

"David Johnston," said Pip. "A scientist who studies volcanoes. He's watching this one closely, to help warn people if it gets dangerous."

"Is it going to erupt?" Zara asked, taking half a step back.

"Not right this second," said Pip gently. "We're just visiting a memory of **May 18, 1980**. Watch, but from a safe distance, like David did."

Right then, the whole side of the mountain slid away in a massive landslide, the biggest ever recorded. A moment later, the mountain blew out sideways in a huge cloud.

"WHOA!" Zara yelped, but Pip's glow wrapped around her like a cozy blanket.

"We're safe," said Pip. "We're just watching, from far away, like you'd watch fireworks."

When the dust cleared, Zara gasped. "The top of the mountain is just... gone!"

"The blast blew off about **1,300 feet** of the summit," said Pip. "That's taller than the tallest skyscrapers, gone in moments."

Zara stared at the new, shorter mountain. "That's wild. And kind of sad for the mountain."

"Scientists like David study volcanoes just like this one," said Pip, "so they can warn people early and keep everyone safe."

Zara nodded slowly. "I like that job. Volcano watcher."

"You're already halfway there, rock detective," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home, With a New Rock
chapters.text:
"Pip, is every trip going to end with a big mountain?" Zara asked, giggling, as the ground firmed up under a grassy field full of steaming pools.

"Not always," said Pip. "This one's hiding its whole volcano UNDER the ground. It's called a **supervolcano**, just means a giant, extra-powerful volcano. This one's at Yellowstone."

"Is it gonna blow up?" Zara asked, eyebrows raised.

"Nope," said Pip. "Its last huge eruption was about **640,000 years ago**. Scientists watch it closely, and right now, there's no sign it's waking up soon."

Zara relaxed. "Okay, good. How DO scientists watch, anyway?"

"Machines called **seismographs**," said Pip, "feel tiny shakes in the ground, too small for us to notice. Satellites way up in space check if the ground is puffing up like a balloon. Both are early clues a volcano might be getting ready."

Zara nodded. "Like a volcano's heartbeat monitor."

"Exactly like that," said Pip, clearly impressed.

The scene shifted one last time, to red, dusty ground under a pink sky.

"Where are we NOW?" Zara asked, looking at nothing but rust-colored dirt.

"Mars," said Pip. "See that huge bump on the horizon? That's Olympus Mons, the biggest volcano anyone's found in the whole solar system. It's about thirteen and a half miles high, almost three Mount Everests stacked up."

Zara tried to imagine climbing that and gave up immediately. "No thank you."

Pip laughed. "Fair. One more thing before home. All that ash volcanoes make breaks down into amazing dirt. **Fertile** means it's perfect for growing plants. That's why farmers still live near volcanoes, even knowing the risk."

Zara thought about that. "So volcanoes build stuff AND grow stuff. Not just boom stuff."

"Rocks are complicated," said Pip. "Kind of like people."

Orange light swirled around them, and the red dust melted back into Zara's soft bedroom rug.

Zara blinked. Her rock piles sat right where she'd left them.

Pip's glow dimmed to a cozy flicker in her hand. "Good trip?"

"Best one yet," Zara said, yawning hugely.

She pulled the smooth black rock from her pocket, the one that used to be lava, now cooled and hard, and set it proudly on her nightstand like a tiny trophy.

"I'm keeping this one right here," she said.

"Good choice," Pip murmured, his glow fading to a sleepy ember.

Zara climbed into bed, her new rock standing guard beside her, and closed her eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Rock on.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is a hole in Earth's crust where hot stuff from underground can escape.
Melted rock is called **magma** underground, and **lava** once it flows out.
The **Ring of Fire** is a horseshoe-shaped loop that holds about three out of every four of Earth's active volcanoes.
**Indonesia** has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes grow over a **hotspot**, a super-hot spot deep down that stays in one place.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been erupting on and off for decades.
**Mauna Loa** is the biggest active volcano on Earth, rising over four thousand meters above the sea.
Wide, gentle volcanoes are called **shield volcanoes**; tall, pointy ones are called **stratovolcanoes**.
In the year **79**, Vesuvius erupted and buried the towns of **Pompeii and Herculaneum** under thick ash.
**Pliny the Younger** watched and wrote about the eruption, so big explosive eruptions are now called **Plinian** eruptions.
**Krakatoa's** 1883 eruption was so loud it was heard about **three thousand miles** away.
In **1963**, a brand-new island named **Surtsey** rose from the sea near Iceland.
On **May 18, 1980**, Mount St. Helens had a giant landslide and then erupted.
Volcanic ash breaks down into **fertile** soil, which is why farmers often live near volcanoes.

story.title: Ben and the Pixel Guide: A Video Game History Adventure
story.subtitle: One glitchy screen takes Ben all the way back to the very first video game ever played.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Green Dot That Bounced (1958)
chapters.text:
Ben was building a pixel pig in his Minecraft world, one tiny block at a time. Snout. Ears. A curly pink tail. It was way, way past bedtime, but the pig needed its tail just right.

His screen flickered. Black, then green, like an old TV that lost its signal.

A small blocky shape popped onto the screen, built out of glowing pixels. It waved both square arms.

"Hiya," it said. "Name's Blip. Wanna see where games came from? Like, the very first one ever?"

Ben sat up straight. "Games have a *before*?"

"Everything does," said Blip. "Follow the green dot."

The screen filled with a round glowing circle, like a tiny TV with no corners.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," said Blip. "A science tool that draws wiggly lines on a round screen. A scientist named **William Higinbotham** used one to make a game, back in **1958**."

A green dot bounced back and forth over a flat line, like a tiny ball over a net.

"It's called **Tennis for Two**," said Blip. "People played it for fun at a science lab called **Brookhaven**, on a day when visitors came to look around."

Two knobs popped up on the screen. Ben grabbed one and turned it. The dot swooped upward.

"It's like... table tennis," Ben said slowly. "But on a screen!"

He turned the knob again. **BOOP.** The dot bounced back the other way.

"You got it," said Blip. "A lot of people say that might be the very first video game anybody ever played just for fun."

Ben kept bouncing the dot, faster and faster, until it zipped clean off the edge of the screen in a long green streak.

"Whoa — where'd it go?" Ben asked.

Blip grinned, all pixels. "Follow it, and find out."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Rocket Fight (1962)
chapters.text:
Ben's screen filled with stars. Two tiny spaceships floated among them, shooting little dots back and forth.

A glowing star sat right in the middle, tugging at both ships like a magnet.

"This is **Spacewar!**," said Blip. "Made in **1962**, by a student named **Steve Russell** and a bunch of his friends."

"On what?" Ben asked. "There's no controller."

"A computer called the **PDP-1**," said Blip. "Big as a fridge. One of the very first computers anywhere in the whole world."

Ben's eyes went wide. "They made a GAME. On a fridge. For fun. At school?"

"Yep," said Blip. "Nobody told them to. They just wanted to see if they could."

Right then, one of the little ships drifted too close to the glowing star.

"It's gonna get pulled in!" Ben shouted. He grabbed the stick that popped up in front of him and yanked the ship sideways.

**WHOOOSH.** The ship zoomed clear, just in time.

"Nice flying," said Blip. "Steve and his friends put that star there on purpose, so it would pull ships in if you weren't careful. Made the game trickier."

Ben grinned and flew a loop all the way around the star, just for the fun of it.

"This is way better than homework," he said.

"Everything's better than homework," said Blip. "C'mon. Next stop."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box (1972)
chapters.text:
The screen glowed to show a cluttered room, wires everywhere, bits of tape stuck to a wooden box.

A man sat hunched over it, flipping switches one at a time.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," said Blip. "Some people call him the father of video games."

"What's he building?" Ben asked. "A robot?"

"Nope," said Blip. "A **Brown Box**. An idea for a game you could play on your very own television. Nobody had ever done that before."

Ben leaned in close. The box had switches and dials, but no screen of its own.

"Does it plug into a TV?" Ben asked. "Like, ANY TV?"

"Yep," said Blip. "A few years later, in **1972**, it came out for real, under a new name: the **Magnavox Odyssey**. The very first home video game console ever made — a box that plugs into your TV and lets you play games right there in your living room."

Ben flipped the little switch. Two small white squares popped onto the screen, bouncing a tiny white dot between them.

"Whoa," Ben said. "That's it? That's the start of EVERY console I've ever played?"

"Every single one," said Blip. "They all say thank you to this box."

Ben reached out and patted the box gently, like it was a good dog.

"Good box," he said. "I want a Brown Box too."

"You basically have one," said Blip. "It's called your TV."

Blip laughed so hard its pixels wobbled sideways.

chapters.heading: Level 4: Pong and the Quarter Jam (1972–1977)
chapters.text:
Next, Ben found himself standing beside a buzzing arcade machine, lights flashing red and blue. A line of people waited behind him, tapping their feet.

**CLUNK.** A coin dropped in. The machine went *bloop*.

"This is **Pong**," said Blip. "Made by **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**. They started a company called **Atari**. Same year as the Odyssey — **1972**."

Ben peeked inside the little coin slot. It was packed to the very top, coins spilling onto the floor.

"It's jammed!" Ben said. "Too many quarters!"

"That's the story people love to tell," said Blip. "Might be a LITTLE bit of a tall tale, if we're honest. But it shows you just how much people loved this game, right from the start."

Ben grabbed the round paddle knob and gave it a spin. **BLOOP. BLOOP.** A little white square bounced between two lines, back and forth.

"It's just like Tennis for Two," Ben said, "but in an arcade, with real quarters!"

"Good eye," said Blip. "Now fast forward five years."

The screen flickered to show a flat plastic rectangle with a label on it.

"The **Atari 2600**," said Blip. "Came out in **1977**. Instead of one game stuck inside the machine forever, you could pop in different **cartridges** — little plastic game boxes that slide in and out — and play something totally new."

Ben slid a cartridge into the slot like a puzzle piece. **CLICK.**

"It's like swapping to a brand new Minecraft world!" Ben said.

"Kind of like that," said Blip. "Same machine. Different adventure every time."

chapters.heading: Level 5: Space Bugs and a Pizza (1978–1980)
chapters.text:
Rows of blocky alien bugs marched across the top of the screen, beeping lower with every step they took.

"Uh oh," said Ben. "Are they gonna win?"

"Only if you let them," said Blip. "Dodge 'em."

Ben grabbed the controls and zipped his little cannon side to side along the bottom. **PEW! PEW!**

"This is **Space Invaders**," said Blip. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**, for a company called Taito. When it came out, people everywhere went completely wild for it — everybody wanted a turn."

Ben blasted the very last alien bug. **POP!** The screen cleared, and a little cheering sound rang out.

"Nice shooting," said Blip. "Ready for something round?"

The screen changed. A yellow circle with a wedge cut out of it went chomping along a maze of dots.

Ben squinted at the shape. "That looks like... a pizza. With a slice missing!"

"Good guess," said Blip. "The man who made this game in **1980**, **Toru Iwatani**, might have gotten the idea from a real pizza that was missing a slice. This is **Pac-Man**, made for a company called Namco."

Ben steered Pac-Man around a tight corner, gobbling up a whole row of dots.

"CHOMP CHOMP CHOMP," Ben said out loud, right along with the game.

Blip's pixels bounced up and down like it was laughing too hard to sit still.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Buried Treasure (1983)
chapters.text:
The screen went bumpy all of a sudden, like riding a bike over gravel.

"What happened?" Ben asked.

"In **1983**, stores got flooded with way too many games, and a lot of them were rushed and not very good," said Blip. "People stopped buying as many. Folks call it the video game **crash** — not a car crash, just a big, sudden drop in how many games people bought."

The screen showed a sandy desert in New Mexico, with big piles of dug-up dirt.

"People say a bunch of unsold game cartridges got buried out here," said Blip. "Including copies of a game based on the movie E.T."

"Buried? Like actual treasure?" Ben asked.

"Diggers actually went looking, and found some, back in **2014**," said Blip. "So that part turned out to be true."

A toy shovel appeared in Ben's hand. He dug into the pixel dirt. **SCRITCH. SCRITCH.**

He pulled out a dusty old cartridge and held it up like buried treasure.

"Found one!" Ben yelled.

"Games had a rough year," said Blip, "but they weren't done. Not even close."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Jumping Plumber and the Falling Blocks (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
A gray rectangle console popped onto the screen, with a little gray controller plugged in beside it.

"This is the **NES**," said Blip. "Nintendo's console, from **1985**. It came packed together with a game that helped bring video games back to life in America."

A pixel plumber in a red cap and blue overalls hopped onto the screen.

"That's **Mario**," said Blip. "Designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto**, in **1985**. Probably the most famous character in all of gaming."

Ben grabbed the controller and pressed a button. The plumber leaped clean over a pixel turtle.

"Nice hop!" said Blip.

"I KNEW it," Ben said. "Mario's been around since before my mom was even — wait, how old is my mom?"

Blip just laughed and didn't answer.

The screen shifted again. Falling blocks of different shapes dropped slowly from the top, one after another.

"Ooh, I know this one!" Ben said. "Tetris!"

"Made in **1984**," said Blip, "by a scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov**, at a computer center in Moscow."

Ben spun a block sideways and slid it into a narrow gap. **THUNK.** A whole row lit up and vanished.

"It's kind of like building with blocks," Ben said, "except they disappear when you do it just right."

"Sounds familiar," said Blip, nodding toward Ben's half-built pixel pig, still waiting back home.

Ben pumped his fist. "Pixel plumbers AND falling blocks. Best level ever."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Blue Spikes and Shiny Discs (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
A blue blur zipped across the screen so fast it left a streak of light behind it.

"Whoa, slow down!" Ben laughed.

"That's **Sonic the Hedgehog**," said Blip. "A company called Sega made him in **1991**, fast on purpose, to race against Mario."

Ben grabbed the controller. Sonic zoomed through a loop so quick the ground blurred. **ZOOOOM.**

"I can't even see where he's going!" Ben said, grinning ear to ear.

The screen changed to show a shiny silver disc, spinning gently in the air.

"In **1994**, a company called Sony made a console called the **PlayStation**," said Blip. "It used **CDs** instead of cartridges — shiny discs like this one — which let games look and sound fuller than ever before."

Ben spun the disc on one finger like a tiny plate.

"Careful with that," said Blip, grabbing it before it could wobble off his finger.

Next, the screen showed two computers sitting side by side, linked together by a long wire.

"In **1993**, a game called **Doom** let people play against each other on separate computers hooked up together," said Blip. "People called it a LAN party — everybody brings their own computer to one room and plugs in to play together."

"That sounds like a sleepover," Ben said, "except everybody brought a computer instead of a sleeping bag."

"Exactly like that," said Blip.

chapters.heading: Level 9: Back to the Blocks (2006–2015)
chapters.text:
The screen showed people waving little white remotes at their TV, swinging their arms like they were really playing tennis.

"That's the **Wii**," said Blip. "Nintendo's console from **2006**. You swing the controller like you're really doing the move, and the game feels it happen."

Ben swung an invisible remote with both hands and nearly knocked his lamp clean off his nightstand.

"Whoops," he said, catching it just in time.

Then the screen turned green and blocky, just like Ben's own world.

"Wait, I know this one," Ben said, sitting up straight. "This is MINECRAFT!"

"Made in **2011**, by a game maker in Sweden named **Markus 'Notch' Persson**," said Blip. "It went on to become the best-selling video game of all time."

Ben puffed up proudly. "I KNEW it was the best one."

Last of all, the screen showed a big building with a glowing glass case full of trophies.

"This is the **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," said Blip. "It opened in **2015**, inside a museum called **The Strong**, in Rochester, New York. Every single game you just saw tonight is in there."

Ben looked at the glowing trophies lined up in rows: the green bouncing dot, the two little spaceships, the brown box, the Pong paddles, the space bugs, Pac-Man, Mario, the falling Tetris blocks, Sonic, and the shiny disc.

"I helped with ALL of those," Ben said.

"You sure did," said Blip.

The green flicker faded from the screen. Ben blinked. He was back in his own room, tablet warm in his hands. His half-built pixel pig sat finished on the screen, curly tail and all, glowing soft and square in the dark.

Blip's tiny pixel shape winked once from the corner of the screen.

"Night, Ben," Blip said. "Game on."

The screen went dark and quiet, ready for tomorrow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game on.

true_facts.text: The first video game people played just for fun was **Tennis for Two**, shown on a round science screen in **1958**.
In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** and his friends made a space game called **Spacewar!** on a computer as big as a fridge.
**Ralph Baer** built an early TV game called the **Brown Box**, and people call him the father of video games.
The **Brown Box** became the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972** — the first game console that plugged right into a TV.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started **Atari** and made the arcade game **Pong**.
The **Atari 2600**, from **1977**, let players pop in different plastic **cartridges** to play new games.
**Space Invaders**, made in **1978** by **Tomohiro Nishikado**, got everybody lining up at arcades.
**Pac-Man**, made in **1980** by **Toru Iwatani**, might have been shaped like a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, too many rushed games made people stop buying as many — folks call it the video game **crash**.
Nintendo's **NES** came out in **1985**, packed together with a game that helped video games bounce back.
**Tetris**, a falling-block puzzle game, was made in **1984** by **Alexey Pajitnov** in Moscow.
**Sonic the Hedgehog** zoomed onto screens in **1991**, made fast on purpose to race against Mario.
In **1994**, Sony's **PlayStation** used shiny **CDs** instead of cartridges.
**Minecraft** came out in **2011**, made by **Markus 'Notch' Persson**, and became the best-selling video game ever.

story.title: Lena and the Keeper's Gloves
story.subtitle: One goalkeeper, one glowing pair of gloves, and two thousand years of soccer.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: A Courtyard in Han China
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep forty minutes ago.

Instead she was diving across her bedroom floor onto a heap of pillows, saving a penalty only she could see. Her new goalkeeper gloves, bright green, lay tossed on the carpet. Under the bed, something else glowed the exact same color.

She pulled out an older pair, cracked at the knuckles, smelling of grass and dust. The moment she tugged them on, they gave a soft hum, and the room filled with pitch-green light. The floor dropped away like a missed stair.

She landed on packed dirt in a courtyard ringed by stone walls. Players in loose tunics kicked a stitched leather ball between them, never once touching it with their hands.

"You're not allowed to catch it," said a boy her age, eyeing her gloves. "This is **cuju** — ball-kick."

"How old is this game?" Lena asked.

"Older than these walls. **People in China have played it for more than 2,000 years** — one of the oldest ball games anyone's ever found."

She couldn't catch the ball, so she popped it up with her knee instead. The courtyard cheered like she'd made the save of the match.

"Not bad, keeper," the boy said. "Come back any century you like."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Chaos in the Streets, 1314
chapters.text:
The green light dropped her onto a muddy English street, right into chaos.

A ball with no fixed shape came barreling down the lane, chased by half the town. Men shoved past market stalls. A cart tipped. A basket of apples rolled everywhere.

Lena's instincts kicked in before her brain caught up. She dove, caught the ball an arm's length from a bread stall, and rolled clear.

"SAVE!" someone yelled, delighted, and half the mob cheered like she'd scored.

"This is **mob football**," said a woman beside her, catching her breath. "No teams, no field — sometimes a whole village against the next one, chasing one ball for miles."

"Is it always this wild?" Lena asked, brushing mud off her gloves.

"Wild enough that the king's had enough," the woman said. "**King Edward II banned the sport in London in 1314** — too many broken stalls, too much noise."

Lena looked at the tipped cart and figured that was fair. Somebody, someday, was going to have to write this game some rules.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Rulebook, Cambridge 1848
chapters.text:
The light dropped her into a university courtyard where two groups of students argued so loudly nobody was playing at all.

"At my school you can carry the ball!" one shouted.

"At mine you can't even touch it below the knee!" shouted another.

Every student had come from a different school with different rules, and nobody agreed on anything.

Lena had sat through enough chaotic recess games to know exactly what this needed.

"Why don't you just write one rulebook," she said. "One everyone agrees to follow, so you can actually play."

The courtyard went quiet. Then a student grabbed a pencil.

"That's the idea that's about to make history," the gloves murmured against her wrist. "**In 1848, Cambridge University students wrote down the Cambridge Rules** — one of the first real attempts at a shared rulebook for football."

Lena grinned. Sometimes the biggest idea in history was just, can we please agree on something.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Laws of the Game, London 1863
chapters.text:
Lena landed in a smoky meeting room above a London pub, where a dozen men in suits argued over handwriting on a page.

"If we don't pick one set of rules," one man was saying, "there's no sport, just arguments."

Lena recognized that frustration. She'd heard it at Cambridge too.

"Who's in charge of the pen?" she asked.

A tall man with ink-stained fingers looked up. "**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," he said. "And yes, I'm writing it right now."

"**The Football Association was founded here, in London, on October 26, 1863**," the gloves murmured. "Morley's writing the very first official Laws of the Game."

Lena scanned the page over his shoulder. One line stopped her cold — no player allowed to carry the ball with their hands.

"Wait," she said, holding up her green gloves. "What about—"

"One problem at a time," Morley said, smiling, and kept writing.

Lena decided that question could wait. Within a decade, this same association would start a tournament still running today — older than any football competition on Earth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Scotland v England, 1872
chapters.text:
The roar of a crowd hit her before her feet hit the ground.

Lena stood pitch-side in Glasgow, where two full teams in long shirts pounded up and down a soggy field. Real teams, real sides, real stakes.

"First time this has ever happened," said a man beside her, waving a scarf. "**Scotland against England — the first official international football match, played right here in Glasgow in 1872**."

Lena watched both goalkeepers dive and claw at everything that came near them, saves piling up at both ends.

"Who's winning?" she asked.

"Nobody, yet," the man said, grinning. "Could stay that way."

It did. The final whistle blew on a **scoreless draw, nil-nil** — boring to most people, but to a goalkeeper, it sounded like two keepers having the games of their lives.

"CLEAN SHEET!" Lena yelled, pumping her fist at both ends of the field, and for once nobody looked at her strangely for celebrating a game with no goals in it at all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Montevideo, 1930
chapters.text:
The air smelled like ocean and cut grass, and a stadium roared loud enough to shake her teeth.

A gold trophy sat on a table near the tunnel, small and plain for something everyone kept staring at.

"What is that?" Lena asked.

"**The first FIFA World Cup**," said a man with a clipboard, practically vibrating with nerves. "**Played right here in Uruguay, in 1930.** Thirteen teams, one winner."

"Who's winning?" Lena asked, already sure she wasn't going to like waiting for the answer.

"Watch," he said.

She watched Uruguay, the host team, beat Argentina to lift the very first trophy of its kind.

"It's named for a person," the clipboard man added, nodding at the gold case. "**Jules Rimet** — the man who pushed hardest to get a world championship built in the first place."

Lena pressed her face to the glass. It looked small for something that would end up mattering to so many people, for so many years after this one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Dog Who Saved the Cup, 1966
chapters.text:
Lena landed in London in the middle of a crisis.

Police paced a stamp exhibition hall, newspapers were read in a panic, and everyone kept saying the same two words: it's gone.

"What's gone?" Lena asked.

"**The World Cup trophy**," said a woman pacing nearby. "Stolen right off its stand. A week before England's about to host the whole tournament."

Lena's stomach dropped — until she noticed something nobody else had. A scruffy little dog on a lead was sniffing hard at something half-hidden by a wall, tail going like a windshield wiper in a storm.

"Over there!" Lena called. "Your dog's found something!"

Sure enough, wrapped up and waiting, was the missing trophy.

"**Found safe, just one week after it disappeared — by a dog named Pickles**," the gloves murmured, delighted. "Good dog."

"PICKLES FOUND IT!" Lena shouted, and the whole hall seemed to exhale at once.

With the trophy back where it belonged, **England went on to host — and win — the 1966 World Cup**, their only title so far. Lena decided dogs didn't get nearly enough credit in the history of soccer.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Three Stars and Two Cards, 1970
chapters.text:
The stadium in Mexico City was so loud Lena felt it in her ribs.

On the field, a player moved like the ball was magnetized to his foot. Everyone around her had come just to watch him.

"Who is that?" she asked.

"**Pele**," said the man next to her, like it was obvious. "Brazilian forward. This is his third World Cup final. **He's the only player who's ever won it three times — in 1958, 1962, and 1970.**"

Lena was still working that out when the referee jogged over to a player and held up a small colored card instead of shouting.

"What's that about?" she asked.

"Brand new this tournament," the man said. "**A referee named Ken Aston invented yellow and red cards, inspired by traffic lights** — yellow to slow down, red to stop completely. First time anyone's used them, right here in 1970."

Lena watched Pele lift the trophy an hour later, and understood why some names in soccer get remembered for a hundred years — and some games invent entirely new rules just to keep up with them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Keepers of the Game
chapters.text:
The light dropped her onto a scrappy field behind a factory, where a women's team ran drills so sharp Lena wanted to join in immediately.

"Who are you?" she asked one player, out of breath from just watching.

"**Lily Parr**," the woman said, slotting a shot past a keeper who never had a chance. "We're one of the most popular teams in England right now."

"Why haven't I heard of you?" Lena asked.

The answer made her jaw tighten. Starting in the 1920s, the people in charge of English football had banned women's teams from their grounds entirely — no good reason, just old rules nobody would budge on.

"It didn't last forever, though," the gloves murmured gently. "**The ban was finally lifted in 1971.**"

Years slid past like turning pages, and Lena found herself in a stadium roaring with noise again.

"**The first official Women's World Cup was held in 1991, in China, and the United States won it**," said a voice over the loudspeaker, and the whole stadium shook with cheering.

"KEEPERS OF THE GAME!" Lena shouted, cheering for everyone who'd ever stood in a net, or kicked a ball, and been told no, and kept playing anyway.

The light turned green once more, and she landed back on her bedroom carpet, gloves warm on her hands, the old pair gone soft and worn like they'd traveled a thousand years to get there.

She set the ancient gloves back under the bed, right where she'd found them, and picked up her own bright green pair off the floor.

Tomorrow, there was a match to get to. She already knew exactly which save she wanted to try first.

story.ending_line: Saturday's match couldn't come soon enough.

The Football Association was founded in London on October 26, 1863, and banned players from carrying the ball with their hands.

story.title: Arjun and the Sleep Sentinel
story.subtitle: A night with Rem, who steps out of comic panels to explain why bodies need to sleep

chapters.heading: Panel One: The Boy Who Blinked
chapters.text:
Arjun lay under his blanket with a flashlight, reading the last page of *Googly Man*, his favorite comic about a cricket-playing superhero. His dad had already said lights out twice.

"Five more minutes," Arjun whispered. He said that every single night.

On the final panel, Googly Man closed his eyes. Then the ink started to move. Tiny lines flicked back and forth across the hero's eyelids, just like real eyes do when they're looking at something fast.

The panel glowed. A figure stepped right off the page — a comic-book sleep hero in a cape stitched from pajama fabric.

"Name's Rem," he said. "Spotted something, did you?"

"His eyes," said Arjun. "They're moving. Is he awake?"

"Nope. Dreaming." Rem grinned. "In **1953**, two scientists in **Chicago** — Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman — watched a sleeping boy's eyes twitch exactly like that under his eyelids. They'd just found **REM sleep**, the stage where your eyes dart around while your brain dreams."

Arjun grinned back. "Show me more."

chapters.heading: Panel Two: The Ninety-Minute Over
chapters.text:
They dropped through the glowing panel into a hallway that smelled like library paper and night air.

"Sleep isn't one long nap," Rem said. "It's cycles. About **ninety minutes** each, back and forth between quiet sleep and REM sleep, all night long."

"Like an over in cricket," said Arjun. "Six balls, then you switch ends."

"Sure. Six balls of quiet sleep, then a dream over." Rem liked that one.

"Here's the strange part." Rem pointed at a sleeping shape drifting past, arms loose at its sides. "During REM, your brain is as busy as if you were awake. But your muscles go floppy. Limp. So you can't jump up and bowl a yorker mid-dream."

Arjun poked the floating sleeper's arm. It really was loose, like a character drawn without any lines holding the joints together.

"Good," Arjun said. "I'd hate to sleep-bowl a wide."

chapters.heading: Panel Three: Growing in the Dark
chapters.text:
A measuring tape unrolled itself across the floor, numbers glowing.

"What's that for?" Arjun asked.

"Growing," said Rem. "The deepest part of quiet sleep is when your body releases the most **growth hormone** — the stuff that helps you get taller."

Arjun eyed the tape. "So sleep is basically training."

"Basically." Rem tapped the tape, and it inched upward on its own, like a scoreboard ticking. "Kids need extra sleep for exactly this reason. You don't grow much during the day. You grow at night, in the deep stuff, without even trying."

Arjun thought about every flashlight-lit five more minutes he'd begged for. "So those minutes were coming out of my height?"

Rem shrugged, cape fluttering. "Maybe half a millimeter. Your call."

Arjun clicked the flashlight off without being asked. First time ever.

chapters.heading: Panel Four: The Editor-in-Chief of the Brain
chapters.text:
They climbed a staircase shaped like a comic book's spine, panels sliding by like windows.

"Who actually decides it's bedtime?" Arjun asked. "Not just Dad."

"Good question." Rem pointed at a tiny glowing office, barely the size of a grain of rice, tucked just behind Arjun's eyes. "That's the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — a speck of brain sitting right where your eye nerves cross. Think of it as the editor-in-chief. It reads how much light's coming in and decides when to print 'sleepy' across the rest of your brain."

"That's a mouthful."

"Call it the body's clock instead. It keeps a rhythm called **circadian** — old Latin for 'about a day' — because it resets roughly every twenty-four hours."

Arjun peeked through the tiny office window. Inside, a cartoon editor stamped files marked DAY and NIGHT. "Busy little guy," he said.

chapters.heading: Panel Five: The Prize for Watching Clocks Tick
chapters.text:
The editor's office suddenly filled with gold confetti.

"What happened?" Arjun asked, batting confetti out of his hair.

"In **2017**," Rem said, "three scientists — Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young — won the **Nobel Prize**, the biggest prize in science, for figuring out which genes build that clock and keep it ticking."

"Genes," Arjun repeated. "Like instructions inside your cells?"

"Exactly. Tiny instructions that tell your body when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake, even without a clock on the wall."

Arjun pictured the three scientists holding a trophy instead of a cricket cup. "Do they get a medal shaped like a clock?"

"Don't know," said Rem. "But they earned it either way."

Arjun decided that was the best kind of prize: one for paying close attention to something everybody else ignored.

chapters.heading: Panel Six: The Sleepy Ink
chapters.text:
Down another staircase, the air smelled like fresh comic ink.

"This part's my favorite," Rem said, holding up a bottle that glowed faint blue. "**Melatonin.** Your brain makes it when it gets dark, and it's basically a signal that says, time to wind down."

"Like a bat-signal, but for sleep."

"Exactly like that. In **1958**, a scientist named Aaron Lerner and his team pulled this stuff out of animal glands for the very first time, in a lab."

Arjun reached a finger near the glowing bottle, careful not to touch. "Does light from my flashlight mess with it?"

"Bright light tells your brain it's still daytime," Rem said. "Which is exactly why somebody's flashlight habit keeps delaying the ink."

Arjun looked guilty. The flashlight, still in his pocket, suddenly felt heavier.

chapters.heading: Panel Seven: The Night Shift
chapters.text:
They reached a room shaped like Arjun's own skull from the inside, lit like a cricket stadium at night.

"Two jobs happen in here while you sleep," Rem said. He flicked a switch, and the day's memories floated by like comic panels — Arjun's cover drive at practice, a joke his friend told, a page of homework.

"Sleep sorts these into long-term memory," said Rem. "Practice a shot, sleep on it, remember it better tomorrow."

"And the second job?"

"Cleaning." A soft whooshing sound rolled through, gentle as stadium sprinklers. "It's called the **glymphatic system** — a nightly rinse that flushes waste out of your brain while you're out cold. Like groundskeepers sweeping the pitch after the last over."

Arjun watched his own cover drive glow brighter, filed neatly away. "Keep that one," he told the room.

chapters.heading: Panel Eight: The Animal Kingdom's Weirdest Sleepers
chapters.text:
A window opened onto an ocean, moonlit and calm.

"Not everyone sleeps like us," Rem said, pointing at a dolphin gliding below. "Bottlenose dolphins sleep with only half their brain at a time. One eye stays open, watching for danger, while the other half naps."

"That's basically keeping one slip fielder awake at all times," said Arjun.

Rem laughed, and the window shifted to tall grass, where a giraffe stood swaying. "Giraffes barely sleep at all — sometimes under **two hours a day**, in short standing naps."

"And bats?" Arjun asked, remembering a cave scene from *Googly Man Annual #3*.

"Some little bats sleep up to **twenty hours a day**. Sleepiest mammals we know of."

"Lucky bats," Arjun muttered, thinking of his own two bedtime battles every single night.

chapters.heading: Panel Nine: Eleven Days Awake
chapters.text:
The window dimmed to a plain garage, a teenager hunched over a science-fair poster.

"This one's a warning, not a dare," Rem said. "In **1964**, a seventeen-year-old named Randy Gardner, from San Diego, stayed awake for about **eleven days** for a science project."

Arjun's eyes went wide. "Eleven days? That's basically a whole Test match series."

"It's one of the longest stretches anybody's ever gone without sleep on record," Rem said. "But doctors don't recommend anyone try to beat it. Go without sleep long enough, and your mood, focus, and memory all fall apart fast."

"So it's a cool fact," Arjun said slowly, "not a plan."

"Exactly." Rem tapped the poster, and it curled shut like a comic nobody needed a sequel to. "Some records aren't worth chasing."

chapters.heading: Panel Ten: Lights Out, For Real
chapters.text:
The staircase folded back into the glowing panel, and Arjun tumbled, blanket and all, back onto his own bedroom floor.

"One more thing," Rem said, already fading at the edges. "Ever seen someone walk in their sleep?"

"My cousin does. Is he dreaming when he does it?"

"Nope. Sleepwalking happens in deep quiet sleep, not during dreams. He's probably not acting out anything at all."

"Good to know. Less weird, somehow."

Rem's cape thinned into comic-panel lines. "Add it all up, and people spend around a third of their whole life asleep. Newborn babies sleep even more — something like **fourteen to seventeen hours a day**, in short bursts."

"A third of my life." Arjun flopped back onto his pillow. "Guess I'd better do it properly, then."

The comic on his nightstand had gone quiet, Googly Man's eyes closed and still. Arjun clicked off the flashlight — no five more minutes tonight — and let his own eyes close.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a match to play, and legs that had earned every minute of growing they got overnight.

Some small bats sleep up to **twenty hours a day**, making them some of the sleepiest mammals known.

story.title: Tom and the Gear That Remembered
story.subtitle: A two-hundred-year ride through the history of the bicycle.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gear in the Toolbox
chapters.text:
Tom was elbow-deep in his dad's old toolbox, hunting for a hex key, when his fingers found something colder than metal should be.

It was a gear, about the size of a cookie, scratched and rust-brown. He wiped it on his jeans. The teeth caught the lamp light and threw it back gold. Then it started spinning, on its own, in his palm.

A low hum rattled the shelves. The gear's teeth blurred into a wheel of light, and a voice clicked out of it, like a freewheel coasting downhill.

"Finally," it said. "Someone who actually knows what a derailleur is."

Tom nearly dropped it. "A talking gear?"

"A Hub," it corrected. "Every bike has one — the middle bit the wheel spins around. I'm the hub of this whole story. Two hundred years of it. Want to see where wheels came from?"

Before he could answer, the garage walls peeled back like wet paper, and the floor dropped into cold morning air that smelled of pine and mud.

WHOOOSH.

He landed standing up, boots crunching gravel, in front of a man straddling the strangest contraption Tom had ever seen.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Running Machine (1817)
chapters.text:
A man in a long coat pushed himself along a dirt path, feet scuffing the ground, wheels wobbling under him.

"Karl von Drais," the Hub whispered. "Built this in **1817**. He called it the Laufmaschine — the running machine. No pedals. You push with your feet, like a kid on a scooter."

The man wobbled, overcorrected, and nearly went into a hedge.

Tom winced. "He's steering with his whole body. Classic beginner mistake."

"Fix it," the Hub said.

Tom cupped his hands. "Look where you want to go, not at your front wheel! Eyes up!"

Von Drais blinked, lifted his chin — and the wobble smoothed out. He rolled a straight line down the path, grinning like he'd invented flight.

"Not bad," the Hub said. "People called it the hobby horse too. Thought it was a toy for grown men who should know better."

Tom laughed. "Grown men on balance bikes. Some things never change."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Pedals and the Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
The gravel became cobblestones, slick with old rain, and a line of men on two-wheelers clattered past, teeth rattling in their skulls.

"The velocipede," the Hub said. "Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel, in the **1860s**. Lallement even patented the design in America, in **1866**."

Tom grabbed the nearest one's handlebars to study it. The crank was welded right onto the front wheel's axle. No chain anywhere.

"Direct drive," he said slowly. "One turn of the pedals, one turn of the wheel. No gears to help you."

"Exactly. Which means—"

"To go fast you'd need a much bigger wheel." Tom grinned, already seeing where this was going.

He hopped on, pedaled ten feet over the cobbles, and nearly bit his tongue. "Okay. I get the nickname."

"Boneshaker," the Hub said cheerfully. "Every bump in the road, straight into your spine."

Tom climbed off, rubbing his jaw. "Someone needs a bigger wheel. Fast."

"Funny you should say that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Giant Wheel (1870s)
chapters.text:
A wheel taller than Tom rolled into view, with a tiny one trailing behind like an afterthought.

"The penny-farthing," said the Hub. "Named for two old British coins — one huge, one tiny. Bigger wheel means more distance per pedal turn. Riders loved the speed."

A man in a bowler hat pedaled past, perched impossibly high, grinning down at them.

"That seat's basically on top of the front axle," Tom said. "If he brakes hard—"

The rider hit a rut. The huge wheel stopped dead. He did not.

He sailed forward over the handlebars in a long, slow arc.

"Taking a header," the Hub said, unbothered. "Happens to everyone eventually. That's genuinely its name."

Tom was already moving, mountain-biking reflexes kicking in. He caught the man's shoulder mid-fall, steering the stumble into a roll instead of a face-plant. The rider popped up, dusted off his hat, entirely fine.

"Nice catch," the Hub said.

"You said it was risky, not that you'd just let him eat gravel."

"I said I was a gear. I didn't say I had arms."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Two Wheels, Same Size (1885)
chapters.text:
The next street belonged to a bicycle that looked almost normal — two matching wheels, no circus-sized front end.

"John Kemp Starley," the Hub said, "built this in **1885**. The Rover Safety Bicycle. A chain and sprockets drive the back wheel, instead of pedals sitting on the front axle."

Tom crouched by the chain, tracing its loop with one finger. "This is basically my bike. Small wheel on the pedals, bigger wheel on the back, chain connects them. You get the penny-farthing's speed without the giant wheel."

"Without the broken collarbones, too," the Hub added.

A woman wheeled hers past, both feet flat on the ground at a stop, easy as anything.

"That's the whole point," Tom said. "Lower seat, even wheels. Anyone can ride it. Not just people tall enough to survive a header."

"Within five years," the Hub said, "this exact shape took over the world. You're basically looking at your own bike's great-great-grandfather."

Tom gave the frame a respectful pat. "Nice to meet you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Air Under the Wheels (1888)
chapters.text:
Down a side street, a man knelt beside a tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around its wheel like a bandage.

"John Boyd Dunlop," the Hub said. "A vet, actually — fixed animals, not bikes. His son kept complaining the tricycle rode rough, so in **1888** Dunlop stuffed the tire full of air instead of solid rubber."

Tom pressed his thumb into the tube. It gave, soft and springy, nothing like the wooden wheels further back down the road.

"Air works like a shock absorber," Tom said. "It squashes down over bumps instead of your spine doing it for you."

"Try it," the Hub said.

Tom wheeled the tricycle over the cobblestones they'd bone-shaken across earlier. It rolled smooth and quiet, barely a rattle.

"That," Tom said, "is the difference between misery and Tuesday."

Dunlop looked up, startled by the praise. His little company would go on to put tires on bikes, and eventually cars, all over the planet.

"You're welcome, world," Tom said, and bowed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
Streets filled suddenly with people, bicycles everywhere, bells ringing nonstop.

"The **1890s**," the Hub said. "The Golden Age of Bicycles. Millions sold across Europe and America, practically overnight."

A woman cycled past confidently, then nearly caught her long skirt in the chain as she pedaled.

Tom cringed. "That's a design problem. Long skirts and chains do not mix."

"Which is exactly why," the Hub said, "bikes helped make bloomers popular — loose, practical trousers women could pedal in safely. An American named Susan B. Anthony said cycling had done more to set women free than anything else in the world."

"Because it actually let them go somewhere," Tom said. "On their own. Whenever they wanted."

"Pretty good upgrade, for two wheels and a chain."

Tom watched the woman swap into a looser skirt from her basket and pedal off without a wobble, grinning the whole way down the street.

"Best safety feature on this entire trip," Tom said, "and it's pockets."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Bicycle Shop in Dayton
chapters.text:
A bell above a shop door jingled as Tom stepped inside, surrounded by wheels, spokes, and the smell of oil.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," the Hub said. "Dayton, Ohio, the **1890s**. They fixed and built bicycles for a living, years before anyone had heard of them doing anything else."

Tom picked up a wheel, spinning it, watching the thin spokes hold their shape.

"These spokes are basically doing the same job as a bridge truss," he said. "Thin, but strong, because the pulling force is spread out evenly."

One of the brothers looked up. "Spread the load, and anything thin can hold weight," he said. "Works on a wheel. Should work on bigger things, too."

"Like wings?" Tom asked.

The brother just smiled and went back to the frame he was welding.

"In **1903**," the Hub said, "that smile builds the first airplane that actually flies. Lightweight tubing, spoked wheels, straight out of this shop."

Tom set the wheel down carefully. "Turns out learning to build a good bike teaches you basically everything."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Gear Comes Home
chapters.text:
The Hub spun faster, and two centuries blurred past the edges of Tom's sight.

"**1903**," the Hub called over the wind, "the first Tour de France — riders now cover about **3,500 kilometers** across France, three straight weeks of pedaling."

"The **1970s**, Marin County, California — riders bolt fat, bumpy tires onto old frames and go bombing down dirt trails. Congratulations, Tom. That's your mountain bike."

The blur slowed. Tom caught a last glimpse of wide, sunlit bike lanes crowded with riders, city after city, more bikes than cars.

Then the garage walls snapped back into place.

Tom stood exactly where he'd started, hex key still in one hand. In the other, the gear sat still and quiet, warm as a held breath.

"We're done?" Tom asked.

"For tonight," the Hub said. "Two hundred years is a lot of ground to cover. Even for me."

Tom turned the gear over once, then set it on his workbench, next to the bike waiting for its chain.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we finish the repair properly."

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a chain to finish — and a gear that remembered everything.

true_facts.text: Karl von Drais built a wooden ride called the Laufmaschine in **1817** — it had no pedals, so riders pushed it along with their feet.

In the **1860s**, Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel, making the velocipede — riders called it the **boneshaker** because cobblestone streets rattled your bones.
Pierre Lallement patented his pedal bicycle design in the United States in **1866**.
In the **1870s**, the penny-farthing arrived, with a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, so one pedal turn carried you much farther.
The penny-farthing got its name from two old British coins, one huge and one tiny.
Falling off a penny-farthing was called **taking a header**, because the rider sat high up and could tip forward over the handlebars.
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built the Rover Safety Bicycle, with two matching wheels and a chain driving the back one.
The safety bicycle's low, even wheels made it far easier and safer to ride, and it quickly became the standard shape worldwide.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop invented the air-filled tire, making rides much smoother than old solid rubber wheels.
Bicycles gave women new freedom to travel on their own in the **1890s**, and Susan B. Anthony said cycling had done more to free women than anything else in the world.
Because long skirts were dangerous near bike chains, the bicycle craze helped make practical clothing like **bloomers** popular.
Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, in the **1890s**, years before they built the first successful airplane in **1903**.
The first Tour de France was held in **1903**, and today riders cover about **3,500 kilometers** across France over three weeks.
Mountain bikes with wide, bumpy tires were built in the **1970s** in Marin County, California, by riders who wanted to bike down rough dirt trails.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Tom returned to his garage holding the Hub, now quiet, and set it beside his mountain bike to finish the repair the next day.
