story.title: Eli and the Sputnik Set
story.subtitle: A beep from 1957 was still on the air. He just had to build the right radio to hear it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Frequency Zero (1957)
chapters.text:
The soldering iron ticked as it cooled, and Eli leaned back from the workbench he'd built out of a door and two sawhorses. Eleven forty on a school night, and he had a dead radio in pieces in front of him — a 1950s shortwave set he'd bought for six dollars at an estate sale because the dial looked like something out of a submarine movie.

His physics fair project was supposed to be about radio propagation: how a signal bounces off the ionosphere and comes back down a thousand miles from where it started. What he had not planned on was the radio turning itself on.

The needle on the dial twitched. A tone came through the dead speaker — not static, something with a shape to it. Beep. Beep. Beep. Steady, mechanical, patient.

Eli's stomach did the thing it did whenever a problem set almost made sense. He grabbed a pencil. The beeps weren't random. They came every six-tenths of a second, like a metronome built by someone very bored or very precise.

"That's not a glitch," he said out loud, to nobody. "That's a transmitter."

The dial glowed amber where his finger landed, right on a frequency scrawled in old grease pencil: 20.005 MHz. He turned it a half-click further, chasing the tone the way you'd chase a radio station through static on a long car ride, and the beep sharpened into something almost bell-clear.

The room didn't so much go dark as go *elsewhere*. The desk lamp became a spotlight on bare concrete. The beeping was louder now, coming from a metal ball the size of a beach ball, bristling with four long antennas, sitting on a stand in front of him.

"You're off by two days," said a voice from the radio speaker, which had somehow followed him. It sounded like a late-night DJ who'd been awake far too long. "This went up October fourth. Nineteen fifty-seven."

Eli walked a slow circle around the ball. It was smaller than he'd pictured — barely two feet across, by his best guess. "Is this—"

"**Sputnik 1**," the radio said. "First man-made object to ever orbit the Earth. About **fifty-eight centimeters** wide, which is roughly the size of a beach ball, and it does exactly one thing: it beeps."

"That beep I heard in my room," Eli said slowly, "was from this. Right now. Well — then."

"The signal was simple enough that **anybody with an ordinary radio could pick it up**,

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Dog, a Rocket, and a Very Bad Week (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
the radio continued, and the beeping ball faded to black along with the concrete floor. When the room came back, it was a different room: fluorescent lights, a smaller satellite shaped more like a cone, and a window with a dog looking out of it.

Eli had read enough to brace himself, but seeing her was different — a scruffy stray with alert ears, strapped into a little compartment, calm the way dogs get when they trust the person holding the leash.

"**Laika**," the radio said quietly. "One month after Sputnik 1, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 with her aboard. **First living creature to orbit the Earth.**"

Eli didn't say anything for a second. He just put his hand near the glass, not touching it, the way you'd greet an animal you respected rather than one you wanted to show off for. "Did she—"

"She mattered," the radio said, which Eli understood was the whole answer he was getting, and decided that was fine.

The scene dissolved into a different kind of room — a briefing hall full of men in dark suits looking like they'd each personally lost a fight. A chalkboard read October 1958.

"The United States got beaten twice in a row by a beeping ball and a dog," the radio said, "and reacted the way you'd expect a sore loser to react: it built an entire agency. **NASA started operating on October 1, 1958.**"

Eli clocked the date on the chalkboard against what he already knew about orbital mechanics, and did the math out loud before the radio could. "So their first satellite had to beat that deadline too. Explorer 1?"

"**January 31, 1958.** Before NASA even existed, actually — the Army launched it. And it didn't just catch up. It found something nobody was looking for."

A band of static-fuzzed light appeared on a projector screen, wrapped around a cartoon Earth like a belt. "The **Van Allen belt**," the radio said. "A ring of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field, out past the atmosphere. Explorer 1's instruments picked it up by accident."

"They were racing to catch up," Eli said, "and tripped over a discovery nobody else had."

"Try not to sound so pleased about it," the radio said. "You're supposed to be rooting for everybody."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Hundred and Eight Minutes (1961)
chapters.text:
The next jump came with a jolt that felt, Eli thought, exactly like what g-force was probably supposed to feel like, which was a strange thing to be proud of at 12:14 in the morning.

He landed in a control room full of men hunched over dials, all of them not breathing. A speaker crackled with a voice speaking Russian, calm as a man reading a grocery list.

"**April 12, 1961**," the radio said. "**Yuri Gagarin.** First human being ever to leave the atmosphere. He went all the way around the planet once, in **about 108 minutes**, aboard a capsule called Vostok 1."

Eli ran the number in his head — low Earth orbit, roughly 17,000 miles an hour, a full lap of the planet faster than most people's commute. "That's insane," he said. "That's basically one really fast homeroom period."

"He landed, got out, and reportedly asked a farmer for directions," the radio said. "Which tells you everything about how little anyone had planned for what happens *after* you get back down."

The room shifted — an ocean, a capsule bobbing in gray water, American flags on the recovery ship. "Three weeks later," the radio said, "**Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, aboard **Freedom 7**. Shorter flight. Didn't orbit. Still counted for plenty."

"Second place," Eli said, "but first to say it out loud, probably."

Then came a podium, a young president gripping both sides of it, a crowd of reporters scribbling. Eli recognized him before the radio said the name.

"**May 25, 1961.** **President Kennedy** stood up and told the country it was going to **land a man on the Moon and bring him home safely — before the decade was out.**"

"That's not a plan," Eli said. "That's a dare with a government budget attached."

"Exactly the kind of sentence an engineer either loves or has nightmares about," the radio agreed. "Tell me, which are you?"

Eli grinned at the glowing dial. "Ask me again after the Moon part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Forty-Eight Times Around (1963)
chapters.text:
The dial hummed low this time, almost thoughtful, before the room resolved into a launch pad under flat gray cloud.

"Guess," the radio said, which Eli had learned by now meant it had a favorite coming up.

He looked at the rocket, the crowd, the calendar someone had taped to a clipboard nearby reading June 1963. "Something that hasn't happened yet in the story," he said. "Gagarin went up. A dog went up. Nobody's sent a woman yet."

"**June 16, 1963.** **Valentina Tereshkova.**" The radio let the name sit there like it deserved its own echo. "**First woman in space.** She'd been a factory worker who did parachute jumping as a hobby — that's how she got noticed in the first place. She orbited Earth **forty-eight times** aboard Vostok 6."

Eli tried to picture it: forty-eight sunrises and sunsets, racing past a window, while down on Earth most people were still arguing about whether women should be allowed to drive race cars. "Forty-eight," he repeated. "That's not a flight. That's basically a very committed vacation."

"She logged more hours in space, on that single mission, than every American astronaut before her put together," the radio said. "Combined."

Eli let out a low whistle, the kind that meant a number had actually impressed him, which did not happen often. "That should be a bigger deal than it is."

"Most of the best ones are," the radio said, and for once it didn't sound like it was joking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Man Who Didn't Exist (1965)
chapters.text:
The next room was colder, somehow, even though nothing in it was actually cold — a capsule floated against a black sky full of stars so sharp they looked fake, and a figure in a bulky white suit drifted on a tether beside it like a kite that had forgotten gravity existed.

"**March 18, 1965.** **Alexei Leonov.** **First spacewalk** in history. About ten minutes floating outside his own capsule, tethered by a cord, looking at the entire planet with nothing between him and it but a suit."

"Ten minutes doesn't sound like long," Eli said.

"Try holding your breath for ten minutes outside a pressurized vehicle sometime," the radio said. "It's long."

Eli watched the tiny figure for a moment, turning slowly, and thought about how every single piece of that suit had to work perfectly or there was no version of the story where Leonov got to tell anyone about it. He filed that thought away rather than saying it out loud; some things didn't need a joke attached.

The view pulled back to a different room entirely — a design office, blueprints everywhere, and a stooped man arguing quietly with three engineers over a drafting table.

"Who's that?" Eli asked.

"**Sergei Korolev.** The chief designer behind basically everything you've seen tonight on the Soviet side — Sputnik, Gagarin, Tereshkova, Leonov. All of it, his program."

"I've genuinely never heard of him," Eli said, which felt wrong given the résumé.

"Nobody had, at the time. His name was kept a state secret. The Soviets were worried a rival country might target him if his identity got out, so the man behind the entire space program was officially nobody, right up until **he died in 1966**. The world only learned who'd been running the show after he was already gone."

Eli looked at the blueprints again, differently this time — not as the work of some faceless agency, but as one guy's handwriting, under one guy's name that nobody was allowed to say. "That's the loneliest kind of famous," he said.

"It's one way to put it," the radio agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Photograph of Everything (1968)
chapters.text:
This time the jump felt different — less like a jolt, more like a slow rise, and the room filled with the hush of a spacecraft cockpit instead of a crowd.

Through a small window, Earth hung against black space: blue, white, impossibly small, impossibly whole.

"**December 1968. Apollo 8.** First humans to ever orbit the Moon. One of the astronauts, **William Anders**, looked up from checking the Moon's surface and saw this instead."

A camera clicked somewhere behind Eli — not his own, not the radio's, just part of the memory replaying itself.

"That's **Earthrise**," the radio said. "Probably the most reproduced photograph in history. Taken by a man whose actual job that day was photographing a dead gray rock, who turned around and photographed the one planet in the universe anybody cared about instead."

Eli stared at it for a long moment. Every physics problem he'd ever solved about orbits and escape velocity had been an abstraction — numbers on a page. This was the same math, wearing a face. "You can't un-see that," he said finally. "Once you've seen the whole planet at once, you can't go back to thinking about it as separate countries having an argument."

"Several people who worked on this program said more or less exactly that," the radio said. "Which is a strange side effect for a rocket to have."

The scene shifted to a hangar bay, where a rocket taller than anything Eli had ever stood next to loomed under work lights, and a precise, accented voice was giving instructions to a team of engineers.

"**Wernher von Braun," the radio said. "Built rockets for Germany before the war, then led the NASA team that built the Saturn V — the rocket you're looking at. Complicated man. Important rocket."

Eli didn't ask about the complicated part. Some things the radio clearly wasn't going to spell out for him, and he suspected that was on purpose.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Three Hundred and Sixty-Three Feet (1969)
chapters.text:
The hangar fell away, and Eli found himself standing on scrubland grass at dawn, a crowd behind him, and in front of him a rocket so tall he had to tip his whole head back to see the top of it.

"**Saturn V**," the radio said. "**Three hundred sixty-three feet tall.** Taller than the Statue of Liberty, pedestal and all."

Eli did the comparison in his head — he'd stood at the base of tall buildings before, but never one built purely to burn itself up on purpose, on a schedule, with people riding on top of it. "That's not a vehicle," he said. "That's a controlled explosion wearing a vehicle costume."

"Most rockets are," the radio said. "That's sort of the whole idea."

The scene jumped — grainy, gray, a screen instead of a sky — and a figure in a bulky suit stepped off a ladder onto powder-white ground.

"**July 20, 1969.** **Neil Armstrong.** First person to ever stand on the Moon."

Eli already knew the line that came next, had known it since before he could read, but hearing it land live still did something to the back of his neck. "A giant leap for mankind," he said along with the fuzzy audio, half a beat behind.

"WE'RE WALKING ON THE MOON," Eli said, too loud for a room that wasn't really a room, and didn't even feel embarrassed about it.

"**Buzz Aldrin** joined him down there a few minutes later," the radio said. "Meanwhile **Michael Collins** stayed up above, alone, orbiting in the command module — Columbia — the whole time they were down on the surface. Every time Columbia passed around the far side of the Moon, he lost radio contact with literally every other human being alive. Most isolated any person has ever been, probably, in the whole history of the species."

Eli looked up — an actual reflex, even though there was no sky here to look at — and thought about that: one guy, alone, circling a rock, while two other guys got all the photographs. "Nobody talks about him," he said.

"You just did," the radio said. "That's something."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Longest Three Days (1970)
chapters.text:
The next room had a different feel entirely — tighter, tenser, the lighting harsher, voices clipped and fast instead of steady.

"**Apollo 13. 1970.**" The radio's tone had changed too, gone careful. "An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon. The mission was over the second that happened — no landing, nothing like it."

Eli felt his chest tighten the way it did during the one part of every movie where something goes wrong, and made himself breathe out slow. "But they got back," he said. It wasn't really a question. He'd have remembered if this story ended the other way.

"They got back," the radio confirmed, immediately, like it wasn't interested in making him wait for that part. "Engineers on the ground — nowhere near as glamorous a job as flying the thing, infinitely harder — worked out a fix using basically whatever was already on board. Spare parts, tape, a plan built from nothing in record time. The crew made it home safely."

Eli let his shoulders drop. "So the story everyone remembers is the landing that worked," he said slowly, "but the one that actually proves these people were good at their jobs is the one that *didn't*."

"That's not a bad way to think about it," the radio said. "Anyone can fly a rocket when nothing's wrong."

Eli looked at the dark console lights around him, imagining a room full of people doing math against a clock that didn't care how good they were. "I think I'd rather be one of the engineers," he said, "than one of the guys in the capsule."

"Funny," the radio said. "Most people say the opposite."

"Most people haven't done the math on reentry angles," Eli said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: A Handshake in Orbit (1975)
chapters.text:
The last jump set him down somewhere brighter — not a launch pad, not a control room, but orbit itself: two spacecraft, one American, one Soviet, nose to nose against the curve of the Earth.

"**Between 1969 and 1972**," the radio said, "**twelve American astronauts** walked on the Moon, across six landing missions. The goal Kennedy set got met with years to spare."

"And then what," Eli said, "everyone just stopped racing?"

"Not stopped," the radio said. "Changed the game. **July 17, 1975.** American and Soviet spacecraft **docked together in orbit**, and the crews climbed through the hatch and shook hands. Apollo-Soyuz. Two countries that had spent eighteen years trying to beat each other to every milestone in the sky, meeting in the middle of it instead."

Eli watched the handshake happen, a small, almost boring gesture given everything that had led up to it — two beeping satellites, a dog, a man whose name was a state secret, a photograph of the whole Earth, an exploded tank, twelve sets of footprints on gray dust. All of it, ending with two guys shaking hands in zero gravity like they'd just finished a group project.

"That's it?" he said. "That's the ending?"

"That's the ending," the radio said. "Races end. Handshakes are harder to pull off, and they tend to matter longer."

The amber dial dimmed, and the cold concrete and the capsule and the whole glowing sky folded back down into his own bedroom — desk lamp, soldering iron, the radio sitting innocently in pieces, as if it had never once sent him anywhere.

Except the needle was still glowing, very faintly, at 20.005 MHz.

Eli reached over, picked up his pencil, and wrote the frequency down on the corner of his physics fair poster board, right next to a hand-drawn sketch of a rocket he'd started three hours ago and never finished.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow he had a poster board to finish — and a radio that clearly still had more to say.

true_facts.text: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the first man-made object to ever orbit Earth — about fifty-eight centimeters wide, roughly the size of a beach ball.
Sputnik 1's signal was so simple that **anybody with an ordinary radio could pick up its beep**.
A month later, Sputnik 2 carried a dog named **Laika** into orbit — the first living creature to ever circle the Earth.
Shocked by the Soviets getting there first, the United States created **NASA**, which began running on October 1, 1958.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched January 31, 1958, and accidentally discovered a ring of charged particles trapped around Earth called the **Van Allen belt**.
On April 12, 1961, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling the whole Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On May 5, 1961, **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space aboard Freedom 7, though his flight didn't make a full orbit.
On May 25, 1961, President **Kennedy** challenged the country to land a man on the Moon and bring him home safely before the decade ended.
On June 16, 1963, **Valentina Tereshkova**, a former factory worker, became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth **48 times**.
On March 18, 1965, **Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk, floating outside his capsule for about ten minutes.
**Sergei Korolev**, the secret mastermind behind the Soviet space program, had his identity kept hidden by the state until after his death in 1966.
In December 1968, the crew of **Apollo 8** became the first humans to orbit the Moon, and astronaut William Anders snapped the famous **Earthrise** photo of the whole Earth.
**Wernher von Braun**, who had built rockets in Germany before the war, led the NASA team that developed the giant **Saturn V** rocket.
The Saturn V rocket stood **363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty.

story.title: Mia and the Stopwatch Under the Bed
story.subtitle: A night of kickoffs, two thousand years in the making

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Stopwatch Under the Bed
chapters.text:
Mia was on the floor of her room, laptop balanced on a pillow, staring at a spreadsheet of every shot she'd taken this season. Column after column: distance, angle, result. She'd missed a penalty that afternoon, and she wanted to know exactly how bad her luck had been, or whether it was something she could actually fix.

Under her bed, in a shoebox that still smelled faintly of grass and polish, sat her grandfather's old referee kit — whistle, flags, and a stopwatch with a dented brass case. He'd been gone two years. She wound it anyway, out of habit, the way you'd check a pulse just to be sure.

The stopwatch didn't just tick. It glowed a flat stadium green, and the numbers on its face started scrolling backward, way too fast: 1990... 1920... 200 BCE. Then the room folded sideways like a sheet being shaken out, and Mia was standing in a dusty courtyard, holding a leather ball stuffed tight with feathers and hair.

A crowd of young men in Han dynasty robes were kicking the ball between two bamboo poles strung with a high net, never once using their hands. **Cuju**, one of them called it, like the word itself was a rule.

Mia, who could not resist counting things even in ancient China, watched for a solid two minutes and did the math in her head. "You've played nine possessions without a single handball," she said. "That's either excellent discipline or you've all had a very scary coach."

The nearest player grinned and passed her the ball with his foot, clearly expecting her to do the same. She tried, missed, tried again, and on the third attempt got it clean through the gap in the poles. The whole courtyard whooped.

Later, catching her breath, she asked how long people had been playing like this. "Longer than anyone can count," the player said, which annoyed the statistician in her more than she expected. Historians would later do better than he could: this game, **cuju**, had been kicked around in China for **more than 2,000 years**, making it one of the very first ancestors of the sport Mia played every Saturday morning.

The stopwatch, still looped around her wrist, buzzed warm. The green numbers started scrolling again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Banned in London
chapters.text:
The green light dropped her into the middle of a dirt street, except the street was a battlefield of elbows. Dozens of men were shoving an inflated ball — if you could even call it that — toward a church at one end of town and a mill at the other, and nobody seemed to be following any rule except win.

A wall collapsed nearby. A pig bolted from someone's yard, trailing an upturned basket. Mia flattened herself against a doorway.

"This," she said, "is the least organized sport I have ever seen. There isn't even a ball size."

An old woman leaning in the doorway beside her laughed. "They call it **mob football**. Whole towns play it, and it gets so wild that the king himself just outlawed the thing, right here in **London** — **1314**."

"Why?"

"Too much noise. Too many broken fences. He's trying to keep the peace."

Mia watched two men tumble into a cart of apples and come up laughing, apples rolling everywhere, nobody hurt, everybody delighted. "Honestly, I get it," she said. "This needs a referee. This needs, at minimum, a rulebook."

The green glow yanked her five centuries forward, and she landed on a tidy lawn in front of a university building, where a cluster of serious young men in waistcoats were arguing over a sheet of paper.

"No hacking an opponent in the shins," one of them read aloud, deeply unimpressed that this needed to be written down at all.

"You're Cambridge students," Mia guessed, looking at the building behind him.

"Correct. And exhausted," the reader said. "Every school we play has different rules. We're writing one set everybody can agree to." That was **1848**, and the paper would be remembered as the **Cambridge Rules** — one of the first serious tries at getting every football match on the same page.

Mia, who had spent her whole life trusting a well-made spreadsheet over chaos, felt something click into place. "You're basically building the first shared database," she said.

The student blinked at her, entirely unsure what a database was, but pleased regardless. "If you say so."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Man Who Wrote It Down
chapters.text:
The glow dropped her onto a cobblestone street in London, outside a pub with frosted windows and a plaque already half-finished: **FREEMASONS' TAVERN**.

Inside, a man in a high collar was dictating to a room of a dozen other serious gentlemen, all of them arguing over whether a player could still pick the ball up and run with it.

"No," the man said firmly, writing as he spoke. "If we allow that, we're not writing football. We're writing a different game entirely, and that game can go start its own club."

Mia leaned in close enough to read over his shoulder. "You're the one actually writing the rulebook," she said. "Everyone else is just talking."

"Ebenezer Cobb Morley," he said, not looking up. "And yes. Somebody has to." It was October, **1863**, and by the end of that meeting the men in that room would found the **Football Association** — the FA, the organization that still runs the sport in England — and Morley's pen would produce the first official **Laws of the Game**, including the rule he'd just finished writing: no carrying the ball with your hands.

Mia thought about every spreadsheet she'd ever built, every stat she'd ever tracked, and felt a strange kinship with a man drafting rule number one by candlelight. "You know this is going to get played on every continent on Earth," she told him.

Morley looked up properly for the first time. "I would settle for England agreeing on it."

Two decades later, in a different room full of different schoolboys, Mia overheard someone shorten "association football" to "assoc," then, because teenagers in the 1880s apparently loved a good nickname as much as teenagers now, to "**soccer**." She laughed out loud. "That word is going to outlive every single person in this room," she said, and nobody believed her, which felt about right.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The First Numbers
chapters.text:
The stopwatch spun her into a crowd roaring outside a muddy pitch, programs clutched in a thousand hands, and Mia — who had never once in her life turned down a stat sheet — grabbed one before she'd even found a seat.

"**FA Cup**," she read. "Started **1871**, finishing **1872**." A man beside her, scarf wound twice around his neck, told her this competition would still be running more than a century and a half later — older than any other football tournament on the planet. Mia tucked that away. Longevity, she thought, was its own kind of statistic.

The scene shifted again, this time to a foggy field in **Glasgow**, where two national teams lined up for what the program called the very **first international match** in the sport's history. Mia watched ninety tense minutes of **Scotland** and **England** cancelling each other out shot for shot, chance for chance, until the final whistle blew on a scoreline of **0–0**.

"That has to be the most anticlimactic first result in sports history," she said.

"Or the most evenly matched," said the man next to her, who turned out to be a club official named McGregor, scribbling in a notebook of his own. "I'm trying to solve a different problem. Too many teams, no order to the season. Everybody plays whoever they like, whenever they like."

Mia looked at his notebook — names scattered with no structure at all — and the statistician in her could not let it stand. "You need a table," she said. "Rank them. Wins worth more than draws, draws worth more than losses, and update it after every single match."

McGregor stared at her like she'd handed him a trophy. "That," he said, "is precisely the plan." In **1888**, William McGregor's **Football League** became the first organized football league in the world, and somewhere in it, Mia liked to think, was a seed of the standings table she checked on her phone every single Sunday morning.
chapters.shout_line: THAT'S A RECORD THAT'LL NEVER GET BROKEN!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Seven Countries and One Old Ball
chapters.text:
The green light set her down on a Paris street in **1904**, outside a room where representatives from **seven countries** were shaking hands over a single piece of paper.

"We need somebody to run this sport once it stops being just England's," one delegate said, in French that the stopwatch, somehow, translated perfectly. That paper founded **FIFA**, the organization that would end up governing football across the entire world, and Mia, watching seven men from seven countries agree on anything at all, thought it was honestly more impressive than any match she'd ever seen.

The dial spun once more, dumping her into a dim stone room that smelled like old dust: a castle, cold even in summer, with a glass case in the corner. Inside sat a lumpy, stitched leather ball, flattened with age.

"That," said the guide waiting for her — a castle historian in a tweed jacket — "is sitting in **Stirling Castle**, in Scotland, and it might be the oldest football in the world."

Mia crouched to look closer. "What's it stuffed with?"

"A pig's bladder," he said, watching her face carefully. "Not as gruesome as it sounds — it's just a stretchy pouch, like a little balloon, that holds air inside the leather shell. Cheapest way to make a ball bounce, back then."

Mia did the math out loud, the way she did everything. "So if nobody's sure exactly when it was made—"

"Historians estimate the **1540s**, based on the stitching and the style of the leather," the historian said. "Which would make it close to five hundred years old."

Mia touched the glass, not the ball, and thought about every ball she'd ever owned, how none of them would survive five centuries in anyone's castle. "Respect," she said quietly, and meant it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Dick, Kerr Ladies
chapters.text:
The next green flash dropped her into a packed stadium roaring for a team of women in matching jerseys, and the player at the center of it all moved like the ball was simply obeying her.

"Who is that?" Mia asked a woman beside her in the stands.

"**Lily Parr**," the woman said, like it was obvious. "Best player most people have never heard of. She plays for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, and right now they're one of the most popular football teams in all of England, women's or men's."

Mia watched Parr bend a shot around two defenders and thought, not for the first time, that talent like that shouldn't need a special introduction. "So why haven't I heard of her?"

The woman's face changed. "Because in **1921**, the men who ran English football decided women shouldn't be allowed to play on their grounds anymore. Banned it outright. No good reason given, just a vote."

Mia felt something sharp and familiar — the specific anger of watching someone get cut from a game they were clearly winning at. "That's not a rule," she said. "That's just somebody being scared of being shown up."

"Fifty years," the woman said. "That's how long it took the **FA** to lift the ban — **1971**." Mia did the subtraction instantly, the number landing heavier than any stat she'd calculated all night: five whole decades, gone.

But the woman was smiling now, pulling Mia forward through the crowd toward a television glowing in a shop window, tuned to **China**, **1991**. "Watch this part, though."

On the screen, a team in white and blue lifted a trophy over their heads: the **United States**, winners of the very first official **Women's World Cup**. Mia grinned so hard her face hurt. "Fifty years to get the door open," she said, "and then they just walked straight to the top."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Uruguay, 1930
chapters.text:
The dial landed her in blazing sun, in a stadium packed with people speaking Spanish faster than she could follow, flags snapping overhead.

"First ever **World Cup**," shouted a boy next to her, grinning, pointing at the pitch. "**1930**. Right here, in **Uruguay**."

A man a few rows back — older, carrying a small golden statue wrapped carefully in cloth — was introduced to her as **Jules Rimet**, the FIFA president who had pushed for this exact tournament to exist. "Thirteen teams," he told her proudly, "all gathered in one place, for one trophy."

Mia watched the host nation attack in waves, and being who she was, she couldn't help calculating shot after shot, chance after chance, building her own mental scoreboard before the real one updated. "Uruguay's going to win this," she said confidently, somewhere around the hour mark. "Look at their shot count versus Argentina's. It's not close."

The boy beside her laughed. "Bold prediction for someone who just got here."

But the numbers held. **Uruguay** beat **Argentina** in the final, and the home crowd came apart with noise loud enough that Mia felt it in her chest rather than just her ears. Jules Rimet handed over his golden trophy, and somewhere in the chaos, Mia realized she'd just watched the very first champion of a tournament that would, one day, stop entire countries just to watch.

"Not bad for a first try," she told the boy.

"Wait until you see what this turns into," he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Dog Who Found the World Cup
chapters.text:
The green glow dropped her onto a gray London pavement outside an exhibition hall, newspapers scattered at her feet, every headline screaming the same thing: **WORLD CUP STOLEN**.

"It vanished right out of a display case," a passerby told her, shaking his head. "Days before **England**'s about to host the whole tournament, and somebody just walks off with the trophy."

Mia, who had spent her whole life finding patterns in messy data, crouched down and read every headline twice. "Okay," she said slowly. "If I'd stolen something and panicked, I wouldn't carry it far. I'd dump it somewhere close, somewhere hidden in plain sight." She looked up. "Like under a hedge."

A week later — the stopwatch fast-forwarded her straight there — a scruffy little dog was dragging his owner down a suburban street, nose jammed into a garden hedge, refusing to budge.

"That's him," somebody near Mia whispered. "That's **Pickles**."

Pickles pulled a newspaper-wrapped package out from under the leaves, and when his owner peeled back the paper, there it was: the missing trophy, completely unharmed.

Mia threw both hands up like she'd scored the winner herself. "I called the hedge!"

"You called *a* hedge," the passerby said. "Pickles called the actual one."

Fair enough, Mia thought. A few months later, in a stadium roaring louder than any she'd stood in yet, she watched **England** lift that same trophy after winning the **1966 World Cup** on home soil — their only title so far, the crowd around her kept reminding each other, like repeating it might make it happen again sooner.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Three Stars and Two Colors
chapters.text:
Four more flashes of green, four more decades, and Mia found herself in Mexico, 1970, watching a number ten glide through defenders like they were cones in a training drill.

"**Pele**," the man beside her said, hardly blinking. "Brazilian. And this is his third World Cup win — **1958**, **1962**, now **1970**. Nobody else in history has three winner's medals."

Mia watched him finish a move with a touch so casual it looked accidental, and did the math anyway, because she always did the math. "Three for three tournaments," she murmured. "That's a hundred percent conversion rate on the only stat that actually matters."

That same celebration would eventually become one line in a much longer stat sheet: by the time Mia's own era rolled around, **Brazil** would have won the World Cup five times — **1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002** — a record nobody else had matched.

Out on the same field, a referee in a black kit was holding up two small colored cards, one yellow, one red, consulting them like they were the most natural thing in the world.

"**Ken Aston**," the man beside her said. "Referee. Got the idea driving home past a set of traffic lights — stop, go, slow down. Figured football needed a signal everybody could understand, no matter what language they spoke. **1970**'s the first World Cup where he gets to use them."

Mia liked that more than almost anything else she'd seen all night. A whole sport running on a simple two-color code, as clean as a well-built spreadsheet. "Green and red I understand," she said. "But why yellow first?"

"Warning," the man said. "Everybody deserves one chance to fix their behavior before it costs them."

One more flash: Brazil, having now kept that original golden trophy for good after their third win, was handed a brand new one in **1974** — bigger, heavier, built to be passed on and never owned outright again. Mia watched it gleam under the stadium lights and thought that was, in its own way, the fairest stat of all: a trophy nobody got to keep forever.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Full Time
chapters.text:
The green light folded shut one last time, and Mia landed back on her bedroom floor exactly where she had started. Her laptop still glowed with the same spreadsheet, the same missed penalty sitting in its same stubborn row.

The stopwatch in her hand had stopped clean on **90:00**, like a match that had just finished. She turned it over in her palm, feeling the dent in the brass her grandfather used to rub with his thumb during tense matches — a habit she hadn't thought about in months.

She looked at her spreadsheet with slightly different eyes now. A missed penalty wasn't nothing. But it also wasn't the whole story — it was one row in a stat sheet that stretched back more than two thousand years, through banned mobs and stolen trophies and a fifty-year door that had finally swung back open. Somewhere in all of that, her name was just the newest entry.

She slid the stopwatch back into the shoebox under her bed, next to the whistle and the flags, and closed the lid gently, the way you'd close a notebook you planned on opening again.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a match of her own to play, and for the first time all night, the number she cared about most wasn't the one from this afternoon.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a ball-kicking game with no hands allowed, was played in China more than **2,000 years ago** — one of soccer's oldest known ancestors.
Medieval street games got so wild that a king banned **mob football** in London in **1314**.
The **Football Association** was founded in **1863**, and its very first rule banned players from carrying the ball with their hands.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote football's first official rulebook, the **Laws of the Game**, in 1863.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871–72**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world.
The first ever international match, **Scotland vs. England** in **Glasgow in 1872**, ended in a **0–0** draw.
In **1888**, William McGregor organized the **Football League** — the world's very first football league, complete with a ranked table.
**FIFA**, football's worldwide governing body, was founded in Paris in **1904** by **seven countries**.
**Lily Parr** was a star player for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular football teams in England at the time.
The FA's ban on women's football lasted **fifty years** before it was finally lifted in **1971**.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **China in 1991**, and the **United States** won it.
The very first **World Cup** was held in **Uruguay in 1930**, with the host country beating Argentina in the final.
In **1966**, the World Cup trophy was stolen in London — then found safe under a hedge a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**Pele** is the only player in history to win three World Cups — in **1958, 1962, and 1970**.

new_recurring.rule: A dented brass stopwatch that glows stadium green and spins its numbers backward when wound, pulling the holder into a real moment in sports history; it stops on 90:00 when the night's journey is over and can be wound again another night.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Mia returns to her bedroom with the stopwatch stopped at 90:00, tucks it back into her grandfather's referee shoebox under the bed, and looks at her own stat spreadsheet with new perspective before heading to tomorrow's match.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Queue Pop, 1953
chapters.text:
The ranked queue had been stuck at ninety-nine percent for four straight minutes, which was somehow worse than losing.

Noah lay flat on his back, phone six inches from his face, blanket up to his chin, bedroom dark except for the screen's cold glow. It was 1:47 a.m. His mom thought he'd been asleep since eleven. The queue was a lie he was willing to tell twice a week.

Then the bar hit one hundred percent, and instead of a lobby, the screen flickered black, then green, then showed two words: **NON-REM 1**.

"That's not a game mode," Noah muttered.

The screen answered him. A glitchy little avatar built out of pixelated eyelids blinked into the corner. "Correct. Name's REM. Not the band, though I get that a lot."

"REM like the sleep thing?"

"REM like the sleep thing. Want to know why you're awake right now instead of doing the one thing your whole species evolved to do at 1:47 a.m.?"

Noah tapped the glowing eyelid icon, mostly out of curiosity, and the room dissolved into black-and-white static.

He landed in a dim lab at the **University of Chicago**, **1953**. A boy about his age lay wired up on a cot, fast asleep. A tired grad student leaned in close, staring at the kid's closed eyes.

"They're twitching," Noah said. "Under the lids. Like a frame drop."

"Good eye," said REM. "That's **Eugene Aserinsky**, and he just noticed the exact same thing you did. He and his professor, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, named it rapid eye movement sleep. REM sleep. Kleitman basically spent his whole career figuring sleep out — people call him the father of the whole field."

Noah grinned. "So the band stole it."

"The band," REM said, "is a coincidence I live with daily."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Playlist
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved into something that looked like a music app, sleep stages laid out like tracks on an album.

"A night of sleep isn't one long black screen," REM said. "It's a playlist. About ninety minutes a loop, over and over till your alarm ruins everything."

Noah scrolled the track list with his finger. "So there's like... chill tracks and loud ones?"

"Close enough. The quiet tracks are **non-REM** — your body doing repair work, nothing flashy. Then every ninety minutes or so you hit a loud one. **REM sleep**. Brain's almost as busy as when you're awake. Dreaming, basically."

"So why doesn't everyone just get up and start swinging during the loud part?"

"Because your body mutes itself." REM grinned, pixel teeth and all. "Muscles go slack during REM — total volume at zero — so you can't act out whatever's happening in the dream. Otherwise half the planet would be sleep-fighting imaginary bosses every night."

Noah thought about cutscenes. "So it's like the controls get disabled during the cinematic."

"That," REM said, "is annoyingly accurate."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Patch Notes
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to Noah's own room — his own bed, him asleep in it, which was deeply weird to watch from the outside.

"Creepy," Noah said.

"Educational," REM corrected. "Watch the deep non-REM stage. The really quiet track."

A soft golden glow pulsed through sleeping-Noah's chest on-screen.

"That's **growth hormone** getting released," REM said, "the chemical that actually helps your body grow, inch by inch. The biggest dose of it comes out during the deepest non-REM stage. It's a big part of why growing bodies — yours, for instance — need real sleep and not four hours and a prayer."

Noah glanced down at the jeans he'd outgrown twice this year. "So it's basically installing the update while I'm offline."

"If that helps you sleep, sure."

"It does not currently help me sleep," Noah said. "I'm standing inside a memory right now."

"Fair," REM said. "Patience. We've got six more stops."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Dark Mode, Factory Installed
chapters.text:
They zoomed in past Noah's skin, past bone, into a brain lit up like a circuit board, down to one tiny cluster of cells glowing blue.

"That speck," REM said, "sits right above where your eye nerves cross. It's called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — basically your body's master clock. It's been running your sleep and wake times since before you had a phone to ignore it with."

"How's a clump of cells a clock?"

"It keeps roughly a twenty-four-hour rhythm. Scientists call that a **circadian** rhythm — the word just comes from Latin for 'about a day.' Your body had a built-in day-and-night schedule a long time before any app did."

Noah blinked. "So I've had dark mode this whole time."

"Factory installed," REM said. "You just keep overriding it at 1 a.m."

"Rude, but accurate," Noah admitted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Achievement Unlocked
chapters.text:
The static resolved into a bright stage, gold curtains, a podium — Noah half expected an esports grand final.

"In **2017**," REM said, "three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, science's biggest trophy, for finding the actual genes that keep your circadian clock ticking."

"They found the clock itself decades earlier, though," Noah said. "Why'd the trophy take so long?"

"Finding the clock is one achievement. Finding the code that runs it is a whole separate quest line. They cracked the genes. The Nobel committee noticed."

Noah nodded slowly. "Respect. That's a long grind for one award."

"Even your cells have patch notes," REM said. "You just can't read the changelog."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Melatonin Mixtape
chapters.text:
Next stop: a cluttered **1958** laboratory, glass bottles everywhere, a scientist squinting through a microscope at something barely visible.

"**Aaron Lerner**," REM said. "His team pulled a brand-new hormone out of a tiny gland in an animal's brain and gave it a name: **melatonin**. It's the chemical that tells your body nighttime has arrived — basically a volume knob that turns alertness down."

"Isn't that the stuff in the gummies my aunt takes before flights?"

"Same molecule. Your own brain makes it for free, usually around the time you should be putting the phone down and are instead opening a fourth app."

Noah slid his phone a few inches further from his face, which felt like progress.

"Baby steps," REM said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Saved Progress
chapters.text:
The scene turned into a loading screen Noah actually recognized — a save icon, spinning.

"Sleep isn't just downtime," REM said. "It's when your brain sorts the whole day into long-term memory. That riff you've been practicing on guitar, that combo you finally landed — sleep is what saves the file."

"So pulling an all-nighter before a test is..."

"Deleting your own save data before it uploads. Yes."

Noah frowned. "What about dreams, though? Like, actual dream content. Is it secretly trying to tell me something?"

"Depends who you ask. Back in **1899**, a scientist named **Sigmund Freud** wrote a whole famous book arguing dreams reveal your secret hidden wishes. Great story. Mostly not how it actually works, according to sleep science today."

"So my dream about failing a boss fight wasn't secretly about my feelings."

"Almost certainly just leftover footage," REM said. "Also — overnight, your brain runs something scientists nicknamed a 'rinse cycle.' It flushes waste out while you sleep, like taking out the trash before the next day loads."

"Gross but useful."

"Most of biology is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Do Not Attempt This Speedrun
chapters.text:
The next scene was a bedroom in San Diego, **1964**. A teenager sat cross-legged on the floor, eyes red, surrounded by notebooks.

"**Randy Gardner**," REM said. "Seventeen years old. Science-fair project. He stayed awake for about **eleven days straight** — one of the longest stretches anyone's ever done on record."

Noah sat up straighter. "Eleven days? No sleep at all?"

"None. And doctors will tell you, flatly, not to try it. Go without sleep that long and your mood tanks, your focus falls apart, your memory gets foggy fast. Randy's story is interesting. It is not a tutorial."

Noah thought about his last three-day gaming weekend, the one where he'd forgotten his own locker combination on day two.

"Noted," he said. "Not a speedrun category I'm entering."

"Wise," said REM. "Very few achievements are worth your whole brain."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Respawn
chapters.text:
The last stop was a blur of animals, flashing past like a nature documentary on fast-forward.

"Quick round," REM said. "**Bottlenose dolphins** sleep with half their brain at a time — one eye stays open, watching for danger, while the other half rests. **Bats**, on the other end, sleep up to **twenty hours a day**. Practically professional sleepers."

"So dolphins are speedrunning sleep and bats are just living in it."

"Pretty much. Point is, sleep isn't some weird human habit. Nearly every animal does some version of it. It's ancient. It matters."

The static began folding back toward black.

"One more thing," REM said, as the room re-formed around him — his own ceiling, his own blanket, his own phone glowing in his hand. "You'll spend roughly a third of your whole life asleep. Might as well stop fighting it."

Noah looked at the time. 2:02 a.m. The ranked queue notification still sat there, untouched.

He closed the app instead. On the lock screen, where the loading bar used to be stuck at ninety-nine percent, a small notification blinked once: **Achievement Unlocked — First Full Cycle.**

He didn't screenshot it. He just put the phone face-down on the nightstand and let his eyes close.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, the queue could wait.

true_facts.text: In 1953, two scientists at the University of Chicago — Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman — discovered REM sleep by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his eyelids.
A night of sleep runs in repeating loops about ninety minutes long, cycling between quiet non-REM sleep and active REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when you're awake, but the muscles go slack so you can't act out your dreams.
The deepest non-REM stage releases the biggest burst of growth hormone, one reason growing bodies need real sleep.
A tiny cluster of brain cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
The word circadian, for the body's roughly 24-hour clock, comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day.'
In 2017, Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young won the Nobel Prize for finding the genes that keep the circadian clock ticking.
In 1958, Aaron Lerner's team isolated the sleep hormone melatonin from a tiny gland in an animal's brain.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memories, so a good night's sleep helps you remember what you practiced.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' flushes waste out of the sleeping brain while you sleep.
In 1964, seventeen-year-old Randy Gardner of San Diego stayed awake for about eleven days as a science-fair project, one of the longest recorded stretches without sleep.
Doctors say going without sleep that long quickly harms mood, focus, and memory, and nobody should try to beat that record.
Bottlenose dolphins sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger.
Some bats sleep up to twenty hours a day, making them some of the sleepiest animals known.

new_recurring.name: REM
new_recurring.rule: A glitchy, pixel-eyed avatar who appears on Noah's phone screen only after midnight, speaks in gaming and music metaphors with dry deadpan humor, and pulls him into real science and history adventures about sleep and the body. Never…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Noah closed his gaming app, saw a glitch-free 'Achievement Unlocked: First Full Cycle' notification on his lock screen instead of the stuck loading bar, and went to sleep without taking a screenshot.
